tutorial.content:
Calculating the circulation of a vector field along a closed, piecewise smooth curve $C$ can be time-consuming because it often requires splitting $C$ into several parts, evaluating a line integral along each one, and calculating their sum. 

However, in such cases, we can often use Stokes' theorem to reduce the amount of work required by converting this sum of line integrals to a single surface integral. 

For example, suppose that $C$ is the intersection of the paraboloid $z=x^2 + y^2$ and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes $x = \pm 1$ and $y=\pm 1.$ Suppose also that $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and 

$$
\mathbf{F} = \bigg\langle 0, \: \dfrac{1}{2}z^2, \: xz \bigg\rangle.
$$

Let's use Stokes' theorem to find the circulation of $\mathbf{F}$ along $C$.

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}
= \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

By computing the curl of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14239092/assets/88f4a6be603e480b46664b6526eea2da6b2b3412f3ebb5add1f8c38d09c282f0.svg)

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-z,\,-z,\,0⟩{|}_{z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨{{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr & ={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 2x+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 2y+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2({x}^{3}+{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}+{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is the region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14239092/assets/dcf7ba14ac2c0f3da12efed6d539817ab1708273f5e8e665fdde14fee28bb4e3.png)

Evaluating this integral using the usual methods, we get

$$
2\int_{-1}^{1} \int_{-1}^{1} x^3 + x^2 y + x y^2 + y^3 \: \textrm{d}y  \: \textrm{d}x = 0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = 0.
$$

**Note**: Stokes theorem tells us that 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

 depends only on the circulation of $\mathbf F$ at the boundary of $S.$ Therefore, we could have evaluated our line integral by selecting *any* surface with $C$ as its bounding curve and integrating $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F$ over this surface.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}
= \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z=x^2+y^2$ and the plane $z=1.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z = g(x,y) = 1.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1)=0 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-xz,\,-yz,\,{z}^{2}+x⟩{|}_{z=1} \\  & =⟨{{-x}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{1+x}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-x)\cdot 0-(-y)\cdot 0+1+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1+x)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Now, note that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle $x^2+y^2=1$ of radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x = r \cos\theta, \qquad
y = r \sin\theta, \qquad
\textrm{d}A = r \, \textrm{d}r \textrm{d}\theta,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1+x)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(1+r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }r+{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[r\theta +{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2\pi r\,\text{d}r \\  & =\pi [{r}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the half-cone $z=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ and the plane $z=-3.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=-3.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3)=0 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨y,\,2yz,\,-{z}^{2}+1⟩{|}_{z=-3} \\  & =⟨{{y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-6y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-8}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y\cdot 0-(-6y)\cdot 0-8)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-8\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ with radius $3$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-8\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}-8\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-8{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}r\,\text{d}r \\  & =-8[\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{r=0}^{r=3} \\  & =-8(2\pi -0)\cdot (\frac{9}{2}-0) \\  & =-72\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨x+y,\,-x+y,\,-2z⟩{|}_{z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}} \\  & =⟨{{x+y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-x+y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-2(x-1)^{2}-2(y+1)^{2}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}

$$

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

question.problem:
Use Stokes' theorem to evaluate 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,
$$

where $\text{curl}\,F=⟨x+y,\,-x+y,\,-2z⟩,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the paraboloid $z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above.
question.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the paraboloid $z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2})=2(x-1) \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2})=2(y+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨x+y,\,-x+y,\,-2z⟩{|}_{z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}} \\  & =⟨{{x+y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-x+y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-2(x-1)^{2}-2(y+1)^{2}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(x+y)\cdot 2(x-1)-(-x+y)\cdot 2(y+1)-2((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2((x+y)(1-x)+(x-y)(y+1)-(x-1)^{2}-(y+1)^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+2x-y-1)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+2x-y-1)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4(-{r}^{2}+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\cdot r\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-{r}^{3}+2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r)\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{[-{r}^{3}\theta +2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}(-2\pi {r}^{3}-2\pi r)\,\text{d}r \\  & =-8\pi {[-\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-8\pi (-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-6\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the plane $z=2+2x-y.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=2+2x-y.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2+2x-y)=2 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2+2x-y)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-y,\,z,\,-2x⟩{|}_{z=2+2x-y} \\  & =⟨{{-y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{2+2x-y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-2x}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-y)\cdot (2)-(2+2x-y)\cdot (-1)-2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2y+2+2x-y-2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2+y)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2+y)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}(2+r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}2r+{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[{r}^{2}+\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(1+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[\theta -\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14239092/assets/b215ec1e3330f96e7e606e085721b2dd1f50d113f0151e36ec98e6d0a6f54e73.png)

$$

question.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the surface $z=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our surface $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})=\frac{-2x}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})=\frac{-2y}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨x,\,y,\,-2z⟩{|}_{z=1/({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)} \\  & =⟨{{x}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-x\cdot \frac{-2x}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}-y\cdot \frac{-2y}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14239092/assets/b215ec1e3330f96e7e606e085721b2dd1f50d113f0151e36ec98e6d0a6f54e73.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\,-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let C be the intersection of the surface z=1x2+y2+1 and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes x=±1, and y=±1. Given that the curve C is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above and curlF=⟨x,y,−2z⟩, the circulation of F along C can be written as ∮CF⋅dr=

a
∫−11∫−11−y2(x2+y2+1)2dydx
b
∫−11∫−11−xy(x2+y2+1)2dydx
c
∫−11∫−11x2(x2+y2+1)2dydx
d
∫−11∫−11−2(x2+y2+1)2dydx
e
∫−11∫−11−4(x2+y2+1)2dydx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let S be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary C with positive orientation. If a vector field F has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains S, then Stokes' theorem states that

∮CF⋅dr=∬ScurlF⋅dS.

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve C representing the intersection of the surface z=1x2+y2+1 and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our surface S with the equation

z=g(x,y)=1x2+y2+1.

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph z=g(x,y):

∂g∂x=∂∂x(1x2+y2+1)=−2x(x2+y2+1)2∂g∂y=∂∂y(1x2+y2+1)=−2y(x2+y2+1)2

Next, we substitute the equation z=g(x,y) into expression for curlF:

curlF|z=g(x,y)=⟨x,y,−2z⟩|z=1/(x2+y2+1)=⟨x⏟P,y⏟Q,−2x2+y2+1⏟R⟩

So, we have

∬ScurlF⋅dS=∬D(−P∂g∂x−Q∂g∂y+R)dA=∬D(−x⋅−2x(x2+y2+1)2−y⋅−2y(x2+y2+1)2−2x2+y2+1)dA=∬D−2(x2+y2+1)2dA,

where D is region enclosed by the projection of C onto the xy-plane, shown below.

Therefore, we obtain

∬D−2(x2+y2+1)2dA=∫−11∫−11−2(x2+y2+1)2dydx.

observed_steps.name: Question 15
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating a Line Integral Using Stokes' Theorem
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨y,\,x,\,2⟩{|}_{z={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨y,\,x,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨{{y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{x}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{2}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y\cdot (2x)-x\cdot (-2y)+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14239092/assets/5f2f4cb03b3b0232c9debd1f4ed64bd683fe788ccba16cfbe395d9c3b629972d.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\,2\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

Let C be the intersection of the hyperbolic paraboloid z=x2−y2 and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes x=±1, y=±2. Given that the curve C is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above and curlF=⟨y,x,2⟩, the circulation of F along C can be written as ∮CF⋅dr=

a
∫−11∫−222xydydx
b
∫−11∫−2xx2−y2dydx
c
∫−11∫−222+2xydydx
d
∫−11∫−222dydx
e
∫−11∫−2x4+2xydydx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let S be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary C with positive orientation. If a vector field F has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains S, then Stokes' theorem states that

∮CF⋅dr=∬ScurlF⋅dS.

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve C representing the intersection of the paraboloid z=x2−y2 and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid S with the equation

z=g(x,y)=x2−y2.

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph z=g(x,y):

∂g∂x=∂∂x(x2−y2)=2x∂g∂y=∂∂y(x2−y2)=−2y

Next, we substitute the equation z=g(x,y) into expression for curlF:

curlF|z=g(x,y)=⟨y,x,2⟩|z=x2−y2=⟨y,x,2⟩=⟨y⏟P,x⏟Q,2⏟R⟩

So, we have

∬ScurlF⋅dS=∬D(−P∂g∂x−Q∂g∂y+R)dA=∬D(−y⋅(2x)−x⋅(−2y)+2)dA=∬D2dA,

where D is region enclosed by the projection of C onto the xy-plane, shown below.

Therefore, we obtain

∬D2dA=∫−11∫−222dydx.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=x\,i-z\,j+y\,k$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=2\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,k$ for $t\in [0,2).$
question.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2,\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i-z\,j+y\,k \\  & =2\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,k \\  & =0\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k) \\  & =2\cdot 0+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\pi \,\text{d}t \\  & =\pi [t]_{0}^{2} \\  & =\pi (2-0) \\  & =2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Calculate the circulation Γ of the vector field F(x,y,z)=xi−zj+yk along the closed curve C given by r(t)=2i+cos⁡(πt)j+sin⁡(πt)k for t∈[0,2).

a
2π
b
π
c
1
d
0
e
2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The circulation Γ measures the total work done by a force F in moving a particle along a closed curve C. It is given by the formula Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

Along the curve C, we have x=2,y=cos⁡(πt),z=sin⁡(πt).

So,

F(r(t))=xi−zj+yk=2i−sin⁡(πt)j+cos⁡(πt)k.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=ddt(2)i+ddt(cos⁡(πt))j+ddt(sin⁡(πt))k=0i−πsin⁡(πt)j+πcos⁡(πt)k.

Therefore,

F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(2i−sin⁡(πt)j+cos⁡(πt)k)⋅(−πsin⁡(πt)j+πcos⁡(πt)k)=2⋅0+(−sin⁡(πt))⋅(−πsin⁡(πt))+cos⁡(πt)⋅πcos⁡(πt)=πsin2⁡(πt)+πcos2⁡(πt)=π.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫02F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫02πdt=π[t]02=π(2−0)=2π

question.html:
Question 1
?

Calculate the circulation Γ of the vector field F(x,y,z)=xi−zj+yk along the closed curve C given by r(t)=2i+cos⁡(πt)j+sin⁡(πt)k for t∈[0,2).

a
2π
b
π
c
1
d
0
e
2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The circulation Γ measures the total work done by a force F in moving a particle along a closed curve C. It is given by the formula Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

Along the curve C, we have x=2,y=cos⁡(πt),z=sin⁡(πt).

So,

F(r(t))=xi−zj+yk=2i−sin⁡(πt)j+cos⁡(πt)k.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=ddt(2)i+ddt(cos⁡(πt))j+ddt(sin⁡(πt))k=0i−πsin⁡(πt)j+πcos⁡(πt)k.

Therefore,

F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(2i−sin⁡(πt)j+cos⁡(πt)k)⋅(−πsin⁡(πt)j+πcos⁡(πt)k)=2⋅0+(−sin⁡(πt))⋅(−πsin⁡(πt))+cos⁡(πt)⋅πcos⁡(πt)=πsin2⁡(πt)+πcos2⁡(πt)=π.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫02F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫02πdt=π[t]02=π(2−0)=2π

feedback.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2,\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i-z\,j+y\,k \\  & =2\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,k \\  & =0\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k) \\  & =2\cdot 0+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\pi \,\text{d}t \\  & =\pi [t]_{0}^{2} \\  & =\pi (2-0) \\  & =2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=-y\,i+x\,j$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+2\,k$ for $t\in [0,2).$
question.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,z=2.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =-y\,i+x\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)\,k \\  & =-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+0\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j)\cdot (-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+0\,k) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+0\cdot 0 \\  & =2\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+2\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2\pi \,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi [t]_{0}^{2} \\  & =2\pi (2-0) \\  & =4\pi \end{aligned}
$$

a

EXPLANATION

The circulation Γ measures the total work done by a force F in moving a particle along a closed curve C. It is given by the formula Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

Along the curve C, we have x=2cos⁡(πt),y=sin⁡(πt),z=2.

So,

F(r(t))=−yi+xj=−sin⁡(πt)i+2cos⁡(πt)j.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=ddt(2cos⁡(πt))i+ddt(sin⁡(πt))j+ddt(2)k=−2πsin⁡(πt)i+πcos⁡(πt)j+0k.

Therefore,

F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(−sin⁡(πt)i+2cos⁡(πt)j)⋅(−2πsin⁡(πt)i+πcos⁡(πt)j+0k)=−sin⁡(πt)⋅(−2πsin⁡(πt))+2cos⁡(πt)⋅πcos⁡(πt)+0⋅0=2πsin2⁡(πt)+2πcos2⁡(πt)=2π.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫02F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫022πdt=2π[t]02=2π(2−0)=4π

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=(y-x)\,i$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=({t}^{2}-t)\,i+({t}^{3}-t)\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)\,k$ for $t\in [0,1).$
question.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}-t,\,y={t}^{3}-t,\,z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y-x)\,i \\  & =({t}^{3}-t-{t}^{2}+t)\,i \\  & =({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})\,i.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)\,)\,k \\  & =(2t-1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-1)\,j+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\,({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})\,i\,)\cdot (\,(2t-1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-1)\,j+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)\,k\,) \\  & =({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})\cdot (2t-1)+0\cdot (3{t}^{2}-1)+0\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t) \\  & =2{t}^{4}-{t}^{3}-2{t}^{3}+{t}^{2} \\  & =2{t}^{4}-3{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\,2{t}^{4}-3{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}\,)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{2{t}^{5}}{5}-\frac{3{t}^{4}}{4}+\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{2}{5}-\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{3})-(0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{60}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Calculate the circulation Γ of the vector field F(x,y,z)=(y−x)i along the closed curve C given by r(t)=(t2−t)i+(t3−t)j+sin⁡(2πt)k for t∈[0,1).

a
−160
b
−16
c
10
d
−1100
e
100
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The circulation Γ measures the total work done by a force F in moving a particle along a closed curve C. It is given by the formula Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

Along the curve C, we have x=t2−t,y=t3−t,z=sin⁡(2πt).

So,

F(r(t))=(y−x)i=(t3−t−t2+t)i=(t3−t2)i.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=ddt(t2−t)i+ddt(t3−t)j+ddt(sin⁡(2πt))k=(2t−1)i+(3t2−1)j+2πcos⁡(2πt)k.

Therefore,

F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=((t3−t2)i)⋅((2t−1)i+(3t2−1)j+2πcos⁡(2πt)k)=(t3−t2)⋅(2t−1)+0⋅(3t2−1)+0⋅2cos⁡(2πt)=2t4−t3−2t3+t2=2t4−3t3+t2.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫01F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫01(2t4−3t3+t2)dt=[2t55−3t44+t33]01=(25−34+13)−(0)=−160

last_observation.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}-t,\,y={t}^{3}-t,\,z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y-x)\,i \\  & =({t}^{3}-t-{t}^{2}+t)\,i \\  & =({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})\,i.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)\,)\,k \\  & =(2t-1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-1)\,j+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\,({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})\,i\,)\cdot (\,(2t-1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-1)\,j+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)\,k\,) \\  & =({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})\cdot (2t-1)+0\cdot (3{t}^{2}-1)+0\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t) \\  & =2{t}^{4}-{t}^{3}-2{t}^{3}+{t}^{2} \\  & =2{t}^{4}-3{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\,2{t}^{4}-3{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}\,)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{2{t}^{5}}{5}-\frac{3{t}^{4}}{4}+\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{2}{5}-\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{3})-(0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{60}\end{aligned}
$$

The circulation Γ measures the total work done by a force F in moving a particle along a closed curve C. It is given by the formula Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=x\,i-z\,k$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=({t}^{2}-t)\,i+({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})\,j+k$ for $t\in [0,1).$
question.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}-t,\,y={t}^{3}-{t}^{2},\,z=1.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i-z\,k \\  & =({t}^{2}-t)\,i-1\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,k \\  & =(2t-1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-2t)\,j+0\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(({t}^{2}-t)\,i-\,k)\cdot ((2t-1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-2t)\,j) \\  & =({t}^{2}-t)\cdot (2t-1)+0\cdot (3{t}^{2}-2t)+(-1)\cdot 0 \\  & =({t}^{2}-t)(2t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}-t)(2t-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{({t}^{2}-t)^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(0-0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}-t,\,y={t}^{3}-{t}^{2},\,z=1.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i-z\,k \\  & =({t}^{2}-t)\,i-1\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,k \\  & =(2t-1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-2t)\,j+0\,k.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(({t}^{2}-t)\,i-\,k)\cdot ((2t-1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-2t)\,j) \\  & =({t}^{2}-t)\cdot (2t-1)+0\cdot (3{t}^{2}-2t)+(-1)\cdot 0 \\  & =({t}^{2}-t)(2t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}-t)(2t-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{({t}^{2}-t)^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(0-0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 5
?

Calculate the circulation Γ of the vector field F(x,y,z)=zj−yk along the closed curve C given by r(t)=(t2−t)i+cos⁡(2πt)j+sin⁡(2πt)k for t∈[0,1)

a
−2π
b
4π
c
2π
d
0
e
−π
Correct
EXPLANATION

The circulation Γ measures the total work done by a force F in moving a particle along a closed curve C. It is given by the formula Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

Along the curve C, we have x=t2−t,y=cos⁡(2πt),z=sin⁡(2πt).

So,

F(r(t))=zj−yk=sin⁡(2πt)j−cos⁡(2πt)k.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=ddt(t2−t)i+ddt(cos⁡(2πt))j+ddt(sin⁡(2πt))k=(2t−1)i−2πsin⁡(2πt)j+2πcos⁡(2πt)k.

Therefore,

F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(sin⁡(2πt)j−cos⁡(2πt)k)⋅((2t−1)i−2πsin⁡(2πt)j+2πcos⁡(2πt)k)=0⋅(2t−1)+sin⁡(2πt)⋅(−2πsin⁡(2πt))+(−cos⁡(2πt))⋅2πcos⁡(2πt)=−2πsin2⁡(2πt)−2πcos2⁡(2πt)=−2π.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫01F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫01(−2π)dt=−2π[t]01=−2π(1−0)=−2π

feedback.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=z\,j-y\,k$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=({t}^{2}-t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)\,k$ for $t\in [0,1)$
feedback.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}-t,\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t),\,z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =z\,j-y\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)\,j-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t))\,k \\  & =(2t-1)\,i-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)\,j+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)\,j-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)\,k)\cdot ((2t-1)\,i-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)\,j+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)\,k) \\  & =0\cdot (2t-1)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)\cdot (-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t))+(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t))\cdot 2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t) \\  & =-2\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(2\pi t)-2\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(2\pi t) \\  & =-2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-2\pi )\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2\pi [t]_{0}^{1} \\  & =-2\pi (1-0) \\  & =-2\pi \end{aligned}

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=({t}^{2}-t)\,i+(t-{t}^{3})\,j+(2{t}^{2}-2t)\,k$ for $t\in [0,1).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=y\,i+x\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$
question.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}-t,\,y=t-{t}^{3},\,z=2{t}^{2}-2t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,k \\  & =(t-{t}^{3})\,i+({t}^{2}-t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-{t}^{3})\,j-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}-2t)\,k \\  & =(2t-1)\,i+(1-3{t}^{2})\,j+(4t-2)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((t-{t}^{3})\,i+({t}^{2}-t)\,k)\cdot ((2t-1)\,i+(1-3{t}^{2})\,j+(4t-2)\,k) \\  & =(t-{t}^{3})\cdot (2t-1)+0\cdot (1-3{t}^{2})+({t}^{2}-t)\cdot (4t-2) \\  & =t-4{t}^{2}+5{t}^{3}-2{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t-4{t}^{2}+5{t}^{3}-2{t}^{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-\frac{4{t}^{3}}{3}+\frac{5{t}^{3}}{4}-\frac{2{t}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{4}{3}+\frac{5}{4}-\frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{60}\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 6
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating a Surface Integral Using Stokes' Theorem
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}-t,\,y=t-{t}^{3},\,z=2{t}^{2}-2t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,k \\  & =(t-{t}^{3})\,i+({t}^{2}-t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-{t}^{3})\,j-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}-2t)\,k \\  & =(2t-1)\,i+(1-3{t}^{2})\,j+(4t-2)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((t-{t}^{3})\,i+({t}^{2}-t)\,k)\cdot ((2t-1)\,i+(1-3{t}^{2})\,j+(4t-2)\,k) \\  & =(t-{t}^{3})\cdot (2t-1)+0\cdot (1-3{t}^{2})+({t}^{2}-t)\cdot (4t-2) \\  & =t-4{t}^{2}+5{t}^{3}-2{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t-4{t}^{2}+5{t}^{3}-2{t}^{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-\frac{4{t}^{3}}{3}+\frac{5{t}^{3}}{4}-\frac{2{t}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{4}{3}+\frac{5}{4}-\frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{60}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Let S be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary C with positive orientation. If a vector field F has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains S, then Stokes' theorem states that

∮CF⋅dr=∬ScurlF⋅dS.

Along the curve C, we have x=t2−t,y=t−t3,z=2t2−2t.

So,

F(r(t))=yi+xk=(t−t3)i+(t2−t)k.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=ddt(t2−t)i+ddt(t−t3)j−ddt(2t2−2t)k=(2t−1)i+(1−3t2)j+(4t−2)k.

Therefore,

F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=((t−t3)i+(t2−t)k)⋅((2t−1)i+(1−3t2)j+(4t−2)k)=(t−t3)⋅(2t−1)+0⋅(1−3t2)+(t2−t)⋅(4t−2)=t−4t2+5t3−2t4.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∬ScurlF⋅dS=∮CF⋅dr=∫01F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫01(t−4t2+5t3−2t4)dt=[t22−4t33+5t34−2t55]01=12−43+54−25=160

solution.reasoning: By Stokes' theorem, the surface integral equals \int_0^1 F(r(t))\cdot r'(t)\,dt. Here F(r(t))=(t-t^3,0,t^2-t) and r'(t)=(2t-1,1-3t^2,4t-2). Their dot product is -2t^4+5t^3-4t^2+t, whose integral is -2/5+5/4-4/3+1/2=1/60. Thus choice c is mathematically correct. question.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=({t}^{2}+t)\,i+({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})\,j+(2{t}^{2}+2t)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,0).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=y\,i+z\,j+x\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$
question.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}+t,\,y={t}^{3}+{t}^{2},\,z=2{t}^{2}+2t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+z\,j+x\,k \\  & =({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})\,i+(2{t}^{2}+2t)\,j+({t}^{2}+t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+2t)\,k \\  & =(2t+1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}+2t)\,j+(4t+2)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})\,i+(2{t}^{2}+2t)\,j+({t}^{2}+t)\,k)\cdot ((2t+1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}+2t)\,j+(4t+2)\,k) \\  & =({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})(2t+1)+(2{t}^{2}+2t)(3{t}^{2}+2t)+({t}^{2}+t)(4t+2) \\  & =2t+11{t}^{2}+17{t}^{3}+8{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(2t+11{t}^{2}+17{t}^{3}+8{t}^{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[{t}^{2}+\frac{11}{3}{t}^{3}+\frac{17}{4}{t}^{4}+\frac{8}{5}{t}^{5}]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-(1-\frac{11}{3}+\frac{17}{4}-\frac{8}{5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{60}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Let S be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve C with positive orientation and parametrization r(t)=(t2+t)i+(t3+t2)j+(2t2+2t)k for t∈[−1,0). Given that F(x,y,z)=yi+zj+xk, evaluate the integral ∬ScurlF⋅dS.

a
215
b
745
c
160
d
115
e
320
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let S be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary C with positive orientation. If a vector field F has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains S, then Stokes' theorem states that ∮CF⋅dr=∬ScurlF⋅dS.

Along the curve C, we have x=t2+t,y=t3+t2,z=2t2+2t.

So, F(r(t))=yi+zj+xk=(t3+t2)i+(2t2+2t)j+(t2+t)k.

Computing r′(t), we get r′(t)=ddt(t2+t)i+ddt(t3+t2)j+ddt(2t2+2t)k=(2t+1)i+(3t2+2t)j+(4t+2)k.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=((t3+t2)i+(2t2+2t)j+(t2+t)k)⋅((2t+1)i+(3t2+2t)j+(4t+2)k)=(t3+t2)(2t+1)+(2t2+2t)(3t2+2t)+(t2+t)(4t+2)=2t+11t2+17t3+8t4.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∬ScurlF⋅dS=∮CF⋅dr=∫−10F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫−10(2t+11t2+17t3+8t4)dt=[t2+113t3+174t4+85t5]−10=0−(1−113+174−85)=160
question.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Surface Integral Using Stokes' Theorem

solution.reasoning: By Stokes' theorem, the integral equals \int_{-1}^0 F(r(t))\cdot r'(t)\,dt. Substitution gives F(r(t))=(t^3+t^2,2t^2+2t,t^2+t) and r'(t)=(2t+1,3t^2+2t,4t+2). Their dot product is 8t^4+17t^3+11t^2+2t. Its integral is 8/5-17/4+11/3-1=1/60, so choice c is mathematically correct. feedback.name: Question 7
feedback.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=({t}^{2}+t)\,i+({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})\,j+(2{t}^{2}+2t)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,0).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=y\,i+z\,j+x\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}+t,\,y={t}^{3}+{t}^{2},\,z=2{t}^{2}+2t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+z\,j+x\,k \\  & =({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})\,i+(2{t}^{2}+2t)\,j+({t}^{2}+t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+2t)\,k \\  & =(2t+1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}+2t)\,j+(4t+2)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})\,i+(2{t}^{2}+2t)\,j+({t}^{2}+t)\,k)\cdot ((2t+1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}+2t)\,j+(4t+2)\,k) \\  & =({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})(2t+1)+(2{t}^{2}+2t)(3{t}^{2}+2t)+({t}^{2}+t)(4t+2) \\  & =2t+11{t}^{2}+17{t}^{3}+8{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(2t+11{t}^{2}+17{t}^{3}+8{t}^{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[{t}^{2}+\frac{11}{3}{t}^{3}+\frac{17}{4}{t}^{4}+\frac{8}{5}{t}^{5}]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-(1-\frac{11}{3}+\frac{17}{4}-\frac{8}{5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{60}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,1).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=y\,i+x\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$
question.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,z=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,k \\  & =-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))+0\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)) \\  & =-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)-\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)-\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\frac{\pi }{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)))\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{[\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)}{2}+\frac{\pi t}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)}{4}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =-[0+\frac{\pi }{2}+0-(0-\frac{\pi }{2}+0)] \\  & =-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Question 8

Let S be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve C with positive orientation and parametrization r(t)=cos⁡(πt)i+sin⁡(πt)j+cos⁡(πt)k for t∈[−1,1). Given that F(x,y,z)=yi+xk, evaluate the integral ∬ScurlF⋅dS.

a
−π
b
2
c
−1
d
2π
e
−2π

EXPLANATION

Let S be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary C with positive orientation. If a vector field F has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains S, then Stokes' theorem states that

∮CF⋅dr=∬ScurlF⋅dS.

Along the curve C, we have x=cos⁡(πt),y=sin⁡(πt),z=cos⁡(πt).

So,

F(r(t))=yi+xk=sin⁡(πt)i+cos⁡(πt)k.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=ddt(cos⁡(πt))i+ddt(sin⁡(πt))j+ddt(cos⁡(πt))k=−πsin⁡(πt)i+πcos⁡(πt)j−πsin⁡(πt)k.

Therefore,

F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(sin⁡(πt)i+cos⁡(πt)k)⋅(−πsin⁡(πt)i+πcos⁡(πt)j−πsin⁡(πt)k)=sin⁡(πt)⋅(−πsin⁡(πt))+0⋅πcos⁡(πt)+cos⁡(πt)⋅(−πsin⁡(πt))=−πsin⁡(πt)cos⁡(πt)−πsin2⁡(πt).

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∬ScurlF⋅dS=∮CF⋅dr=∫−11F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫−11(−πsin⁡(πt)cos⁡(πt)−πsin2⁡(πt))dt=−∫−11(πsin⁡(πt)cos⁡(πt)+π2(1−cos⁡(2πt)))dt=−[sin2⁡(πt)2+πt2−sin⁡(2πt)4]−11=−[0+π2+0−(0−π2+0)]=−π

last_observation.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,z=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,k \\  & =-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))+0\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)) \\  & =-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)-\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)-\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\frac{\pi }{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)))\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{[\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)}{2}+\frac{\pi t}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)}{4}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =-[0+\frac{\pi }{2}+0-(0-\frac{\pi }{2}+0)] \\  & =-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))+0\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)) \\  & =-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)-\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t).\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)-\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\frac{\pi }{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)))\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{[\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)}{2}+\frac{\pi t}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)}{4}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =-[0+\frac{\pi }{2}+0-(0-\frac{\pi }{2}+0)] \\  & =-\pi \end{aligned}

solution.reasoning: By Stokes' theorem, the surface integral equals the circulation. Here F(r(t))=(\sin(\pi t),0,\cos(\pi t)) and r'(t)=(-\pi\sin(\pi t),\pi\cos(\pi t),-\pi\sin(\pi t)). Their dot product is -\pi\sin^2(\pi t)-\pi\sin(\pi t)\cos(\pi t). Over [-1,1], the squared-sine integral is 1 and the mixed term is odd, giving -\pi, choice a. question.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=({t}^{3}-t)\,i+(2{t}^{2}+1)\,j+({t}^{2}-1)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,1).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=y\,i+3\,j+yz\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$
question.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{3}-t,\,y=2{t}^{2}+1,\,z={t}^{2}-1.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+3\,j+yz\,k \\  & =(2{t}^{2}+1)\,i+3\,j+(2{t}^{2}+1)({t}^{2}-1)\,k \\  & =(2{t}^{2}+1)\,i+3\,j+(2{t}^{4}-{t}^{2}-1)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)\,k \\  & =(3{t}^{2}-1)\,i+4t\,j+2t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((2{t}^{2}+1)\,i+3\,j+(2{t}^{4}-{t}^{2}-1)\,k)\cdot ((3{t}^{2}-1)\,i+4t\,j+2t\,k) \\  & =(2{t}^{2}+1)(3{t}^{2}-1)+3(4t)+(2{t}^{4}-{t}^{2}-1)(2t) \\  & =-1+10t+{t}^{2}-2{t}^{3}+6{t}^{4}+4{t}^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-1+10t+{t}^{2}-2{t}^{3}+6{t}^{4}+4{t}^{5})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-t+5{t}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{4}+\frac{6}{5}{t}^{5}+\frac{2}{3}{t}^{6}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-1+5+\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{6}{5}+\frac{2}{3})-(1+5-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{6}{5}+\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =-2+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{12}{5} \\  & =\frac{16}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 9
question.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=({t}^{3}-t)\,i+(2{t}^{2}+1)\,j+({t}^{2}-1)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,1).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=y\,i+3\,j+yz\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$
question.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{3}-t,\,y=2{t}^{2}+1,\,z={t}^{2}-1.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+3\,j+yz\,k \\  & =(2{t}^{2}+1)\,i+3\,j+(2{t}^{2}+1)({t}^{2}-1)\,k \\  & =(2{t}^{2}+1)\,i+3\,j+(2{t}^{4}-{t}^{2}-1)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)\,k \\  & =(3{t}^{2}-1)\,i+4t\,j+2t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((2{t}^{2}+1)\,i+3\,j+(2{t}^{4}-{t}^{2}-1)\,k)\cdot ((3{t}^{2}-1)\,i+4t\,j+2t\,k) \\  & =(2{t}^{2}+1)(3{t}^{2}-1)+3(4t)+(2{t}^{4}-{t}^{2}-1)(2t) \\  & =-1+10t+{t}^{2}-2{t}^{3}+6{t}^{4}+4{t}^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-1+10t+{t}^{2}-2{t}^{3}+6{t}^{4}+4{t}^{5})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-t+5{t}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{4}+\frac{6}{5}{t}^{5}+\frac{2}{3}{t}^{6}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-1+5+\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{6}{5}+\frac{2}{3})-(1+5-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{6}{5}+\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =-2+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{12}{5} \\  & =\frac{16}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Let S be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary C with positive orientation. If a vector field F has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains S, then Stokes' theorem states that ∮CF⋅dr=∬ScurlF⋅dS.

Along the curve C, we have x=t3−t,y=2t2+1,z=t2−1.

So, F(r(t))=yi+3j+yzk=(2t2+1)i+3j+(2t2+1)(t2−1)k=(2t2+1)i+3j+(2t4−t2−1)k.

Computing r′(t), we get r′(t)=ddt(t3−t)i+ddt(2t2+1)j+ddt(t2−1)k=(3t2−1)i+4tj+2tk.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=((2t2+1)i+3j+(2t4−t2−1)k)⋅((3t2−1)i+4tj+2tk)=(2t2+1)(3t2−1)+3(4t)+(2t4−t2−1)(2t)=−1+10t+t2−2t3+6t4+4t5.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∬ScurlF⋅dS=∮CF⋅dr=∫−11F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫−11(−1+10t+t2−2t3+6t4+4t5)dt=[−t+5t2+13t3−12t4+65t5+23t6]−11=(−1+5+13−12+65+23)−(1+5−13−12−65+23)=−2+23+125=1615

solution.reasoning: By Stokes' theorem, the surface integral equals \int_{-1}^1 F(r(t))\cdot r'(t)\,dt. The dot product is (2t^2+1)(3t^2-1)+12t+2t(2t^2+1)(t^2-1). The last two terms are odd and integrate to zero. Thus the result is \int_{-1}^1(6t^4+t^2-1)\,dt=12/5+2/3-2=16/15, choice c. question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,1).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=2y\,i-2x\,j+{e}^{z-2y}\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$
question.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,z=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2y\,i-2x\,j+{e}^{z-2y}\,k \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)}\,k \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$

d

Let S be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary C with positive orientation. If a vector field F has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains S, then Stokes' theorem states that

∮CF⋅dr=∬ScurlF⋅dS.

Along the curve C, we have x=cos⁡(πt),y=sin⁡(πt),z=2sin⁡(πt).

So,

Computing r′(t), we get

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∬ScurlF⋅dS=∮CF⋅dr=∫−11F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫−11(−2π+2πcos⁡(πt))dt=[−2πt+2sin⁡(πt)]−11=(−2π(1)+0)−(−2π(−1)+0)=−4π

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,z=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2y\,i-2x\,j+{e}^{z-2y}\,k \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)}\,k \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,k \\  & =-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+k)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+1\cdot 2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =-2\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)-2\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =-2\pi +2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-2\pi +2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =[-2\pi t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-2\pi (1)+0)-(-2\pi (-1)+0) \\  & =-4\pi \end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+k)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+1\cdot 2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =-2\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)-2\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =-2\pi +2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-2\pi +2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =[-2\pi t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-2\pi (1)+0)-(-2\pi (-1)+0) \\  & =-4\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 11
question.problem:
Use Stokes' theorem to evaluate 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,
$$

where $\text{curl}\,F=⟨y,\,2yz,\,-{z}^{2}+1⟩,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the half-cone $z=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ and the plane $z=-3.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above.
question.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the half-cone $z=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ and the plane $z=-3.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=-3.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3)=0 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨y,\,2yz,\,-{z}^{2}+1⟩{|}_{z=-3} \\  & =⟨{{y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-6y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-8}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y\cdot 0-(-6y)\cdot 0-8)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-8\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ with radius $3$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-8\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}-8\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-8{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}r\,\text{d}r \\  & =-8[\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{r=0}^{r=3} \\  & =-8(2\pi -0)\cdot (\frac{9}{2}-0) \\  & =-72\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the half-cone $z=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ and the plane $z=-3.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=-3.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3)=0 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨y,\,2yz,\,-{z}^{2}+1⟩{|}_{z=-3} \\  & =⟨{{y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-6y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-8}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

question.name: Question 12
question.problem:
Use Stokes' theorem to evaluate 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,
$$

where $\text{curl}\,F=⟨x+y,\,-x+y,\,-2z⟩,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the paraboloid $z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above.
question.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the paraboloid $z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2})=2(x-1) \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2})=2(y+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨x+y,\,-x+y,\,-2z⟩{|}_{z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}} \\  & =⟨{{x+y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-x+y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-2(x-1)^{2}-2(y+1)^{2}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(x+y)\cdot 2(x-1)-(-x+y)\cdot 2(y+1)-2((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2((x+y)(1-x)+(x-y)(y+1)-(x-1)^{2}-(y+1)^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+2x-y-1)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+2x-y-1)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4(-{r}^{2}+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\cdot r\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-{r}^{3}+2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r)\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{[-{r}^{3}\theta +2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}(-2\pi {r}^{3}-2\pi r)\,\text{d}r \\  & =-8\pi {[-\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-8\pi (-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-6\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the paraboloid $z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2})=2(x-1) \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2})=2(y+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨x+y,\,-x+y,\,-2z⟩{|}_{z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}} \\  & =⟨{{x+y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-x+y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-2(x-1)^{2}-2(y+1)^{2}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(x+y)\cdot 2(x-1)-(-x+y)\cdot 2(y+1)-2((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2((x+y)(1-x)+(x-y)(y+1)-(x-1)^{2}-(y+1)^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+2x-y-1)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+2x-y-1)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4(-{r}^{2}+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\cdot r\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-{r}^{3}+2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r)\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{[-{r}^{3}\theta +2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}(-2\pi {r}^{3}-2\pi r)\,\text{d}r \\  & =-8\pi {[-\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-8\pi (-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-6\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Use Stokes' theorem to evaluate 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,
$$

where $\text{curl}\,F=⟨-y,\,z,\,-2x⟩,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the plane $z=2+2x-y.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above.
question.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the plane $z=2+2x-y.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=2+2x-y.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2+2x-y)=2 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2+2x-y)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-y,\,z,\,-2x⟩{|}_{z=2+2x-y} \\  & =⟨{{-y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{2+2x-y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-2x}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-y)\cdot (2)-(2+2x-y)\cdot (-1)-2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2y+2+2x-y-2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2+y)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2+y)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}(2+r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}2r+{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[{r}^{2}+\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(1+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[\theta -\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2+y)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}(2+r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}2r+{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[{r}^{2}+\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(1+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[\theta -\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,
$$

where $\text{curl}\,F=⟨-y,\,z,\,-2x⟩,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the plane $z=2+2x-y.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above.
feedback.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the plane $z=2+2x-y.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=2+2x-y.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2+2x-y)=2 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2+2x-y)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-y,\,z,\,-2x⟩{|}_{z=2+2x-y} \\  & =⟨{{-y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{2+2x-y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-2x}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-y)\cdot (2)-(2+2x-y)\cdot (-1)-2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2y+2+2x-y-2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2+y)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2+y)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}(2+r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}2r+{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[{r}^{2}+\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(1+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[\theta -\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}

$$
question.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the surface $z=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our surface $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})=\frac{-2x}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})=\frac{-2y}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨x,\,y,\,-2z⟩{|}_{z=1/({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)} \\  & =⟨{{x}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-x\cdot \frac{-2x}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}-y\cdot \frac{-2y}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14239092/assets/b215ec1e3330f96e7e606e085721b2dd1f50d113f0151e36ec98e6d0a6f54e73.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\,-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$
