Question 14
?

Let C be the intersection of the surface z=1x2+y2+1 and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes x=±1, and y=±1. Given that the curve C is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above and curlF=⟨x,y,−2z⟩, the circulation of F along C can be written as ∮CF⋅dr=

a
∫−11∫−11−y2(x2+y2+1)2dydx
b
∫−11∫−11−xy(x2+y2+1)2dydx
c
∫−11∫−11x2(x2+y2+1)2dydx
d
∫−11∫−11−2(x2+y2+1)2dydx
e
∫−11∫−11−4(x2+y2+1)2dydx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let S be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary C with positive orientation. If a vector field F has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains S, then Stokes' theorem states that

∮CF⋅dr=∬ScurlF⋅dS.

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve C representing the intersection of the surface z=1x2+y2+1 and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our surface S with the equation

z=g(x,y)=1x2+y2+1.

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph z=g(x,y):

∂g∂x=∂∂x(1x2+y2+1)=−2x(x2+y2+1)2∂g∂y=∂∂y(1x2+y2+1)=−2y(x2+y2+1)2

Next, we substitute the equation z=g(x,y) into expression for curlF:

curlF|z=g(x,y)=⟨x,y,−2z⟩|z=1/(x2+y2+1)=⟨x⏟P,y⏟Q,−2x2+y2+1⏟R⟩

So, we have

∬ScurlF⋅dS=∬D(−P∂g∂x−Q∂g∂y+R)dA=∬D(−x⋅−2x(x2+y2+1)2−y⋅−2y(x2+y2+1)2−2x2+y2+1)dA=∬D−2(x2+y2+1)2dA,

where D is region enclosed by the projection of C onto the xy-plane, shown below.

Therefore, we obtain

∬D−2(x2+y2+1)2dA=∫−11∫−11−2(x2+y2+1)2dydx.

last_observation.name: Question 14
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating a Line Integral Using Stokes' Theorem
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the surface $z=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our surface $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})=\frac{-2x}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})=\frac{-2y}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨x,\,y,\,-2z⟩{|}_{z=1/({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)} \\  & =⟨{{x}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-x\cdot \frac{-2x}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}-y\cdot \frac{-2y}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14239092/assets/b215ec1e3330f96e7e606e085721b2dd1f50d113f0151e36ec98e6d0a6f54e73.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\,-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the surface $z=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our surface $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})=\frac{-2x}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})=\frac{-2y}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨x,\,y,\,-2z⟩{|}_{z=1/({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)} \\  & =⟨{{x}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-x\cdot \frac{-2x}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}-y\cdot \frac{-2y}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14239092/assets/b215ec1e3330f96e7e606e085721b2dd1f50d113f0151e36ec98e6d0a6f54e73.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\,-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

Let C be the intersection of the surface z=1x2+y2+1 and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes x=±1, and y=±1. Given that the curve C is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above and curlF=⟨x,y,−2z⟩, the circulation of F along C can be written as ∮CF⋅dr=

a
∫−11∫−11−y2(x2+y2+1)2dydx
b
∫−11∫−11−xy(x2+y2+1)2dydx
c
∫−11∫−11x2(x2+y2+1)2dydx
d
∫−11∫−11−2(x2+y2+1)2dydx
e
∫−11∫−11−4(x2+y2+1)2dydx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let S be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary C with positive orientation. If a vector field F has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains S, then Stokes' theorem states that

∮CF⋅dr=∬ScurlF⋅dS.

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve C representing the intersection of the surface z=1x2+y2+1 and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our surface S with the equation

z=g(x,y)=1x2+y2+1.

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph z=g(x,y):

∂g∂x=∂∂x(1x2+y2+1)=−2x(x2+y2+1)2∂g∂y=∂∂y(1x2+y2+1)=−2y(x2+y2+1)2

Next, we substitute the equation z=g(x,y) into expression for curlF:

curlF|z=g(x,y)=⟨x,y,−2z⟩|z=1/(x2+y2+1)=⟨x⏟P,y⏟Q,−2x2+y2+1⏟R⟩

So, we have

∬ScurlF⋅dS=∬D(−P∂g∂x−Q∂g∂y+R)dA=∬D(−x⋅−2x(x2+y2+1)2−y⋅−2y(x2+y2+1)2−2x2+y2+1)dA=∬D−2(x2+y2+1)2dA,

where D is region enclosed by the projection of C onto the xy-plane, shown below.

Therefore, we obtain

∬D−2(x2+y2+1)2dA=∫−11∫−11−2(x2+y2+1)2dydx.
question.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Line Integral Using Stokes' Theorem

solution.reasoning: Use the graph z=g(x,y)=1/(x^2+y^2+1) over [-1,1]^2, oriented upward to match C. Writing q=x^2+y^2+1 gives g_x=-2x/q^2 and g_y=-2y/q^2. By Stokes' theorem, the integrand is -x g_x-y g_y-2g=2(x^2+y^2)/q^2-2/q=-2/q^2. Thus choice d is mathematically correct. feedback.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the surface $z=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our surface $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})=\frac{-2x}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})=\frac{-2y}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨x,\,y,\,-2z⟩{|}_{z=1/({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)} \\  & =⟨{{x}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-x\cdot \frac{-2x}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}-y\cdot \frac{-2y}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14239092/assets/b215ec1e3330f96e7e606e085721b2dd1f50d113f0151e36ec98e6d0a6f54e73.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\,-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨y,\,x,\,2⟩{|}_{z={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨y,\,x,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨{{y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{x}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{2}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y\cdot (2x)-x\cdot (-2y)+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14239092/assets/5f2f4cb03b3b0232c9debd1f4ed64bd683fe788ccba16cfbe395d9c3b629972d.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\,2\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

Let C be the intersection of the hyperbolic paraboloid z=x2−y2 and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes x=±1, y=±2. Given that the curve C is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above and curlF=⟨y,x,2⟩, the circulation of F along C can be written as ∮CF⋅dr=

a
∫−11∫−222xydydx
b
∫−11∫−2xx2−y2dydx
c
∫−11∫−222+2xydydx
d
∫−11∫−222dydx
e
∫−11∫−2x4+2xydydx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let S be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary C with positive orientation. If a vector field F has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains S, then Stokes' theorem states that

∮CF⋅dr=∬ScurlF⋅dS.

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve C representing the intersection of the paraboloid z=x2−y2 and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid S with the equation

z=g(x,y)=x2−y2.

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph z=g(x,y):

∂g∂x=∂∂x(x2−y2)=2x∂g∂y=∂∂y(x2−y2)=−2y

Next, we substitute the equation z=g(x,y) into expression for curlF:

curlF|z=g(x,y)=⟨y,x,2⟩|z=x2−y2=⟨y,x,2⟩=⟨y⏟P,x⏟Q,2⏟R⟩

So, we have

∬ScurlF⋅dS=∬D(−P∂g∂x−Q∂g∂y+R)dA=∬D(−y⋅(2x)−x⋅(−2y)+2)dA=∬D2dA,

where D is region enclosed by the projection of C onto the xy-plane, shown below.

Therefore, we obtain

∬D2dA=∫−11∫−222dydx.

last_observation.name: Question 15
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating a Line Integral Using Stokes' Theorem
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨y,\,x,\,2⟩{|}_{z={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨y,\,x,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨{{y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{x}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{2}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y\cdot (2x)-x\cdot (-2y)+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14239092/assets/5f2f4cb03b3b0232c9debd1f4ed64bd683fe788ccba16cfbe395d9c3b629972d.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\,2\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

Let C be the intersection of the hyperbolic paraboloid z=x2−y2 and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes x=±1, y=±2. Given that the curve C is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above and curlF=⟨y,x,2⟩, the circulation of F along C can be written as ∮CF⋅dr=

a
∫−11∫−222xydydx
b
∫−11∫−2xx2−y2dydx
c
∫−11∫−222+2xydydx
d
∫−11∫−222dydx
e
∫−11∫−2x4+2xydydx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let S be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary C with positive orientation. If a vector field F has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains S, then Stokes' theorem states that

∮CF⋅dr=∬ScurlF⋅dS.

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve C representing the intersection of the paraboloid z=x2−y2 and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid S with the equation

z=g(x,y)=x2−y2.

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph z=g(x,y):

∂g∂x=∂∂x(x2−y2)=2x∂g∂y=∂∂y(x2−y2)=−2y

Next, we substitute the equation z=g(x,y) into expression for curlF:

curlF|z=g(x,y)=⟨y,x,2⟩|z=x2−y2=⟨y,x,2⟩=⟨y⏟P,x⏟Q,2⏟R⟩

So, we have

∬ScurlF⋅dS=∬D(−P∂g∂x−Q∂g∂y+R)dA=∬D(−y⋅(2x)−x⋅(−2y)+2)dA=∬D2dA,

where D is region enclosed by the projection of C onto the xy-plane, shown below.

Therefore, we obtain

∬D2dA=∫−11∫−222dydx.

solution.reasoning: For z=x^2-y^2, the upward area vector is (-2x,2y,1) dA. Stokes' theorem gives integrand (y,x,2)\cdot(-2x,2y,1)=2 over [-1,1]×[-2,2], exactly choice d, with value 16. Choice c also evaluates to 16 because its extra term 2xy integrates to zero, so the choices are not mathematically unique. Choice d is the direct Stokes representation. feedback.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨y,\,x,\,2⟩{|}_{z={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨y,\,x,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨{{y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{x}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{2}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y\cdot (2x)-x\cdot (-2y)+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14239092/assets/5f2f4cb03b3b0232c9debd1f4ed64bd683fe788ccba16cfbe395d9c3b629972d.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\,2\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.html:
Question 15
?

Let C be the intersection of the hyperbolic paraboloid z=x2−y2 and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes x=±1, y=±2. Given that the curve C is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above and curlF=⟨y,x,2⟩, the circulation of F along C can be written as ∮CF⋅dr=

a
∫−11∫−222xydydx
b
∫−11∫−2xx2−y2dydx
c
∫−11∫−222+2xydydx
d
∫−11∫−222dydx
e
∫−11∫−2x4+2xydydx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let S be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary C with positive orientation. If a vector field F has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains S, then Stokes' theorem states that

∮CF⋅dr=∬ScurlF⋅dS.

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve C representing the intersection of the paraboloid z=x2−y2 and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid S with the equation

z=g(x,y)=x2−y2.

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph z=g(x,y):

∂g∂x=∂∂x(x2−y2)=2x∂g∂y=∂∂y(x2−y2)=−2y

Next, we substitute the equation z=g(x,y) into expression for curlF:

curlF|z=g(x,y)=⟨y,x,2⟩|z=x2−y2=⟨y,x,2⟩=⟨y⏟P,x⏟Q,2⏟R⟩

So, we have

∬ScurlF⋅dS=∬D(−P∂g∂x−Q∂g∂y+R)dA=∬D(−y⋅(2x)−x⋅(−2y)+2)dA=∬D2dA,

where D is region enclosed by the projection of C onto the xy-plane, shown below.

Therefore, we obtain

∬D2dA=∫−11∫−222dydx.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.worked_solution:
The function $\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(2x+8)}{2-x}$ is well defined for $x>-4,$ and $x\ne 2$ and so to find this limit we substitute $x=1$ into the above expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(2x+8)}{2-x} & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(2(1)+8)}{2-1} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(10)}{1} \\  & =\operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{1}) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the following limit:
limx→1log⁡(2x+8)2−x=

questions.worked_solution:
The function ${log}_{2}⁡(4x)$ is well defined for $x>0,$ and so to find this limit we substitute $x=4$ into the above expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}{log}_{2}⁡(4x) & ={log}_{2}⁡(4\cdot 4) \\  & ={log}_{2}⁡(16) \\  & ={log}_{2}⁡({2}^{4}) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Evaluating Using Direct Substitution
canonical_examples.problem: Find $\lim_\limits{x \to 4}\log_2 (x+4) .$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The function $\log_2 (x+4)$ is defined for $x>-4,$ so the limit as $x \to 4$ exists.

To find this limit, we substitute $x=4$ into the expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}{log}_{2}⁡(x+4) & ={log}_{2}⁡(4+4) \\  & ={log}_{2}⁡(8) \\  & ={log}_{2}⁡({2}^{3}) \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Let's look at the graph of $y=\log_2{x}$ below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14246608/assets/004265d2269924c6ce8905b6b92e9050b84066b3b5a3cc5383c75dd08e62f413.png)

From the graph, we see that

$$
\lim_{x\to3}\log_2{x} = \log_2{3}\approx 1.58.
$$

For logarithmic functions, the limit at a point is equal to the value of the function at that point, so for any base $b \gt 1$ we have

$$
\lim_{x\to c}\log_b{x} = \log_b{c}.
$$

Remember that logarithms are only defined for positive inputs $x\gt 0,$ so we must have $c>0.$ Otherwise, the limit does not exist $\textrm{(DNE}).$

Let's take a look again at the function $y=\log_2(x).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14246608/assets/30a66b56ea1422fc61941d22aedbbf3f17e06810e66e6590490bd4b7188fd361.png)

As $x$ gets larger and larger, the curve increases without bound. So, we have

$$
\lim_{x\to\infty} \log_2{x}= \infty.
$$

The curve is not defined for $x\leq 0,$ but as $x$ approaches zero from the right the curve *decreases* without bound. So

$$
\lim_{x\to0^+}\log_2{x} = -\infty.
$$

Also, note that

$$
\lim_{x\to0^-}\log_2{x} = \textrm{DNE},\qquad\qquad \lim_{x\to0}\log_2{x} = \textrm{DNE}.
$$

These properties are true for logarithms of any base $b\gt 1.$

tutorial.problem:
Let's look at the graph of $y=\log_2{x}$ below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14246608/assets/004265d2269924c6ce8905b6b92e9050b84066b3b5a3cc5383c75dd08e62f413.png)

From the graph, we see that

$$
\lim_{x\to3}\log_2{x} = \log_2{3}\approx 1.58.
$$

For logarithmic functions, the limit at a point is equal to the value of the function at that point, so for any base $b \gt 1$ we have

$$
\lim_{x\to c}\log_b{x} = \log_b{c}.
$$

Remember that logarithms are only defined for positive inputs $x\gt 0,$ so we must have $c>0.$ Otherwise, the limit does not exist $\textrm{(DNE}).$

observed_steps.name: Example: Evaluating Using Direct Substitution
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The function $\log_2 (x+4)$ is defined for $x>-4,$ so the limit as $x \to 4$ exists.

To find this limit, we substitute $x=4$ into the expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}{log}_{2}⁡(x+4) & ={log}_{2}⁡(4+4) \\  & ={log}_{2}⁡(8) \\  & ={log}_{2}⁡({2}^{3}) \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating Using Direct Substitution
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The function $\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(2x+8)}{2-x}$ is well defined for $x>-4,$ and $x\ne 2$ and so to find this limit we substitute $x=1$ into the above expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(2x+8)}{2-x} & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(2(1)+8)}{2-1} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(10)}{1} \\  & =\operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{1}) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let's sketch the graph of $y = \ln(x-2).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14246608/assets/bfe277aaf4c57d73d2649d8ade756cf04411ba23a049a6e1283d18c3e711a7fa.png)

The function is not defined for $x\leq 2.$ Therefore,

$$
\lim_\limits{x \to 2^{-}} \ln (x-2) = \textrm{DNE}.
$$

However, the function is defined for $x\gt 2.$ Therefore,

$$
\lim_\limits{x \to 2^{+}} \ln (x-2) = -\infty.
$$

Since the left and right-sided limits are not equal, we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x \to 2} \ln (x-2) = \textrm{DNE}.
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.worked_solution:
The function $\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(2x+8)}{2-x}$ is well defined for $x>-4,$ and $x\ne 2$ and so to find this limit we substitute $x=1$ into the above expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(2x+8)}{2-x} & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(2(1)+8)}{2-1} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(10)}{1} \\  & =\operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{1}) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.worked_solution:
Let's sketch the graph of $y={log}_{3}⁡(4-2x).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14246608/assets/b1d65d2df4e6a5a6b66e908ed8f776e2a1b8a4b24896506d3625e6569d9ea4e6.png)

The function is not defined for $x\ge 2.$ Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}{log}_{3}⁡(4-2x)=\text{DNE}.
$$

However, the function is defined for $x<2.$ Moreover,

$$
{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}{log}_{3}⁡(4-2x)=-\infty .
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating One-Sided Infinite Limits of Logarithmic Functions
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(6-2x).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14246608/assets/bba697be09903e54cffc4bf0c0e05cbd30cbfc11975cac5097e964415baca113.png)

The function is not defined for $x>3.$ Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to {3}^{+}}\operatorname{ln}⁡(6-2x)=\text{DNE}.
$$

However, the function is defined for $x<3.$ Moreover,

$$
{lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}\operatorname{ln}⁡(6-2x)=-\infty .
$$

question.name: Question 7
question.problem: Calculate ${lim}_{x\to -3}{log}_{7}⁡(x+3).$
question.worked_solution:
Let's sketch the graph of $y={log}_{7}⁡(x+3).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14246608/assets/0b45cd648830ad88c2f21865c1bfd704783a7b5d9ce3510646ae55e98d2d95ac.png)

The function is not defined for $x\le -3.$ Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to (-3)^{-}}{log}_{7}⁡(x+3)=\text{DNE}.
$$

However, the function is defined for $x>-3.$ Moreover,

$$
{lim}_{x\to (-3)^{+}}{log}_{7}⁡(x+3)=-\infty .
$$

Since the left and right-sided limits are not equal, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to -3}{log}_{7}⁡(x+3)=\text{DNE}.
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14236103/assets/931f7cc1fe4cc6a45c1f586bb017bb3eda8f7745aa3973c13f08aa8521c39400.png)

A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ what are the nonzero singular values of $A?$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=4={\sigma }_{1},$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=2={\sigma }_{2}.$

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=4$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=2.$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: A $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=2\sqrt{3},$ find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.
questions.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=9,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={9}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={9}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=9.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=9.$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues

- $||A{v}_{2}||=8={\sigma }_{2},$ which means that ${\lambda }_{2}={8}^{2}=64.$

Therefore, an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=100$ of ${A}^{T}A$ is ${v}_{1}.$

question.html:
Question 1
?

A 2×3 matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto an ellipse in R2. The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that v1 and v2 are unit eigenvectors of ATA, what are the nonzero singular values of A?

a
16 and 4
b
2 and 2
c
v1 and v1
d
4 and 2
e
4v1 and 2v1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose A is an m×n matrix. Let

{v1,v2…,vn} be an orthonormal basis of Rn consisting of the eigenvectors of ATA with corresponding eigenvalues

λ1≥λ2≥…≥λn.

Then,

  • σ1=λ1 is the length of Av1,

  • σ2=λ2 is the length of Av2,

  • ⋯

In our example, we see that

  • ||Av1||=4=σ1, and

  • ||Av2||=2=σ2.

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of A are σ1=4 and σ2=2.

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=9,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={9}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={9}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=9.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=9.$

Question 2
?

A 2×2 matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto an ellipse in R2. Given that the singular values of A are σ1=9 and σ2=23, find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.

a
3
b
25
c
3
d
9
e
23
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto the ellipse {Ax|‖x‖=1} in R2.

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point Ax on our ellipse, as follows:

‖Ax‖2=(Ax)T(Ax)=(xTAT)(Ax)=xT(ATA)x,

where xT(ATA)x is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ATA.

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ATA.

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ATA are called the singular values of A. Since the largest singular value of A is σ1=9, the largest eigenvalue of ATA must be λ1=σ12=92. So, we obtain that

max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖2}=92⟹max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖}=9.

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is σ1=9.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=5={\sigma }_{1},$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=3={\sigma }_{2}.$

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=3.$

A 2×3 matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto an ellipse in R2. The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that v1 and v2 are unit eigenvectors of ATA, what are the nonzero singular values of A?

a
7 and 3
b
11 and 7
c
6 and 4
d
5 and 3
e
25 and 9
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Suppose A is an m×n matrix. Let

{v1,v2…,vn} be an orthonormal basis of Rn consisting of the eigenvectors of ATA with corresponding eigenvalues

λ1≥λ2≥…≥λn.

Then,

  • σ1=λ1 is the length of Av1,

  • σ2=λ2 is the length of Av2,

  • ⋯

In our example, we see that

  • ||Av1||=5=σ1, and

  • ||Av2||=3=σ2.

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of A are σ1=5 and σ2=3.

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=10={\sigma }_{1},$ which means that ${\lambda }_{1}={10}^{2}=100,$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=8={\sigma }_{2},$ which means that ${\lambda }_{2}={8}^{2}=64.$

Therefore, an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=100$ of ${A}^{T}A$ is ${v}_{1}.$

question.html:
Question 1
?

A 2×3 matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto an ellipse in R2. The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that v1 and v2 are unit eigenvectors of ATA, what are the nonzero singular values of A?

a
16 and 4
b
2 and 2
c
v1 and v1
d
4 and 2
e
4v1 and 2v1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose A is an m×n matrix. Let

{v1,v2…,vn} be an orthonormal basis of Rn consisting of the eigenvectors of ATA with corresponding eigenvalues

λ1≥λ2≥…≥λn.

Then,

  • σ1=λ1 is the length of Av1,

  • σ2=λ2 is the length of Av2,

  • ⋯

In our example, we see that

  • ||Av1||=4=σ1, and

  • ||Av2||=2=σ2.

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of A are σ1=4 and σ2=2.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: A $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=2\sqrt{3},$ find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.
question.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=9,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={9}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={9}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=9.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=9.$

question.html:
Question 3
?

A 2×2 matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto an ellipse in R2. Given that the singular values of A are σ1=8 and σ2=33, find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.

a
9
b
3
c
33
d
4
e
8
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto the ellipse {Ax|‖x‖=1} in R2.

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point Ax on our ellipse, as follows:

‖Ax‖2=(Ax)T(Ax)=(xTAT)(Ax)=xT(ATA)x,

where xT(ATA)x is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ATA.

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ATA.

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ATA are called the singular values of A. Since the largest singular value of A is σ1=8, the largest eigenvalue of ATA must be λ1=σ12=82. So, we obtain that

max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖2}=82⟹max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖}=8.

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is σ1=8.

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14236103/assets/6df3639cb222756221803446ebc735cf1e7cbcf4a922ed7fce835c0c44fb9aa1.png)

A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ what are the nonzero singular values of $A?$
question.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=5={\sigma }_{1},$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=3={\sigma }_{2}.$

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=3.$

question.html:
Question 4
?

A 2×3 matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto an ellipse in R2. The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that v1 and v2 are unit eigenvectors of ATA, what are the nonzero singular values of A?

a
7 and 3
b
11 and 7
c
6 and 4
d
5 and 3
e
25 and 9
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Suppose A is an m×n matrix. Let

{v1,v2…,vn} be an orthonormal basis of Rn consisting of the eigenvectors of ATA with corresponding eigenvalues

λ1≥λ2≥…≥λn.

Then,

  • σ1=λ1 is the length of Av1,

  • σ2=λ2 is the length of Av2,

  • ⋯

In our example, we see that

  • ||Av1||=5=σ1, and

  • ||Av2||=3=σ2.

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of A are σ1=5 and σ2=3.

A $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ which of the following is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $100$ of ${A}^{T}A?$
question.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=10={\sigma }_{1},$ which means that ${\lambda }_{1}={10}^{2}=100,$ and

question.html:
Question 5
?

A 2×2 matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto an ellipse in R2. The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that v1 and v2 are unit eigenvectors of ATA, which of the following is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue 100 of ATA?

a
Av1
b
v2
c
v1
d
Av2
e
AATv1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose A is an m×n matrix. Let

{v1,v2…,vn} be an orthonormal basis of Rn consisting of the eigenvectors of ATA with corresponding eigenvalues

λ1≥λ2≥…≥λn.

Then,

  • σ1=λ1 is the length of Av1,

  • σ2=λ2 is the length of Av2,

  • ⋯

In our example, we see that

  • ||Av1||=10=σ1, which means that λ1=102=100, and

  • ||Av2||=8=σ2, which means that λ2=82=64.

Therefore, an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue λ1=100 of ATA is v1.

questions.name: Question 2
questions.worked_solution:
For similar polygons, the ratios of lengths of the corresponding sides should be the same.

- Let's check for this in option I:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{AB}{{A}^{′}{B}^{′}} & =\frac{4}{16}=\frac{1}{4}, \\ \frac{BC}{{B}^{′}{C}^{′}} & =\frac{6}{24}=\frac{1}{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So, option I does give possible values of ${A}^{′}{B}^{′}$ and ${B}^{′}{C}^{′}.$

- For option II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{AB}{{A}^{′}{B}^{′}} & =\frac{4}{20}=\frac{1}{5}, \\ \frac{BC}{{B}^{′}{C}^{′}} & =\frac{6}{30}=\frac{1}{5}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So, option II does give possible values of ${A}^{′}{B}^{′}$ and ${B}^{′}{C}^{′}.$

- For option III, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{AB}{{A}^{′}{B}^{′}} & =\frac{4}{32}=\frac{1}{8}, \\ \frac{BC}{{B}^{′}{C}^{′}} & =\frac{6}{42}=\frac{1}{7}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So, option III does not give possible values of ${A}^{′}{B}^{′}$ and ${B}^{′}{C}^{′}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14245089/assets/99212835e0eec95ac4ebd0c7d0fd49e1bb7e1a392f53251aa49510ac8ef5b65d.png)

Which of the above quadrilaterals are similar to $T$ (other than $T$ itself)?
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $T$ is a right trapezoid with one pair of parallel opposite sides.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given polygons.

- $K$ is *not* similar to $T.$ The polygon $K$ is a right trapezoid, and the corresponding angles are congruent, but the ratios of the lengths of the corresponding sides are not the same: 

$$
\frac{7}{14}\ne \frac{6}{6}
$$

- $R$ is *not* similar to $T$ because $R$ is not a trapezoid (it's a rectangle since it has $2$ pairs of opposite parallel sides, and $2$ pairs of right angles).

- $M$ is similar to $T.$ Indeed, $M$ is a right trapezoid. Furthermore, the corresponding angles are congruent, and the ratios of the lengths of the corresponding sides are the same:

$$
\frac{7}{14}=\frac{3}{6}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$M$ only".

Question 1

The two pentagons shown above are similar. What is the correct similarity statement?

a
 ABCDE∼YUVWX
b
 ABCDE∼UVWXY
c
 EABCD∼XYUVW
d
 EABCD∼YUVXW
e
 ABCDE∼UYXWV
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since, ∠A≅∠U,∠B≅∠V,∠C≅∠W,∠D≅∠X,∠E≅∠Y,

we conclude that

  • A corresponds to U,

  • B corresponds to V,

  • C corresponds to W,

  • D corresponds to X,

  • E corresponds to Y.

Therefore, ABCDE∼UVWXY.

question.name: Question 2
question.worked_solution:
For similar polygons, the ratios of lengths of the corresponding sides should be the same.

- Let's check for this in option I:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{AB}{{A}^{′}{B}^{′}} & =\frac{4}{16}=\frac{1}{4}, \\ \frac{BC}{{B}^{′}{C}^{′}} & =\frac{6}{24}=\frac{1}{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So, option I does give possible values of ${A}^{′}{B}^{′}$ and ${B}^{′}{C}^{′}.$

- For option II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{AB}{{A}^{′}{B}^{′}} & =\frac{4}{20}=\frac{1}{5}, \\ \frac{BC}{{B}^{′}{C}^{′}} & =\frac{6}{30}=\frac{1}{5}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So, option II does give possible values of ${A}^{′}{B}^{′}$ and ${B}^{′}{C}^{′}.$

Which of the above quadrilaterals are similar to $T$ (other than $T$ itself)?
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that $T$ is a right trapezoid with one pair of parallel opposite sides.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given polygons.

- $K$ is *not* similar to $T.$ The polygon $K$ is a right trapezoid, and the corresponding angles are congruent, but the ratios of the lengths of the corresponding sides are not the same: 

$$
\frac{7}{14}\ne \frac{6}{6}
$$

- $R$ is *not* similar to $T$ because $R$ is not a trapezoid (it's a rectangle since it has $2$ pairs of opposite parallel sides, and $2$ pairs of right angles).

- $M$ is similar to $T.$ Indeed, $M$ is a right trapezoid. Furthermore, the corresponding angles are congruent, and the ratios of the lengths of the corresponding sides are the same:

$$
\frac{7}{14}=\frac{3}{6}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$M$ only".

question.html:
Question 3
?

Which of the above quadrilaterals are similar to T (other than T itself)?

a
K and M only
b
M and R only
c
R only
d
M only
e
K only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that T is a right trapezoid with one pair of parallel opposite sides.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given polygons.

  • K is not similar to T. The polygon K is a right trapezoid, and the corresponding angles are congruent, but the ratios of the lengths of the corresponding sides are not the same: 714≠66

  • R is not similar to T because R is not a trapezoid (it's a rectangle since it has 2 pairs of opposite parallel sides, and 2 pairs of right angles).

  • M is similar to T. Indeed, M is a right trapezoid. Furthermore, the corresponding angles are congruent, and the ratios of the lengths of the corresponding sides are the same: 714=36

Therefore, the correct answer is "M only".

solution.reasoning: M has the same corresponding angles as T and matching side scale factors: 3/6=7/14=1/2. K fails proportionality because 6/6≠7/14. R has four right angles, unlike T. Thus only M is similar to T. No Math Academy answer or grade is captured.

Which of the above quadrilaterals are similar to $T$ (other than $T$ itself)?
feedback.worked_solution:
First, notice that $T$ is a right trapezoid with one pair of parallel opposite sides.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given polygons.

- $K$ is *not* similar to $T.$ The polygon $K$ is a right trapezoid, and the corresponding angles are congruent, but the ratios of the lengths of the corresponding sides are not the same: 

$$
\frac{7}{14}\ne \frac{6}{6}
$$

- $R$ is *not* similar to $T$ because $R$ is not a trapezoid (it's a rectangle since it has $2$ pairs of opposite parallel sides, and $2$ pairs of right angles).

- $M$ is similar to $T.$ Indeed, $M$ is a right trapezoid. Furthermore, the corresponding angles are congruent, and the ratios of the lengths of the corresponding sides are the same:

$$
\frac{7}{14}=\frac{3}{6}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$M$ only".

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Let $L$ be the line with equation $y=-x$ in ${R}^{2}.$ Which of the following statements are true? 

I. $L$ contains the zero-vector

II. $L$ is closed under vector addition

III. $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication

IV. $L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $L$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ -x\end{aligned}],\,x\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. The coordinates of the zero-vector satisfy the equation $y=-x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-x \\ (0) & =-(0) \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}a \\ -a\end{aligned}]\in L$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}b \\ -b\end{aligned}]\in L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =[\begin{aligned}a \\ -a\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}b \\ -b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a+b \\ (-a)+(-b)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a+b \\ -(a+b)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $y=-x.$ Therefore, $a+b\in L.$

- Statement III is true. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}a \\ -a\end{aligned}]\in L$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot [\begin{aligned}a \\ -a\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}ka \\ k(-a)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}ka \\ -(ka)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $y=-x.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in L.$

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are true, $L$ must be a subspace of ${R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "All the statements are true."

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Let $L$ be the line with equation $x+y=1$ in ${R}^{2}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $L$ contains the zero-vector

II. $L$ is closed under vector addition

III. $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication

IV. $L$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $L$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ 1-x\end{aligned}],\,x\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The coordinates of the zero-vector do not satisfy the equation $x+y=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & =1 \\ (0)+(0) & =1 \\ 0 & =1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ from $L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0+1 \\ 1+0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 
However, $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\notin L$ since substituting the coordinates into the equation, we obtain the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & =1 \\ (1)+(1) & =1 \\ 2 & =1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin L,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only."

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Let $L$ be the line with equation $2x-y=3$ in ${R}^{2}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $L$ contains the zero-vector

II. $L$ is closed under vector addition

III. $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication

IV. $L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $L$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ 2x-3\end{aligned}],\,x\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The coordinates of the zero-vector do not satisfy the equation $2x-y=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-y & =3 \\ 2(0)-(0) & =3 \\ 0 & =3\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ from $L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0+1 \\ -3-1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 
However, $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\notin L$ since substituting the coordinates into the equation, we obtain the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-y & =3 \\ 2(1)-(-4) & =3 \\ 6 & =3\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin L,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is false. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}t \\ -2t \\ 3t\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

for $t\in R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$

I. $Π$ contains the zero-vector

II. $Π$ is closed under vector addition

III. $Π$ is closed under scalar multiplication

IV. $Π$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}^{3}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $Π$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1+2y-z \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],\,y,z\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The line does not pass through the origin since

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2y+z & =1 \\ (0)-2(0)+(0) & =1 \\ 0 & =1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Let's consider $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\in Π$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\in Π.$ Then 

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1+0 \\ 0+0 \\ 0+1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

However, $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ does not belong to $Π$ since 

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2y+z & =1 \\ (1)-2(0)+(1) & =1 \\ 2 & =1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin Π,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only."

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem:
Let $Π$ be the plane with equation $z=2x-y$ in ${R}^{3}.$ Which of the following statements are true? 

I. $Π$ contains the zero-vector

II. $Π$ is closed under vector addition

III. $Π$ is closed under scalar multiplication

IV. $Π$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}^{3}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $Π$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ 2x-y\end{aligned}],\,x,y\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. The coordinates of the zero-vector satisfy the equation $z=2x-y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2x-y \\ (0) & =2(0)-(0) \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ 2{a}_{1}-{a}_{2}\end{aligned}]\in Π$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2} \\ 2{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}\end{aligned}]\in Π.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ 2{a}_{1}-{a}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2} \\ 2{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}+{b}_{2} \\ (2{a}_{1}-{a}_{2})+(2{b}_{1}-{b}_{2})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}+{b}_{2} \\ 2({a}_{1}+{b}_{1})-({a}_{2}+{b}_{2})\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $z=2x-y.$ Therefore, $a+b\in Π.$

- Statement III is true. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ 2{a}_{1}-{a}_{2}\end{aligned}]\in Π$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot [\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ 2{a}_{1}-{a}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}k{a}_{1} \\ k{a}_{2} \\ k(2{a}_{1}-{a}_{2})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}k{a}_{1} \\ k{a}_{2} \\ 2(k{a}_{1})-k{a}_{2}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $z=2x-y.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in Π.$

- Statement IV is false. Since statements II and III are true, $Π$ must be a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only."

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem:
Let $Π$ be the plane with equation $3x+2y+z=1$ in ${R}^{3}.$ Which of the following statements are true? 

I. $Π$ contains the zero-vector

II. $Π$ is closed under vector addition

III. $Π$ is closed under scalar multiplication

IV. $Π$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $Π$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ 1-3x-2y\end{aligned}],\,x,y\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The line does not pass through the origin since

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+2y+z & =1 \\ 3(0)+2(0)+(0) & =1 \\ 0 & =1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Let's consider $a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\in Π$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\in Π.$ Then 

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0+1 \\ 0+(-1) \\ 1+0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

However, $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ does not belong to $Π$ since 

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+2y+z & =1 \\ 3(1)+2(-1)+(1) & =1 \\ 2 & =1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin Π,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is false. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Determining Whether a Line Is a Subspace of Two-Dimensional Space
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $L$ be the line with equation $y=5+3x$ in $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $L$ contains the zero-vector

II. $L$ is closed under vector addition

III. $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication

IV. $L$ is **not** a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0 \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ for any vector $\mathbf{v}$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $L$ contains vectors of the form 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/7202d8cbdd95abf0bce85cd66490b29abe5737259def341fcb3202a06c6140a0.svg)

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The coordinates of the zero-vector do not satisfy the equation $y=5+3x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5+3x \\ (0) & =5+3(0) \\ 0 & =5\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Let, for example, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/9b7dd489c2bd902529876d678dd3e21d3503f1d42aafba6aa6b3c40dad8f61da.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/911a47012bbfefca8e19f14c023c3924a5e6e02470d6825ad8e4525816bcf2a2.svg) from $L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0+(-1) \\ 5+2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 
However, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/dbbce97422b8e84b3408bc64d43a250bcba2bd5f2ba5ea5a6aa282e884fa8750.svg) since substituting the coordinates into the equation $y=5+3x$ gives the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5+3x \\ 7 & =5+3(-1) \\ 7 & =2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $\mathbf{0} \not\in L,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining Whether a Line Is a Subspace of Two-Dimensional Space

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Determining Whether a Line Is a Subspace of Three-Dimensional Space
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $L$ be the line in $\mathbb{R}^3$ that passes through the points $(1,2,2)$ and $(2,1,1).$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $L$ contains the zero-vector

II. $L$ is closed under vector addition

III. $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication

IV. $L$ is **not** a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0 \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ for any vector $\mathbf{v}$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The direction vector of the line $L$ is 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/cd632a2491479baa770168dc5d143944fa72fe7264f27ee51e5518f9e9b9cbe2.svg)
This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in\mathbb R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
{x-1}=\dfrac{y-2}{-1}=\dfrac{z-2}{-1}.
$$

But this line does not pass through the origin since 

$$
{(0)-1}\neq\dfrac{(0)-2}{-1}=\dfrac{(0)-2}{-1}.  \quad {\color{red}\times}
$$

- Statement II is false. Let's consider the vectors $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ and $[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ from $L$ (the position vectors of the given points). Then,
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/c58eba4b7130df4c9e588d2792fc1cb1f2b465504ae0859edd213735ca690c97.svg)
However, the point $(3,3,3)$ does not belong to $L$ since

$$
{(3)-1}\neq\dfrac{(3)-2}{-1}=\dfrac{(3)-2}{-1}. \quad {\color{red}\times}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $\mathbf{0} \not\in L,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only."

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Determining Whether a Plane Is a Subspace of Three-Dimensional Space
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $\Pi$ be the plane with equation $x+4y-3z=2$ in $\mathbb{R}^3.$ Which of the following statements are true? 

I. $\Pi$ contains the zero-vector

II. $\Pi$ is closed under vector addition

III. $\Pi$ is closed under scalar multiplication

IV. $\Pi$ is **not** a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0 \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ for any vector $\mathbf{v}$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $\Pi$ contains vectors of the form 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/70061c1d04780e7a3db2b0c6b41a91c791f029666dff632f35c0ba8d3fd608b0.svg)

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The plane does not pass through the origin since

$$
\begin{aligned}x+4y-3z & =2 \\ (0)+4(0)-3(0) & =2 \\ 0 & =2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Let's consider ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/d0cf195a83c36291bae09c62f542449734d024fadae23b99cecbb4507f03c430.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/13f8e15407cd0dbdfc080f19f906df1ed4bf984635cb2eb30b01f95d50695d53.svg) Then 

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2+1 \\ 0+1 \\ 0+1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

However, $[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ does not belong to $\Pi$ since 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+4y-3z & =2 \\ (3)+4(1)-3(1) & =2 \\ 4 & =2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $\mathbf{0} \not\in \Pi,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are false, $\Pi$ is *not* a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining Whether a Plane Is a Subspace of Three-Dimensional Space

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
A **subspace** of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a subset of $\mathbb R^n$ that is closed  under vector addition and scalar multiplication. In other words: 

$H\subseteq \mathbb R^n$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ if and only if it satisfies the following properties:

- *Closure under vector addition:* 

$\qquad$ If $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are in $H,$ then their sum $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$ is also in $H.$

- *Closure under scalar multiplication:* 

$\qquad$ If $\mathbf{u}$ is in $H,$ then $c\cdot \mathbf{u}$ is also in $H$ for any scalar number $c.$

For example, consider the line $L$ with equation $y=3x$ in $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Is $L$ a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2?$ 

First, notice that we can express the points on $L$ as the following set:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/1f380f9928da2dd44ff157a72fce97c02ae44626df515d52ece6ff5feee302d2.svg)

In other words, $L$ contains all vectors of the form ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/90996c2ffae29c3bd9cd3ab398cca4dd7e1b8fbe275de8520a72a16e504fb0f3.svg) where $x$ is a real number.

To determine whether $L$ is a subspace of $\mathbb R^2,$ we need to check the two conditions above. 

- Let's pick two arbitrary vectors in $L,$ namely, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/59be22e80d0be32c84a8c2bdb2f2c96b23a0941d4aba26bdefa078fd299c137c.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/d78ea4fcfbd469e88b7fe46e28ac6f396a538c577f4defdd1b3d60e60df3c4b7.svg) If we compute their sum, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}u+v & =[\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} \\ 3{u}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} \\ 3{v}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}+{v}_{1} \\ 3{u}_{1}+3{v}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}+{v}_{1} \\ 3\cdot ({u}_{1}+{v}_{1})\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $y=3x.$ Therefore, $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v} \in L. \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}$

- Let's pick an arbitrary vector in $L,$ namely, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/759c7883ad2772f20a090ad2f8c5dfe01031ca31e2b5f0e7681c945c9256c91d.svg) Then, for any scalar $c$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}c\cdot u & =c\cdot [\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} \\ 3{u}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}c{u}_{1} \\ 3\cdot c{u}_{1}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $y=3x.$ Therefore, $c\cdot \mathbf{u}\in L. \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}$

The set $L$ satisfies both conditions. So, we can conclude that it is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2.$

**Note:** Since the second condition must be satisfied for any $c,$ including $c=0,$ we can conclude that every subspace must contain the zero vector $\mathbf{0}.$ So, if a set does not contain $\mathbf{0}$ then it is *not* a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n.$

For instance, the set 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/a15e0b4fc4544421e572d15b8fd016c3fa8721e0ecf3f8808a469c3252d1f6d6.svg)

does *not* contain the zero vector (since $0 \neq 0 + 1$), and consequently it is *not* a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2.$

tutorials.content:
A **subspace** of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a subset of $\mathbb R^n$ that is closed  under vector addition and scalar multiplication. In other words: 

$H\subseteq \mathbb R^n$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ if and only if it satisfies the following properties:

- *Closure under vector addition:* 

$\qquad$ If $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are in $H,$ then their sum $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$ is also in $H.$

- *Closure under scalar multiplication:* 

$\qquad$ If $\mathbf{u}$ is in $H,$ then $c\cdot \mathbf{u}$ is also in $H$ for any scalar number $c.$

For example, consider the line $L$ with equation $y=3x$ in $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Is $L$ a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2?$ 

First, notice that we can express the points on $L$ as the following set:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/1f380f9928da2dd44ff157a72fce97c02ae44626df515d52ece6ff5feee302d2.svg)

In other words, $L$ contains all vectors of the form ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/90996c2ffae29c3bd9cd3ab398cca4dd7e1b8fbe275de8520a72a16e504fb0f3.svg) where $x$ is a real number.

To determine whether $L$ is a subspace of $\mathbb R^2,$ we need to check the two conditions above. 

- Let's pick two arbitrary vectors in $L,$ namely, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/59be22e80d0be32c84a8c2bdb2f2c96b23a0941d4aba26bdefa078fd299c137c.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/d78ea4fcfbd469e88b7fe46e28ac6f396a538c577f4defdd1b3d60e60df3c4b7.svg) If we compute their sum, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}u+v & =[\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} \\ 3{u}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} \\ 3{v}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}+{v}_{1} \\ 3{u}_{1}+3{v}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}+{v}_{1} \\ 3\cdot ({u}_{1}+{v}_{1})\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $y=3x.$ Therefore, $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v} \in L. \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}$

- Let's pick an arbitrary vector in $L,$ namely, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/759c7883ad2772f20a090ad2f8c5dfe01031ca31e2b5f0e7681c945c9256c91d.svg) Then, for any scalar $c$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}c\cdot u & =c\cdot [\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} \\ 3{u}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}c{u}_{1} \\ 3\cdot c{u}_{1}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $y=3x.$ Therefore, $c\cdot \mathbf{u}\in L. \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}$

The set $L$ satisfies both conditions. So, we can conclude that it is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2.$

**Note:** Since the second condition must be satisfied for any $c,$ including $c=0,$ we can conclude that every subspace must contain the zero vector $\mathbf{0}.$ So, if a set does not contain $\mathbf{0}$ then it is *not* a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n.$

For instance, the set 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/a15e0b4fc4544421e572d15b8fd016c3fa8721e0ecf3f8808a469c3252d1f6d6.svg)

does *not* contain the zero vector (since $0 \neq 0 + 1$), and consequently it is *not* a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2.$

tutorials.problem:
Recall that $H$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ if and only if it satisfies the following properties:

*Closure under vector addition:* 

 $\qquad$ If $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are in $H,$ then their sum $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$ is also in $H.$

*Closure under scalar multiplication:* 

 $\qquad$ If $\mathbf{u}$ is in $H,$ then $c\cdot \mathbf{u}$ is also in $H$ for any scalar number $c.$

Let $L$ be the line in $\mathbb{R}^3$ that passes through the points $(0,0,0)$ and $(4,1,-2).$ Is $L$ a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3?$ 

First, note that the direction vector of the line $L$ is 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/25fa34994b33e0d11fd8990dddbfda276857e699018b4701c6e2eaf13acb0c20.svg)
This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4t \\ t \\ -2t\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in\mathbb R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
\dfrac x4=y=\dfrac z{-2}.
$$

To determine whether $L$ is a subspace, we need to check the two conditions above:

- Let's pick two arbitrary vectors in $L,$ namely, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/d7f1a3cf1625ff12bc96324dc428e1c95d271d8a72de603b671f722b9173281d.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/255fc61225b017a51ae60b1d157787ac4b60fe596ebaa8296b48053b87b2eae7.svg) If we compute their sum, we get

$$

$$

which satisfies the condition $\dfrac x4=y=\dfrac z{-2}.$ Therefore, $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\in L. \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}$

- Let's pick an arbitrary vector in $L,$ namely, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/7f7df4272eae1975b5802d54dfae499c528661ba0ae82faff45bb26f6cfab276.svg) Then, for any scalar $c,$ we have

$$

which satisfies the condition $\dfrac x4=y=\dfrac z{-2}.$ Therefore, $c\cdot \mathbf{u}\in L. \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}$

The set $L$ satisfies both conditions. So, we can conclude that it is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3.$

Recall that $H$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ if and only if it satisfies the following properties:

*Closure under vector addition:* 

 $\qquad$ If $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are in $H,$ then their sum $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$ is also in $H.$

*Closure under scalar multiplication:* 

 $\qquad$ If $\mathbf{u}$ is in $H,$ then $c\cdot \mathbf{u}$ is also in $H$ for any scalar number $c.$

Let $L$ be the line in $\mathbb{R}^3$ that passes through the points $(0,0,0)$ and $(4,1,-2).$ Is $L$ a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3?$ 

First, note that the direction vector of the line $L$ is 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/25fa34994b33e0d11fd8990dddbfda276857e699018b4701c6e2eaf13acb0c20.svg)
This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4t \\ t \\ -2t\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in\mathbb R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
\dfrac x4=y=\dfrac z{-2}.
$$

To determine whether $L$ is a subspace, we need to check the two conditions above:

- Let's pick two arbitrary vectors in $L,$ namely, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/d7f1a3cf1625ff12bc96324dc428e1c95d271d8a72de603b671f722b9173281d.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/255fc61225b017a51ae60b1d157787ac4b60fe596ebaa8296b48053b87b2eae7.svg) If we compute their sum, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}u+v & =[\begin{aligned}4{u}_{1} \\ {u}_{1} \\ -2{u}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4{v}_{1} \\ {v}_{1} \\ -2{v}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4{u}_{1}+4{v}_{1} \\ {u}_{1}+{v}_{1} \\ (-2{u}_{1})+(-2{v}_{1})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4\cdot ({u}_{1}+{v}_{1}) \\ {u}_{1}+{v}_{1} \\ (-2)\cdot ({u}_{1}+{v}_{1})\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $\dfrac x4=y=\dfrac z{-2}.$ Therefore, $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\in L. \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}$

- Let's pick an arbitrary vector in $L,$ namely, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246322/assets/7f7df4272eae1975b5802d54dfae499c528661ba0ae82faff45bb26f6cfab276.svg) Then, for any scalar $c,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}c\cdot u & =c\cdot [\begin{aligned}4{u}_{1} \\ {u}_{1} \\ -2{u}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4\cdot c{u}_{1} \\ c{u}_{1} \\ (-2)\cdot c{u}_{1}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $\dfrac x4=y=\dfrac z{-2}.$ Therefore, $c\cdot \mathbf{u}\in L. \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}$

The set $L$ satisfies both conditions. So, we can conclude that it is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3.$
