questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$
Q=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}],\,R=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 6 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 6 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}33 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}=33 \\ 2{x}_{2}=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-3.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-5(-3) & =33 \\ 3{x}_{1} & =18 \\ {x}_{1} & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$
Q=\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}-7 & 24 \\ -24 & -7\end{aligned}],\,R=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 10\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ is orthogonal, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}-7 & -24 \\ 24 & -7\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 10\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}-11 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-11 \\ {x}_{2}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-(2) & =-11 \\ {x}_{1} & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$
Q=\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & \sqrt{2} \\ 3\sqrt{5} & 3\sqrt{2} \\ 2\sqrt{5} & -5\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,R=\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 3\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{2} & 3\sqrt{2} & -5\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}-10\sqrt{5} \\ -10\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2}=-10\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{2}{x}_{2}=-10\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-10.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{5}(-10) & =-10\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5}{x}_{1} & =10\sqrt{5} \\ {x}_{1} & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -10\end{aligned}].$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem:
Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$
Q=\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}8 & -1 \\ 4 & 4 \\ -1 & 8\end{aligned}],\,R=\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}9 & 8 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}9 & 8 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}8 & 4 & -1 \\ -1 & 4 & 8\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}9 & 8 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}9{x}_{1}+8{x}_{2}=-9 \\ {x}_{2}=9.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=9.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}_{1}+8(9) & =-9 \\ 9{x}_{1} & =-81 \\ {x}_{1} & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 9\end{aligned}].$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem:
Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$
Q=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}1 & \sqrt{2} \\ 2 & -\sqrt{2} \\ 1 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,R=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ \sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}20 \\ -4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=20 \\ 2\sqrt{2}{x}_{2}=-4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-(-2) & =20 \\ 2{x}_{1} & =18 \\ {x}_{1} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying an Expression for a Least-Squares Solution in Terms of the Matrices Q and R
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
\bbox[5px, border: 1px solid black]{\phantom{A}} \, \mathbf{x} = \bbox[5px, border: 1px solid black]{\phantom{A}} \, \mathbf{b}
$$

Let $A=QR$  be a QR decomposition of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, and the matrix equation above gives the least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}.$ From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
A^T A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b}.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, it satisfies $Q^T Q = I,$ and we get

$$
R^T R \mathbf{x} = R^T \! Q^T \mathbf{b}.
$$

Finally, since $R^T$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $(R^T)^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ \bbox[5px,border:1px solid black]{\,R\phantom{|}}\,\,x & ={Q}^{T}\,b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are $R$ and $Q^T.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System Given a QR Factorization

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Let's consider the least-squares problem for the system

$$
A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}.
$$

We can use QR factorization to construct the least-squares solution of this system. Recall that finding the QR factorization of $A$ means expressing $A$ in the form

$$
A = QR,
$$

where

- $Q$ has orthonormal columns, and

- $R$ is an upper triangular matrix with positive entries on its main diagonal.

To see how QR factorization can be used to solve a least-squares problem, we first recall that the least-squares solution satisfies the normal equation

$$
A^T A \mathbf{x} = A^T \mathbf{b}.
$$

Substituting $A = QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, we have $Q^T Q = I.$ Therefore, the above equation becomes

$$
R^TR\mathbf{x} = R^TQ^T\mathbf{b}.
$$

Since $R^T$ is invertible, pre-multiplying our equation by $(R^T)^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

which simplifies as

$$
R \mathbf{x} = Q^T \mathbf{b}.  \qquad\qquad (\ast)
$$

The least-squares solution $\hat{\mathbf x}$ can now be found by solving this equation using back-substitution or row operations. This is usually the fastest way.

If we want an explicit formula for the least-squares solution, then we note that since $R$ is invertible, pre-multiplying $(\ast)$ by $R^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{-1}\cdot Rx & ={R}^{-1}\cdot {Q}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

which simplifies as

$$
\mathbf{x} = R^{-1} Q^T \mathbf{b}.
$$

The least-squares solution is unique if $A$ has linearly independent columns.

Let's find the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b},$ where $A = QR,$ and
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14246885/assets/4e2433312f3a424aa161d5aeec63df38787c43435a9c2af44ba6b3d63f9ef065.svg)

Previously, we showed that the normal equation corresponding to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ where $A=QR,$ can be reduced to

$$
R \mathbf{x} = Q^T \mathbf{b}.
$$

Substituting our matrices into this equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=2 \\ 3{x}_{2}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $x_2=2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$

tutorials.title: Using QR Factorization to Solve a Least-Squares Problem

tutorial.name: Introduction
tutorial.problem:
Let's consider the least-squares problem for the system

$$
A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}.
$$

We can use QR factorization to construct the least-squares solution of this system. Recall that finding the QR factorization of $A$ means expressing $A$ in the form

$$
A = QR,
$$

where

- $Q$ has orthonormal columns, and

- $R$ is an upper triangular matrix with positive entries on its main diagonal.

To see how QR factorization can be used to solve a least-squares problem, we first recall that the least-squares solution satisfies the normal equation

$$
A^T A \mathbf{x} = A^T \mathbf{b}.
$$

Substituting $A = QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, we have $Q^T Q = I.$ Therefore, the above equation becomes

$$
R^TR\mathbf{x} = R^TQ^T\mathbf{b}.
$$

Since $R^T$ is invertible, pre-multiplying our equation by $(R^T)^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

which simplifies as

$$
R \mathbf{x} = Q^T \mathbf{b}.  \qquad\qquad (\ast)
$$

The least-squares solution $\hat{\mathbf x}$ can now be found by solving this equation using back-substitution or row operations. This is usually the fastest way.

If we want an explicit formula for the least-squares solution, then we note that since $R$ is invertible, pre-multiplying $(\ast)$ by $R^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{-1}\cdot Rx & ={R}^{-1}\cdot {Q}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

which simplifies as

$$
\mathbf{x} = R^{-1} Q^T \mathbf{b}.
$$

The least-squares solution is unique if $A$ has linearly independent columns.

?

Ax=QTA

Let A=QR be a QR decomposition of an m×n matrix A with linearly independent columns, and the matrix equation above gives the least-squares solution of Ax=b. From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?

a
RT and bT
b
R and mb
c
R and b
d
R−1 and mb
e
R−1 and b
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the normal equation

ATAx=ATb.

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

Since Q has orthonormal columns, QTQ=I, and we get

RTRx=RTQTb.

Finally, since RT is invertible, pre-multiplying by (RT)−1 gives

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb.

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are R and b.

question.html:
Question 2
?

x=AQTb

Let A=QR be a QR decomposition of an m×n matrix A with linearly independent columns, and the expression above gives the least-squares solution of Ax=b. What is the missing part of the equation?

a
(R−I)
b
RT
c
(R−m⋅I)
d
RTR
e
R−1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the normal equation

ATAx=ATb.

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

Since Q has orthonormal columns, QTQ=I, and we get

RTRx=RTQTb.

Then, since RT is invertible, pre-multiplying by (RT)−1 gives

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb.

Finally, since R is invertible, pre-multiplying by R−1 gives

R−1⋅Rx=R−1⋅QTbx=R−1QTb.

Therefore, the missing part of the equation is R−1.
question.knowledge_point: Identifying an Expression for a Least-Squares Solution in Terms of the Matrices Q and R

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying an Expression for a Least-Squares Solution in Terms of the Matrices Q and R
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Then, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $R$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by ${R}^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{-1}\cdot Rx & ={R}^{-1}\cdot {Q}^{T}b \\ x & =\bbox[6px,border:1px solid black]{\,\phantom{|}\,\,{R}^{-1}\,}\,{Q}^{T}\,b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are ${R}^{-1}$ and ${Q}^{T}.$

question.html:
Question 4
?

RA=QTA

Let A=QR be a QR decomposition of an m×n matrix A with linearly independent columns, and the matrix equation above gives the least-squares solution of Ax=b. From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?

a
x and bT
b
b and x
c
x and 1‖b‖⋅b
d
1‖b‖⋅b and x
e
x and b
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the normal equation

ATAx=ATb.

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

Since Q has orthonormal columns, QTQ=I, and we get

RTRx=RTQTb.

Finally, since RT is invertible, pre-multiplying by (RT)−1 gives

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb.

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are x and b.

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying an Expression for a Least-Squares Solution in Terms of the Matrices Q and R
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Then, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $R$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by ${R}^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{-1}\cdot Rx & ={R}^{-1}\cdot {Q}^{T}b \\ x & =\bbox[4px,border:1px solid black]{{R}^{-1}\phantom{|}}\,\,{Q}^{T}\,\,b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are ${R}^{-1}$ and $b.$

question.problem:
$$
x=\bbox[5px,border:1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,{Q}^{T}\,\bbox[5px,border:1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}
$$

Let $A=QR$  be a QR decomposition of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, and the expression above gives the least-squares solution of $Ax=b.$ From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?
question.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Then, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $R$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by ${R}^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{-1}\cdot Rx & ={R}^{-1}\cdot {Q}^{T}b \\ x & =\bbox[4px,border:1px solid black]{{R}^{-1}\phantom{|}}\,\,{Q}^{T}\,\,b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are ${R}^{-1}$ and $b.$

x=AQTA

Let A=QR be a QR decomposition of an m×n matrix A with linearly independent columns, and the expression above gives the least-squares solution of Ax=b. From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?

a
bT and A
b
AT and b
c
R and b
d
R−1 and b
e
bT and R
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the normal equation

ATAx=ATb.

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

RTRx=RTQTb.

Let's find the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b},$ where $A = QR,$ and
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14246885/assets/37659acbbe3bd173fc178ce445d66a0edb529648f9a89a76356efd14d46fd92a.svg)

Previously, we showed that the normal equation corresponding to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ where $A=QR,$ can be reduced to

$$
R \mathbf{x} = Q^T \mathbf{b}.
$$

Substituting our matrices into this equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=2 \\ 3{x}_{2}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $x_2=2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-4(2) & =2 \\ 2{x}_{1} & =10 \\ {x}_{1} & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
A^T A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b}
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, it satisfies $Q^T Q = I,$ and we get

$$
R^T R \mathbf{x} = R^T \! Q^T \mathbf{b}.
$$

Finally, since $R^T$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $(R^T)^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{7}[\begin{aligned}7 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{7}[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 & 2 \\ -6 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}7 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}28 \\ 14\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}7{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=28 \\ 2{x}_{2}=14.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $x_2=7.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}7{x}_{1}-3(7) & =28 \\ 7{x}_{1} & =49 \\ {x}_{1} & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 6
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System Given a QR Factorization
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 6 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}33 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}=33 \\ 2{x}_{2}=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-3.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-5(-3) & =33 \\ 3{x}_{1} & =18 \\ {x}_{1} & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ is orthogonal, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}-7 & -24 \\ 24 & -7\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 10\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}-11 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-11 \\ {x}_{2}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-(2) & =-11 \\ {x}_{1} & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.

\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

\{\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2}=-10\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{2}{x}_{2}=-10\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Given the QR decomposition A=QR, find the least-squares solution to Ax=b, where Q=170[52353225−52],R=170[52502],b=[−1−30].

a
[1030]
b
[10−10]
c
[−1030]
d
[2030]
e
[−1020]
Submit

EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

ATAx=ATb

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

Since Q has orthonormal columns, QTQ=I, and we get

RTRx=RTQTb.

Finally, since RT is invertible, pre-multiplying by (RT)−1 gives

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb.

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

170[52502]⏞Rx=170[53525232−52]⏞QT[−1−30]⏞b[52502]x=[−105−102]

which gives the system

{5x1+25x2=−1052x2=−102.

From the second equation, we get x2=−10. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

5x1+25(−10)=−1055x1=105x1=10.

Therefore, the least-squares solution to Ax=b is [10−10].

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System Given a QR Factorization
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}9 & 8 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}8 & 4 & -1 \\ -1 & 4 & 8\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}9 & 8 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}9{x}_{1}+8{x}_{2}=-9 \\ {x}_{2}=9.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=9.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}_{1}+8(9) & =-9 \\ 9{x}_{1} & =-81 \\ {x}_{1} & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 9\end{aligned}].$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
$$
\bbox[5px,border:1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,x={Q}^{T}\,\bbox[5px,border:1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}
$$

Let $A=QR$  be a QR decomposition of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, and the matrix equation above gives the least-squares solution of $Ax=b.$ From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?
question.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ \,R\,\,\,x & ={Q}^{T}\,\,\,b\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are $R$ and $b.$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying an Expression for a Least-Squares Solution in Terms of the Matrices Q and R
last_observation.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ \,R\,\,\,x & ={Q}^{T}\,\,\,b\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are $R$ and $b.$

feedback.html:
Question 1
?

Ax=QTA

Let A=QR be a QR decomposition of an m×n matrix A with linearly independent columns, and the matrix equation above gives the least-squares solution of Ax=b. From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?

a
RT and bT
b
R and mb
c
R and b
d
R−1 and mb
e
R−1 and b
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the normal equation

ATAx=ATb.

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

Since Q has orthonormal columns, QTQ=I, and we get

RTRx=RTQTb.

Finally, since RT is invertible, pre-multiplying by (RT)−1 gives

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb.

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are R and b.
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying an Expression for a Least-Squares Solution in Terms of the Matrices Q and R

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
$$
x=\bbox[5px,border:1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,{Q}^{T}\,b
$$

Let $A=QR$  be a QR decomposition of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, and the expression above gives the least-squares solution of $Ax=b.$ What is the missing part of the equation?
question.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Then, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $R$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by ${R}^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{-1}\cdot Rx & ={R}^{-1}\cdot {Q}^{T}b \\ x & ={R}^{-1}\,\,{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing part of the equation is ${R}^{-1}.$

Question 2
?

x=AQTb

Let A=QR be a QR decomposition of an m×n matrix A with linearly independent columns, and the expression above gives the least-squares solution of Ax=b. What is the missing part of the equation?

a
(R−I)
b
RT
c
(R−m⋅I)
d
RTR
e
R−1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the normal equation

ATAx=ATb.

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

RTRx=RTQTb.

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb.

question.html:
Question 2
?

x=AQTb

Let A=QR be a QR decomposition of an m×n matrix A with linearly independent columns, and the expression above gives the least-squares solution of Ax=b. What is the missing part of the equation?

a
(R−I)
b
RT
c
(R−m⋅I)
d
RTR
e
R−1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the normal equation

ATAx=ATb.

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

Since Q has orthonormal columns, QTQ=I, and we get

RTRx=RTQTb.

Then, since RT is invertible, pre-multiplying by (RT)−1 gives

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb.

Finally, since R is invertible, pre-multiplying by R−1 gives

R−1⋅Rx=R−1⋅QTbx=R−1QTb.

Therefore, the missing part of the equation is R−1.
question.knowledge_point: Identifying an Expression for a Least-Squares Solution in Terms of the Matrices Q and R

solution.reasoning: Because Q^TQ=I, the normal equations reduce to Rx=Q^Tb. The independent columns of A ensure R is invertible, so x=R^{-1}Q^Tb. Thus option e is mathematically correct. The captured example establishes Rx=Q^Tb but does not explicitly state the current missing factor or reveal this question's grading key.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem:
$$
x=\bbox[5px,border:1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,{Q}^{T}\,b
$$

Let $A=QR$  be a QR decomposition of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, and the expression above gives the least-squares solution of $Ax=b.$ What is the missing part of the equation?
feedback.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Then, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $R$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by ${R}^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{-1}\cdot Rx & ={R}^{-1}\cdot {Q}^{T}b \\ x & ={R}^{-1}\,\,{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing part of the equation is ${R}^{-1}.$

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying an Expression for a Least-Squares Solution in Terms of the Matrices Q and R
last_observation.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Then, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $R$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by ${R}^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{-1}\cdot Rx & ={R}^{-1}\cdot {Q}^{T}b \\ x & =\bbox[6px,border:1px solid black]{\,\phantom{|}\,\,{R}^{-1}\,}\,{Q}^{T}\,b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are ${R}^{-1}$ and ${Q}^{T}.$

question.html:
Question 3
?

x=AAb

Let A=QR be a QR decomposition of an m×n matrix A with linearly independent columns, and the expression above gives the least-squares solution of Ax=b. From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?

a
R−1 and Q
b
R and QT
c
Q and R−1
d
Q and R
e
R−1 and QT
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the normal equation

ATAx=ATb.

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

Since Q has orthonormal columns, QTQ=I, and we get

RTRx=RTQTb.

Then, since RT is invertible, pre-multiplying by (RT)−1 gives

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb

Finally, since R is invertible, pre-multiplying by R−1 gives

R−1⋅Rx=R−1⋅QTbx=|R−1QTb.

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are R−1 and QT.

solution.reasoning: The normal equations and Q^TQ=I give Rx=Q^Tb. Since R is invertible, x=R^{-1}Q^Tb, so the missing factors are R^{-1} and Q^T, in that order: option e. The captured example gives Rx=Q^Tb with different blank positions; it does not explicitly give the current answer or grading key.

feedback.html:
Question 3
?

x=AAb

Let A=QR be a QR decomposition of an m×n matrix A with linearly independent columns, and the expression above gives the least-squares solution of Ax=b. From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?

a
R−1 and Q
b
R and QT
c
Q and R−1
d
Q and R
e
R−1 and QT
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the normal equation

ATAx=ATb.

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

Since Q has orthonormal columns, QTQ=I, and we get

RTRx=RTQTb.

Then, since RT is invertible, pre-multiplying by (RT)−1 gives

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb

Finally, since R is invertible, pre-multiplying by R−1 gives

R−1⋅Rx=R−1⋅QTbx=|R−1QTb.

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are R−1 and QT.
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying an Expression for a Least-Squares Solution in Terms of the Matrices Q and R

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
$$
R\,\bbox[5px,border:1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}={Q}^{T}\,\bbox[5px,border:1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}
$$

Let $A=QR$  be a QR decomposition of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, and the matrix equation above gives the least-squares solution of $Ax=b.$ From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?
question.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ R\,\,x & ={Q}^{T}\,\,b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are $x$ and $b.$

Question 4
?

RA=QTA

Let A=QR be a QR decomposition of an m×n matrix A with linearly independent columns, and the matrix equation above gives the least-squares solution of Ax=b. From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?

a
x and bT
b
b and x
c
x and 1‖b‖⋅b
d
1‖b‖⋅b and x
e
x and b
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the normal equation

ATAx=ATb.

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

Since Q has orthonormal columns, QTQ=I, and we get

RTRx=RTQTb.

Finally, since RT is invertible, pre-multiplying by (RT)−1 gives

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb.

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are x and b.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying an Expression for a Least-Squares Solution in Terms of the Matrices Q and R
last_observation.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ R\,\,x & ={Q}^{T}\,\,b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are $x$ and $b.$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ R\,\,x & ={Q}^{T}\,\,b.\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 4
?

RA=QTA

Let A=QR be a QR decomposition of an m×n matrix A with linearly independent columns, and the matrix equation above gives the least-squares solution of Ax=b. From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?

a
x and bT
b
b and x
c
x and 1‖b‖⋅b
d
1‖b‖⋅b and x
e
x and b
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the normal equation

ATAx=ATb.

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

Since Q has orthonormal columns, QTQ=I, and we get

RTRx=RTQTb.

Finally, since RT is invertible, pre-multiplying by (RT)−1 gives

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb.

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are x and b.
question.knowledge_point: Identifying an Expression for a Least-Squares Solution in Terms of the Matrices Q and R

solution.reasoning: Substituting A=QR into the normal equations and using Q^TQ=I gives R^TRx=R^TQ^Tb. Cancelling invertible R^T yields Rx=Q^Tb, so the blanks are x and b: option e. The captured worked example explicitly supports this equation, although the current question's grading key is not captured.

feedback.html:
Question 4
?

RA=QTA

Let A=QR be a QR decomposition of an m×n matrix A with linearly independent columns, and the matrix equation above gives the least-squares solution of Ax=b. From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?

a
x and bT
b
b and x
c
x and 1‖b‖⋅b
d
1‖b‖⋅b and x
e
x and b
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the normal equation

ATAx=ATb.

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

Since Q has orthonormal columns, QTQ=I, and we get

RTRx=RTQTb.

Finally, since RT is invertible, pre-multiplying by (RT)−1 gives

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb.

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are x and b.
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying an Expression for a Least-Squares Solution in Terms of the Matrices Q and R

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
$$
x=\bbox[5px,border:1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,{Q}^{T}\,\bbox[5px,border:1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}
$$

Let $A=QR$  be a QR decomposition of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, and the expression above gives the least-squares solution of $Ax=b.$ From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?
question.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Then, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $R$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by ${R}^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{-1}\cdot Rx & ={R}^{-1}\cdot {Q}^{T}b \\ x & =\bbox[4px,border:1px solid black]{{R}^{-1}\phantom{|}}\,\,{Q}^{T}\,\,b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are ${R}^{-1}$ and $b.$

x=AQTA

Let A=QR be a QR decomposition of an m×n matrix A with linearly independent columns, and the expression above gives the least-squares solution of Ax=b. From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?

a
bT and A
b
AT and b
c
R and b
d
R−1 and b
e
bT and R

Correct

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the normal equation

ATAx=ATb.

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

RTRx=RTQTb.

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb.

R−1⋅Rx=R−1⋅QTbx=R−1|QTb.

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying an Expression for a Least-Squares Solution in Terms of the Matrices Q and R
last_observation.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Then, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $R$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by ${R}^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{-1}\cdot Rx & ={R}^{-1}\cdot {Q}^{T}b \\ x & =\bbox[4px,border:1px solid black]{{R}^{-1}\phantom{|}}\,\,{Q}^{T}\,\,b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are ${R}^{-1}$ and $b.$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$

Then, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

x=AQTA

Let A=QR be a QR decomposition of an m×n matrix A with linearly independent columns, and the expression above gives the least-squares solution of Ax=b. From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?

a
bT and A
b
AT and b
c
R and b
d
R−1 and b
e
bT and R
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the normal equation

ATAx=ATb.

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

Since Q has orthonormal columns, QTQ=I, and we get

RTRx=RTQTb.

Then, since RT is invertible, pre-multiplying by (RT)−1 gives

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb.

Finally, since R is invertible, pre-multiplying by R−1 gives

R−1⋅Rx=R−1⋅QTbx=R−1|QTb.

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are R−1 and b.

solution.reasoning: The normal equations simplify to Rx=Q^Tb because Q^TQ=I and R^T is invertible. Multiplying by R^{-1} gives x=R^{-1}Q^Tb, so the blanks are R^{-1} and b: option d. The captured example does not explicitly state these current missing parts, and no current grading key is captured.

feedback.html:
Question 5
?

x=AQTA

Let A=QR be a QR decomposition of an m×n matrix A with linearly independent columns, and the expression above gives the least-squares solution of Ax=b. From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?

a
bT and A
b
AT and b
c
R and b
d
R−1 and b
e
bT and R
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the normal equation

ATAx=ATb.

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

Since Q has orthonormal columns, QTQ=I, and we get

RTRx=RTQTb.

Then, since RT is invertible, pre-multiplying by (RT)−1 gives

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb.

Finally, since R is invertible, pre-multiplying by R−1 gives

R−1⋅Rx=R−1⋅QTbx=R−1|QTb.

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are R−1 and b.
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying an Expression for a Least-Squares Solution in Terms of the Matrices Q and R

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$
Q=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}],\,R=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 6 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 6 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}33 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}=33 \\ 2{x}_{2}=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-3.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-5(-3) & =33 \\ 3{x}_{1} & =18 \\ {x}_{1} & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Given the QR decomposition A=QR, find the least-squares solution to Ax=b, where Q=13[2−1221−2],R=13[3−502],b=[865].

a
[−32]
b
[2−3]
c
[−3−6]
d
[6−3]
e
[56]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

ATAx=ATb

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

Since Q has orthonormal columns, QTQ=I, and we get

RTRx=RTQTb.

Finally, since RT is invertible, pre-multiplying by (RT)−1 gives

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb.

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

13[3−502]⏞Rx=13[221−12−2]⏞QT[865]⏞b[3−502]x=[33−6]

which gives the system

{3x1−5x2=332x2=−6.

From the second equation, we get x2=−3. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

3x1−5(−3)=333x1=18x1=6.

Therefore, the least-squares solution to Ax=b is [6−3].

last_observation.name: Question 6
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System Given a QR Factorization
last_observation.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 6 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}33 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}=33 \\ 2{x}_{2}=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-3.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-5(-3) & =33 \\ 3{x}_{1} & =18 \\ {x}_{1} & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$

EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

ATAx=ATb

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

Since Q has orthonormal columns, QTQ=I, and we get

RTRx=RTQTb.

Finally, since RT is invertible, pre-multiplying by (RT)−1 gives

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb.

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

13[3−502]⏞Rx=13[221−12−2]⏞QT[865]⏞b[3−502]x=[33−6]

which gives the system

{3x1−5x2=332x2=−6.

From the second equation, we get x2=−3. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

3x1−5(−3)=333x1=18x1=6.

Therefore, the least-squares solution to Ax=b is [6−3].

solution.reasoning: Q^Tb=(11,-2)^T. Solving Rx=Q^Tb gives (2/3)x_2=-2, hence x_2=-3; then x_1-(5/3)(-3)=11 gives x_1=6. Thus option d is mathematically correct. The captured worked example uses different matrices, so it does not establish MA's answer for this question.

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

ATAx=ATb

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

Since Q has orthonormal columns, QTQ=I, and we get

RTRx=RTQTb.

Finally, since RT is invertible, pre-multiplying by (RT)−1 gives

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb.

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

13[3−502]⏞Rx=13[221−12−2]⏞QT[865]⏞b[3−502]x=[33−6]

which gives the system

{3x1−5x2=332x2=−6.

From the second equation, we get x2=−3. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

Therefore, the least-squares solution to Ax=b is [6−3].

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$
Q=\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}-7 & 24 \\ -24 & -7\end{aligned}],\,R=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 10\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ is orthogonal, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}-7 & -24 \\ 24 & -7\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 10\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}-11 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-11 \\ {x}_{2}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-(2) & =-11 \\ {x}_{1} & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

last_observation.name: Question 7
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System Given a QR Factorization
last_observation.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ is orthogonal, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}-7 & -24 \\ 24 & -7\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 10\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}-11 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-11 \\ {x}_{2}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-(2) & =-11 \\ {x}_{1} & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

which gives the system

{x1−x2=−11x2=2.

From the second equation, we get x2=2. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

x1−(2)=−11x1=−9.

Therefore, the least-squares solution to Ax=b is [−92].

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$
Q=\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & \sqrt{2} \\ 3\sqrt{5} & 3\sqrt{2} \\ 2\sqrt{5} & -5\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,R=\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 3\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{2} & 3\sqrt{2} & -5\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}-10\sqrt{5} \\ -10\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2}=-10\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{2}{x}_{2}=-10\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-10.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{5}(-10) & =-10\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5}{x}_{1} & =10\sqrt{5} \\ {x}_{1} & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -10\end{aligned}].$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System Given a QR Factorization
last_observation.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 3\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{2} & 3\sqrt{2} & -5\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}-10\sqrt{5} \\ -10\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2}=-10\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{2}{x}_{2}=-10\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-10.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{5}(-10) & =-10\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5}{x}_{1} & =10\sqrt{5} \\ {x}_{1} & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -10\end{aligned}].$

Question 8
?

Given the QR decomposition A=QR, find the least-squares solution to Ax=b, where Q=170[52353225−52],R=170[52502],b=[−1−30].

a
[1030]
b
[10−10]
c
[−1030]
d
[2030]
e
[−1020]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

ATAx=ATb

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

Since Q has orthonormal columns, QTQ=I, and we get

RTRx=RTQTb.

Finally, since RT is invertible, pre-multiplying by (RT)−1 gives

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb.

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

170[52502]⏞Rx=170[53525232−52]⏞QT[−1−30]⏞b[52502]x=[−105−102]

which gives the system

{5x1+25x2=−1052x2=−102.

From the second equation, we get x2=−10. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

5x1+25(−10)=−1055x1=105x1=10.

Therefore, the least-squares solution to Ax=b is [10−10].

solution.reasoning: Q^Tb=(-10\sqrt{5},-10\sqrt{2})^T/\sqrt{70}. Solving Rx=Q^Tb cancels the common factor 1/\sqrt{70}, giving x_2=-10 and x_1+2x_2=-10. Thus x_1=10, so option b is mathematically correct. The captured example uses different matrices; no current answer key or grade is provided.

question.name: Question 9
question.problem:
Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$
Q=\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}8 & -1 \\ 4 & 4 \\ -1 & 8\end{aligned}],\,R=\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}9 & 8 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}9 & 8 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}8 & 4 & -1 \\ -1 & 4 & 8\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}9 & 8 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}9{x}_{1}+8{x}_{2}=-9 \\ {x}_{2}=9.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=9.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}_{1}+8(9) & =-9 \\ 9{x}_{1} & =-81 \\ {x}_{1} & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 9\end{aligned}].$

last_observation.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}9 & 8 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}8 & 4 & -1 \\ -1 & 4 & 8\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}9 & 8 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}9{x}_{1}+8{x}_{2}=-9 \\ {x}_{2}=9.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=9.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}_{1}+8(9) & =-9 \\ 9{x}_{1} & =-81 \\ {x}_{1} & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 9\end{aligned}].$

$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 9\end{aligned}].$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$
Q=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}1 & \sqrt{2} \\ 2 & -\sqrt{2} \\ 1 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,R=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ \sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}20 \\ -4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=20 \\ 2\sqrt{2}{x}_{2}=-4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-(-2) & =20 \\ 2{x}_{1} & =18 \\ {x}_{1} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$

last_observation.name: Question 10
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System Given a QR Factorization
last_observation.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ \sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}20 \\ -4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=20 \\ 2\sqrt{2}{x}_{2}=-4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-(-2) & =20 \\ 2{x}_{1} & =18 \\ {x}_{1} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$

question.problem:

$$
Q=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}1 & \sqrt{2} \\ 2 & -\sqrt{2} \\ 1 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,R=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ \sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}20 \\ -4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=20 \\ 2\sqrt{2}{x}_{2}=-4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-(-2) & =20 \\ 2{x}_{1} & =18 \\ {x}_{1} & =9.\end{aligned}

Question 10
?

Given the QR decomposition A=QR, find the least-squares solution to Ax=b, where Q=16[122−212],R=16[2−1022],b=[282].

a
[92]
b
[9−2]
c
[3−2]
d
[−32]
e
[23]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

ATAx=ATb

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

Since Q has orthonormal columns, QTQ=I, and we get

RTRx=RTQTb.

Finally, since RT is invertible, pre-multiplying by (RT)−1 gives

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb.

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

16[2−1022]⏞Rx=16[1212−22]⏞QT[282]⏞b[2−1022]x=[20−42]

which gives the system

{2x1−x2=2022x2=−42.

From the second equation, we get x2=−2. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

2x1−(−2)=202x1=18x1=9.

Therefore, the least-squares solution to Ax=b is [9−2].

solution.reasoning: Since Q has orthonormal columns, solve Rx=Q^Tb. Here Q^Tb=(20,-4\sqrt{2})^T/\sqrt{6}. Cancelling 1/\sqrt{6} gives 2\sqrt{2}x_2=-4\sqrt{2} and 2x_1-x_2=20, so x_2=-2 and x_1=9. Option b is mathematically correct. The captured example uses different matrices; the current MA key is not captured.

\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=20 \\ 2\sqrt{2}{x}_{2}=-4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-(-2) & =20 \\ 2{x}_{1} & =18 \\ {x}_{1} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$

Question 10
?

Given the QR decomposition A=QR, find the least-squares solution to Ax=b, where Q=16[122−212],R=16[2−1022],b=[282].

a
[92]
b
[9−2]
c
[3−2]
d
[−32]
e
[23]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

ATAx=ATb

Substituting A=QR, we obtain

ATAx=ATb(QR)TQRx=(QR)TbRT(QTQ)Rx=RTQTb.

Since Q has orthonormal columns, QTQ=I, and we get

RTRx=RTQTb.

Finally, since RT is invertible, pre-multiplying by (RT)−1 gives

(RT)−1⋅RTRx=(RT)−1⋅RTQTbRx=QTb.

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

16[2−1022]⏞Rx=16[1212−22]⏞QT[282]⏞b[2−1022]x=[20−42]

which gives the system

{2x1−x2=2022x2=−42.

From the second equation, we get x2=−2. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

2x1−(−2)=202x1=18x1=9.

Therefore, the least-squares solution to Ax=b is [9−2].

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Evaluate $z=\frac{2y-x}{{x}^{3}-{y}^{2}-4}$ at the point $(2,-2).$
questions.worked_solution:
To evaluate our multivariable function at the point $(2,-2),$ we substitute $x=2$ and $y=-2$ into the function expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,{|}_{(2,-2)} & =\frac{2y-x}{{x}^{3}-{y}^{2}-4}\,{|}_{(2,-2)} \\  & =\frac{2(-2)-2}{{2}^{3}-(-2)^{2}-4} \\  & =\frac{-4-2}{8-4-4} \\  & =\frac{(-6)}{0},\end{aligned}
$$

which is undefined.

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Evaluate $z={2}^{-x}+\frac{1}{y}$ at the point $(2,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
To evaluate our multivariable function at the point $(2,2),$ we substitute $x=2$ and $y=2$ into the function expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,{|}_{(2,2)} & =({2}^{-x}+\frac{1}{y}){|}_{(2,2)} \\  & ={2}^{-2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The function $f(x,y)$ is defined as 

$$
f(x,y)=x\operatorname{arccos}⁡(y+1).
$$

Evaluate this function at the point $(-3,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
To evaluate our multivariable function at the point $(-3,1),$ we substitute $x=-3$ and $y=1$ into the function expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-3,1) & =x\operatorname{arccos}⁡(y+1)\,{|}_{(-3,1)} \\  & =-3\operatorname{arccos}⁡(1+1) \\  & =-3\operatorname{arccos}⁡2,\end{aligned}
$$

which is undefined.

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Evaluate $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x-2y+4)$ at the point $(-4,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
To evaluate our multivariable function at the point $(-4,1),$ we substitute $x=-4$ and $y=1$ into the function expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,{|}_{(-4,1)} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x-2y+4)\,{|}_{(-4,1)} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3(-4)-2(1)+4) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-12-2+4) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-10),\end{aligned}
$$

which is undefined.

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{2x+y}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
2x+y\ne 0
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,2x+y\ne 0\}.
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}-1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
{x}^{2}-1\ne 0\,⟹\,{x}^{2}\ne 1
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}\ne 1\}.
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem: Find the domain of the function $z=\frac{\sqrt{y-{x}^{2}}}{2x-y}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

- the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y-{x}^{2}\ge 0 \\ 2x-y\ne 0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}y\ge {x}^{2} \\ y\ne 2x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y\ge {x}^{2},\,y\ne 2x\}.
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 0
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 0\}.
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem: Find the domain of the function $z=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

- the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<1\}.
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem: Find the domain of the function $z=\frac{{x}^{3}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities: 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\ne 0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0 \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0,\,{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 1\}.
$$

\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,-1<x<1,\,y\ne 0\}.

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡y}{{x}^{3}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities: 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y>0 \\ {x}^{3}\ne 0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}y>0 \\ x\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y>0,\,x\ne 0\}.
$$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-y)}{{e}^{x}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

Notice that ${e}^{x}>0$ for all $x.$ Therefore, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y>0\,⟹\,x>y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,x>y\}.
$$
