questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-y)}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities: 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x-y>0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x-y)\ne 0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}x-y>0 \\ x-y\ne 1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,x-y>0,\,x-y\ne 1\}.
$$

questions.name: Question 16
questions.problem: Which of the following shaded regions corresponds to the domain of the function $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2})?$
questions.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
4-{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}>0\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}<4\,⟹\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}<1
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}<1\}.
$$

Since the expression involves the $<$ sign, the curve is *not* part of the domain. Therefore, we draw the dashed curve $\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}<1$ and shade the region *inside* the curve.

The resulting domain is as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246566/assets/59ac983361be7dd9a991e1cf134e7193256891a5587eab6bff5edf906fef3688.png)

questions.name: Question 17
questions.problem: Which of the following shaded regions corresponds to the domain of the function $g(x,y)=\frac{1}{{x}^{3}+y}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
{x}^{3}+y\ne 0\,⟹\,y\ne -{x}^{3}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y\ne -{x}^{3}\}.
$$

Since the expression involves the $\ne $ sign, the line is *not* part of the domain. Therefore, we draw the dashed curve $y=-{x}^{3}$ and shade *above* and *below* the curve.

questions.name: Question 18
questions.problem: Which of the following shaded regions corresponds to the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{y+{x}^{2}}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

$$
y+{x}^{2}\ge 0\,⟹\,y\ge -{x}^{2}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y\ge -{x}^{2}\}.
$$

Since the inequality involves the $\ge $ sign, the curve is part of the domain. Therefore, we draw a solid curve $y=-{x}^{2}$ and shade the area *outside* the curve.

The resulting domain is as follows:

questions.problem: Which of the following shaded regions corresponds to the domain of the function $g(x,y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-y}}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression under the square root is non-negative, and

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
x-y>0\,⟹\,y<x
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y<x\}.
$$

Since the inequality involves the $>$ sign, the line is not part of the domain. Therefore, we draw a dashed line $y=x$ and shade the area *below* the line.

The resulting domain is as follows:

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Evaluating a Two-Variable Function
canonical_examples.problem:
The function $f(x,y)$ is defined as 

$$
f(x,y) = y^2 - \log_3(x - 7).
$$

Evaluate this function at the point $(10,3).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To evaluate our multivariable function at the point $(10,3),$ we substitute $x = 10$ and $y = 3$ into the function expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(10,3) & =({y}^{2}-{log}_{3}⁡(x-7)){|}_{(10,3)} \\  & ={3}^{2}-{log}_{3}⁡(10-7) \\  & =9-{log}_{3}⁡(3) \\  & =9-1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(10,3)=8.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    The Domain of a Function Involving Reciprocals and Radicals
canonical_examples.problem: Find the domain of the function $z = \dfrac {\sqrt {y+1}}{x+y}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

- the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246566/assets/5b534c95f0105645223836a1b44f38db3f14bf61425b6f53ee7815742a86a068.svg)

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\big\{ (x,y)\in\mathbb R^2 \,:\, y \geq -1, \: y \neq -x \big\}.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    The Domain of a Function Containing Exponential, Logarithmic, and Trigonometric Functions
canonical_examples.problem: Find the domain of the function $z= \dfrac{\ln (2x+y)}{\sqrt{x}}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive,

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

- the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities: 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2x+y>0 \\ x>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\big\{(x, y)\in\mathbb R^2 \,:\, 2x+y >0, \: x > 0 \big\}.
$$

Example: 
                    Sketching the Domain of a Multivariable Function
canonical_examples.problem: Sketch the domain of $g(x,y)=\dfrac{1}{\ln(x+y)}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246566/assets/68197b31685c209b98416f8e137dca514d7fbbf382d400688d411fa633ffd3c0.svg)

Therefore, the domain is

$$
D = \left \{ (x,y)\in\mathbb R^2 \, : \, y \gt -x, \, y \neq 1-x \right \}.
$$

Now, we plot the corresponding domain. 

- Starting with $y> -x,$ we draw a dashed line $y=-x$ and shade the region *above* the line.

- Then, we draw a dashed line $y=1-x$ through the shaded region.

The resulting domain is as follows:

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Sketching the Domain of a Multivariable Function

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
A function $f(x,y)$ of two variables is a rule that maps each pair of numbers $(x,y)\in D$ to a unique real number. Under this notation, $D\subseteq \mathbb R^2$ is the **domain** of $f.$

For instance, consider the following two-variable function: 

$$
f(x,y) = \dfrac{\sin(xy)}{\sqrt{x-1}}
$$

We can evaluate this function by substituting concrete pairs of numbers for $x$ and $y{:}$

- Let's evaluate $f(x,y)$ at the point $(2, \pi).$ To do that, we substitute $x=2$ and $y=\pi$ into the function expression: 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,\pi ) & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)}{\sqrt{x-1}}{|}_{(2,\pi )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \pi )}{\sqrt{2-1}} \\  & =\frac{0}{1} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(2,\pi)$ returned a unique real number, this means that $(2,\pi)$ belongs to the domain of $f,$ i.e., $(2,\pi)\in D.$

- Let's now try to evaluate $f(x,y)$ at the point $(0, \pi).$ To do that, we substitute $x=0$ and $y=\pi$ into the function expression: 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,\pi ) & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)}{\sqrt{x-1}}{|}_{(0,\pi )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(0\cdot \pi )}{\sqrt{0-1}} \\  & =\frac{0}{\sqrt{-1}}\end{aligned}
$$

which is undefined over the real numbers.

Since $f(0,\pi)$ did not return a unique *real* number, this means that $(0,\pi)\notin D.$

We can also have functions of three variables $f(x,y,z),$ functions of four variables, $f(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4),$ etc. There is no limit to the number of variables a function can have. Functions with more than one variable are called **multivariable functions.**

tutorials.title: Introduction

tutorials.name: The Domain and Range of a Two-Variable Function
tutorials.problem:
The **domain** of a multivariable function is the set of points where the function is defined. 

For example, consider the function 

$$
z = f(x,y) =  \sqrt{1 -x^2 -y^2}.
$$

The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the expression under the square root is non-negative. As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
1 - x^2 - y^2 \geq 0 
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x^2 + y^2 \leq 1
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y)\in\mathbb R^2 \,:\, x^2 + y^2 \leq 1 \big\}.
$$

Geometrically, the domain of our function is a disc of radius $1$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane, as shown on the left diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246566/assets/8642db9fd933ec2f15c6712c713cfaec8fb20052066dcca3915904190d3551fa.png)

Each point in this domain is uniquely mapped to a real number $z.$ Possible values of $z$ can be visualized on a separate axis (depicted by the diagram on the right). 

If $(x,y)$ is allowed to run over the entire domain, the set of points on the $z$-axis where the values of $f(x,y)$ land is called the **range** of the function. For this function, the range is $z\in [0,1].$

Note the following:

- When discussing a function's domain, we usually refer to the so-called **natural domain**, the largest set of values for which the function is defined.

- We can also *restrict* the domain of a function to a subset of the natural domain. For example, we might restrict the domain of $f$ to all values of $y$ in the upper-half plane. In this case, we'd write

$$
f(x,y) =  \sqrt{1 -x^2 -y^2}, \quad (x,y)\in D, \quad D = \big\{ (x,y)\in\mathbb R^2 \,:\, x^2 + y^2 \leq 1, \: y\geq 0 \big\}.
$$

This gives a domain/range diagram that looks as follows.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246566/assets/fbab832d984232b0b3b951579e5ee2727e92c9f4bf496d4fffe82f7230cfbb14.png)

In this case, restricting the domain does not affect the range. However, in general, restricting the domain *will* affect the range.

f(x,y) =  \sqrt{1 -x^2 -y^2}, \quad (x,y)\in D, \quad D = \big\{ (x,y)\in\mathbb R^2 \,:\, x^2 + y^2 \leq 1, \: y\geq 0 \big\}.
$$

This gives a domain/range diagram that looks as follows.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246566/assets/fbab832d984232b0b3b951579e5ee2727e92c9f4bf496d4fffe82f7230cfbb14.png)

In this case, restricting the domain does not affect the range. However, in general, restricting the domain *will* affect the range.

tutorials.name: The Graph of a Two-Variable Function
tutorials.problem:
Another way of visualizing a two-variable function is to draw its graph as a **surface** in a three-dimensional coordinate system. 

For example, consider the function

$$
z = f(x,y) = x^2 +y^2, \quad (x,y)\in D
$$

where the (restricted) domain is given by the unit disc 

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y)\in\mathbb R^2 \: : \: x^2+y^2 \leq 1 \big\}.
$$

The graph of $f$ is a surface that consists of all the points with coordinates

$$
(x, \, y, \, f(x,y)), \quad (x,y) \in D,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246566/assets/a3c9c7eca49a0f828e53c0775afac16335033c1a8881367e49098bf7125ee2e6.png)

  

Notice that range of $f$ is represented by the interval $R=[0,1]$ on the vertical $z$-axis. It consists of the possible $z$-coordinates of the points on our surface.

tutorial.name: Introduction
tutorial.problem:
A function $f(x,y)$ of two variables is a rule that maps each pair of numbers $(x,y)\in D$ to a unique real number. Under this notation, $D\subseteq \mathbb R^2$ is the **domain** of $f.$

For instance, consider the following two-variable function: 

$$
f(x,y) = \dfrac{\sin(xy)}{\sqrt{x-1}}
$$

We can evaluate this function by substituting concrete pairs of numbers for $x$ and $y{:}$

- Let's evaluate $f(x,y)$ at the point $(2, \pi).$ To do that, we substitute $x=2$ and $y=\pi$ into the function expression: 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,\pi ) & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)}{\sqrt{x-1}}{|}_{(2,\pi )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \pi )}{\sqrt{2-1}} \\  & =\frac{0}{1} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(2,\pi)$ returned a unique real number, this means that $(2,\pi)$ belongs to the domain of $f,$ i.e., $(2,\pi)\in D.$

- Let's now try to evaluate $f(x,y)$ at the point $(0, \pi).$ To do that, we substitute $x=0$ and $y=\pi$ into the function expression: 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,\pi ) & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)}{\sqrt{x-1}}{|}_{(0,\pi )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(0\cdot \pi )}{\sqrt{0-1}} \\  & =\frac{0}{\sqrt{-1}}\end{aligned}
$$

which is undefined over the real numbers.

Since $f(0,\pi)$ did not return a unique *real* number, this means that $(0,\pi)\notin D.$

We can also have functions of three variables $f(x,y,z),$ functions of four variables, $f(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4),$ etc. There is no limit to the number of variables a function can have. Functions with more than one variable are called **multivariable functions.**

observed_steps.name: Example: Evaluating a Two-Variable Function
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To evaluate our multivariable function at the point $(10,3),$ we substitute $x = 10$ and $y = 3$ into the function expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(10,3) & =({y}^{2}-{log}_{3}⁡(x-7)){|}_{(10,3)} \\  & ={3}^{2}-{log}_{3}⁡(10-7) \\  & =9-{log}_{3}⁡(3) \\  & =9-1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(10,3)=8.$

tutorial.name: The Domain and Range of a Two-Variable Function
tutorial.problem:
The **domain** of a multivariable function is the set of points where the function is defined. 

For example, consider the function 

$$
z = f(x,y) =  \sqrt{1 -x^2 -y^2}.
$$

The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the expression under the square root is non-negative. As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
1 - x^2 - y^2 \geq 0 
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x^2 + y^2 \leq 1
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y)\in\mathbb R^2 \,:\, x^2 + y^2 \leq 1 \big\}.
$$

Geometrically, the domain of our function is a disc of radius $1$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane, as shown on the left diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246566/assets/8642db9fd933ec2f15c6712c713cfaec8fb20052066dcca3915904190d3551fa.png)

Each point in this domain is uniquely mapped to a real number $z.$ Possible values of $z$ can be visualized on a separate axis (depicted by the diagram on the right). 

If $(x,y)$ is allowed to run over the entire domain, the set of points on the $z$-axis where the values of $f(x,y)$ land is called the **range** of the function. For this function, the range is $z\in [0,1].$

Note the following:

- When discussing a function's domain, we usually refer to the so-called **natural domain**, the largest set of values for which the function is defined.

- We can also *restrict* the domain of a function to a subset of the natural domain. For example, we might restrict the domain of $f$ to all values of $y$ in the upper-half plane. In this case, we'd write

$$
f(x,y) =  \sqrt{1 -x^2 -y^2}, \quad (x,y)\in D, \quad D = \big\{ (x,y)\in\mathbb R^2 \,:\, x^2 + y^2 \leq 1, \: y\geq 0 \big\}.
$$

This gives a domain/range diagram that looks as follows.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246566/assets/fbab832d984232b0b3b951579e5ee2727e92c9f4bf496d4fffe82f7230cfbb14.png)

In this case, restricting the domain does not affect the range. However, in general, restricting the domain *will* affect the range.

tutorial.name: The Graph of a Two-Variable Function
tutorial.problem:
Another way of visualizing a two-variable function is to draw its graph as a **surface** in a three-dimensional coordinate system. 

For example, consider the function

$$
z = f(x,y) = x^2 +y^2, \quad (x,y)\in D
$$

where the (restricted) domain is given by the unit disc 

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y)\in\mathbb R^2 \: : \: x^2+y^2 \leq 1 \big\}.
$$

The graph of $f$ is a surface that consists of all the points with coordinates

$$
(x, \, y, \, f(x,y)), \quad (x,y) \in D,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246566/assets/a3c9c7eca49a0f828e53c0775afac16335033c1a8881367e49098bf7125ee2e6.png)

  

Notice that range of $f$ is represented by the interval $R=[0,1]$ on the vertical $z$-axis. It consists of the possible $z$-coordinates of the points on our surface.

observed_steps.name: Question 6
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: The Domain of a Function Involving Reciprocals and Radicals
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
2x+y\ne 0
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,2x+y\ne 0\}.
$$

?

Find the domain of the function f(x,y)=12x+y.

a
{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y≠−1}
b
The domain is the entire xy−plane
c
{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y≠0}
d
{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y<1}
e
{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y>0}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following condition is satisfied:

  • The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

2x+y≠0

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y≠0}.

Question 7
?

Find the domain of the function f(x,y)=yx2−1.

a
{(x,y)∈R2:x2>1}
b
{(x,y)∈R2:x2>0}
c
 The domain is the entire xy−plane
d
{(x,y)∈R2:x2≠1}
e
{(x,y)∈R2:x2=1}
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following condition is satisfied:

  • The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

x2−1≠0⟹x2≠1

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:x2≠1}.
question.knowledge_point: The Domain of a Function Involving Reciprocals and Radicals

observed_steps.name: Question 8
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: The Domain of a Function Involving Reciprocals and Radicals
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

- the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y-{x}^{2}\ge 0 \\ 2x-y\ne 0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}y\ge {x}^{2} \\ y\ne 2x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y\ge {x}^{2},\,y\ne 2x\}.
$$

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y\ge {x}^{2},\,y\ne 2x\}.

question.html:
Question 8
?

Find the domain of the function z=y−x22x−y.

a
{(x,y)∈R2:y≥x2,y>2x}
b
{(x,y)∈R2:y≥x2,y≠2x}
c
{(x,y)∈R2:y=x2,y>2x}
d
The domain is the entire xy−plane
e
{(x,y)∈R2:y<x2,y≠2x}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

  • the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

{y−x2≥02x−y≠0⟹{y≥x2y≠2x

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:y≥x2,y≠2x}.

observed_steps.name: Question 9
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: The Domain of a Function Involving Reciprocals and Radicals
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 0
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 0\}.
$$

question.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}.$
question.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 0
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 0\}.
$$

question.html:
Question 9
?

Find the domain of the function f(x,y)=x2+y2x2−y2.

a
The domain is the entire xy−plane
b
{(x,y)∈R2:x2+y≠0}
c
{(x,y)∈R2:x2−y2≠1}
d
{(x,y)∈R2:x2−y2≠0}
e
{(x,y)∈R2:x2−y2=0}
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following condition is satisfied:

  • The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

x2−y2≠0

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:x2−y2≠0}.
question.knowledge_point: The Domain of a Function Involving Reciprocals and Radicals

observed_steps.name: Question 10
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: The Domain of a Function Involving Reciprocals and Radicals
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

- the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<1\}.
$$

question.problem: Find the domain of the function $z=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}.$
question.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

- the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<1\}.
$$

Find the domain of the function z=11−x2−y2.

a
{(x,y)∈R2:x2+y2<0}
b
{(x,y)∈R2:x2+y2≤1}
c
{(x,y)∈R2:x2+y2>1}
d
The domain is the entire xy-plane
e
{(x,y)∈R2:x2+y2<1}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

  • the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

1−x2−y2>0⟹x2+y2<1

Therefore, the domain is {(x,y)∈R2:x2+y2<1}.

Find the domain of the function f(x,y)=ln2⁡yx3.

a
The domain is the entire xy-plane
b
{(x,y)∈R2:y>0}
c
{(x,y)∈R2:y≥0,x≠0}
d
{(x,y)∈R2:y≠0,x≠0}
e
{(x,y)∈R2:y>0,x≠0}
Submit

EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

  • the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

{y>0x3≠0⟹{y>0x≠0

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:y>0,x≠0}.

observed_steps.name: Question 14
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: The Domain of a Function Containing Exponential, Logarithmic, and Trigonometric Functions
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

Notice that ${e}^{x}>0$ for all $x.$ Therefore, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y>0\,⟹\,x>y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,x>y\}.
$$

question.name: Question 14
question.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-y)}{{e}^{x}}.$
question.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

Notice that ${e}^{x}>0$ for all $x.$ Therefore, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y>0\,⟹\,x>y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,x>y\}.
$$

Question 14
?

Find the domain of the function f(x,y)=ln⁡(x−y)ex.

a
{(x,y)∈R2:x≠y}
b
The domain is the entire xy-plane
c
{(x,y)∈R2:x>y}
d
{(x,y)∈R2:x≠y,x≠0}
e
{(x,y)∈R2:x>y,x≠0}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

  • the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

Notice that ex>0 for all x. Therefore, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

x−y>0⟹x>y Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:x>y}.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Sketching the Domain of a Multivariable Function
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
4-{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}>0\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}<4\,⟹\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}<1
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}<1\}.
$$

Since the expression involves the $<$ sign, the curve is *not* part of the domain. Therefore, we draw the dashed curve $\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}<1$ and shade the region *inside* the curve.

The resulting domain is as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14246566/assets/59ac983361be7dd9a991e1cf134e7193256891a5587eab6bff5edf906fef3688.png)

question.name: Question 16
question.problem: Which of the following shaded regions corresponds to the domain of the function $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2})?$
question.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
4-{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}>0\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}<4\,⟹\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}<1
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}<1\}.
$$

Since the expression involves the $<$ sign, the curve is *not* part of the domain. Therefore, we draw the dashed curve $\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}<1$ and shade the region *inside* the curve.

The resulting domain is as follows:

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Evaluate $z=\frac{2y-x}{{x}^{3}-{y}^{2}-4}$ at the point $(2,-2).$
question.worked_solution:
To evaluate our multivariable function at the point $(2,-2),$ we substitute $x=2$ and $y=-2$ into the function expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,{|}_{(2,-2)} & =\frac{2y-x}{{x}^{3}-{y}^{2}-4}\,{|}_{(2,-2)} \\  & =\frac{2(-2)-2}{{2}^{3}-(-2)^{2}-4} \\  & =\frac{-4-2}{8-4-4} \\  & =\frac{(-6)}{0},\end{aligned}
$$

which is undefined.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Evaluate $z={2}^{-x}+\frac{1}{y}$ at the point $(2,2).$
question.worked_solution:
To evaluate our multivariable function at the point $(2,2),$ we substitute $x=2$ and $y=2$ into the function expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,{|}_{(2,2)} & =({2}^{-x}+\frac{1}{y}){|}_{(2,2)} \\  & ={2}^{-2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,{|}_{(-4,1)} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x-2y+4)\,{|}_{(-4,1)} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3(-4)-2(1)+4) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-12-2+4) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-10),\end{aligned}

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{2x+y}.$
question.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
2x+y\ne 0
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,2x+y\ne 0\}.
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Find the domain of the function f(x,y)=12x+y.

a
{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y≠−1}
b
The domain is the entire xy−plane
c
{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y≠0}
d
{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y<1}
e
{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y>0}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following condition is satisfied:

  • The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

2x+y≠0

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y≠0}.

question.html:
Question 6
?

Find the domain of the function f(x,y)=12x+y.

a
{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y≠−1}
b
The domain is the entire xy−plane
c
{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y≠0}
d
{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y<1}
e
{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y>0}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following condition is satisfied:

  • The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

2x+y≠0

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y≠0}.
question.knowledge_point: The Domain of a Function Involving Reciprocals and Radicals

solution.reasoning: The denominator must be nonzero, so the domain is all real pairs (x,y) satisfying 2x+y≠0, option c. There are no other restrictions. The supplied example concerns a different function; no captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes the current question's key.

feedback.name: Question 6
feedback.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{2x+y}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
2x+y\ne 0
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,2x+y\ne 0\}.
$$

Question 6
?

Find the domain of the function f(x,y)=12x+y.

a
{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y≠−1}
b
The domain is the entire xy−plane
c
{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y≠0}
d
{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y<1}
e
{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y>0}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following condition is satisfied:

  • The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

2x+y≠0

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:2x+y≠0}.

question.name: Question 7
question.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}-1}.$
question.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
{x}^{2}-1\ne 0\,⟹\,{x}^{2}\ne 1
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}\ne 1\}.
$$

 The domain is the entire xy−plane

last_observation.name: Question 7
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: The Domain of a Function Involving Reciprocals and Radicals
last_observation.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
{x}^{2}-1\ne 0\,⟹\,{x}^{2}\ne 1
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}\ne 1\}.
$$

question.html:
Question 7
?

Find the domain of the function f(x,y)=yx2−1.

a
{(x,y)∈R2:x2>1}
b
{(x,y)∈R2:x2>0}
c
 The domain is the entire xy−plane
d
{(x,y)∈R2:x2≠1}
e
{(x,y)∈R2:x2=1}
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following condition is satisfied:

  • The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

x2−1≠0⟹x2≠1

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:x2≠1}.
question.knowledge_point: The Domain of a Function Involving Reciprocals and Radicals

solution.reasoning: The denominator must satisfy x²−1≠0, equivalently x²≠1 (x≠±1), while y can be any real number. Thus option d is correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key; the worked example concerns a different function.

feedback.name: Question 7
feedback.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}-1}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
{x}^{2}-1\ne 0\,⟹\,{x}^{2}\ne 1
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}\ne 1\}.
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem: Find the domain of the function $z=\frac{\sqrt{y-{x}^{2}}}{2x-y}.$
question.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

- the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y-{x}^{2}\ge 0 \\ 2x-y\ne 0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}y\ge {x}^{2} \\ y\ne 2x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y\ge {x}^{2},\,y\ne 2x\}.
$$

Question 8
?

Find the domain of the function z=y−x22x−y.

a
{(x,y)∈R2:y≥x2,y>2x}
b
{(x,y)∈R2:y≥x2,y≠2x}
c
{(x,y)∈R2:y=x2,y>2x}
d
The domain is the entire xy−plane
e
{(x,y)∈R2:y<x2,y≠2x}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

  • the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

{y−x2≥02x−y≠0⟹{y≥x2y≠2x

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:y≥x2,y≠2x}.

last_observation.name: Question 8
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: The Domain of a Function Involving Reciprocals and Radicals
last_observation.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

- the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y-{x}^{2}\ge 0 \\ 2x-y\ne 0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}y\ge {x}^{2} \\ y\ne 2x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y\ge {x}^{2},\,y\ne 2x\}.
$$

question.html:
Question 8
?

Find the domain of the function z=y−x22x−y.

a
{(x,y)∈R2:y≥x2,y>2x}
b
{(x,y)∈R2:y≥x2,y≠2x}
c
{(x,y)∈R2:y=x2,y>2x}
d
The domain is the entire xy−plane
e
{(x,y)∈R2:y<x2,y≠2x}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

  • the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

{y−x2≥02x−y≠0⟹{y≥x2y≠2x

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:y≥x2,y≠2x}.
question.knowledge_point: The Domain of a Function Involving Reciprocals and Radicals

solution.reasoning: The square root requires y−x²≥0, and the denominator requires 2x−y≠0. Thus y≥x² and y≠2x, which is option b. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key; the supplied worked example concerns a different function.

feedback.name: Question 8
feedback.problem: Find the domain of the function $z=\frac{\sqrt{y-{x}^{2}}}{2x-y}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

- the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y-{x}^{2}\ge 0 \\ 2x-y\ne 0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}y\ge {x}^{2} \\ y\ne 2x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y\ge {x}^{2},\,y\ne 2x\}.
$$

a

b

The domain is the entire xy−plane
e
{(x,y)∈R2:y<x2,y≠2x}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

  • the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

{y−x2≥02x−y≠0⟹{y≥x2y≠2x

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:y≥x2,y≠2x}.

question.name: Question 9
question.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}.$
question.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 0
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 0\}.
$$

last_observation.name: Question 9
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: The Domain of a Function Involving Reciprocals and Radicals
last_observation.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 0
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 0\}.
$$

question.html:
Question 9
?

Find the domain of the function f(x,y)=x2+y2x2−y2.

a
The domain is the entire xy−plane
b
{(x,y)∈R2:x2+y≠0}
c
{(x,y)∈R2:x2−y2≠1}
d
{(x,y)∈R2:x2−y2≠0}
e
{(x,y)∈R2:x2−y2=0}
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following condition is satisfied:

  • The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

x2−y2≠0

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:x2−y2≠0}.
question.knowledge_point: The Domain of a Function Involving Reciprocals and Radicals

solution.reasoning: The denominator must be nonzero: x²−y²≠0, equivalently x≠y and x≠−y. The numerator imposes no restrictions, so option d is correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key; the worked example concerns a different function.

feedback.name: Question 9
feedback.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 0
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 0\}.
$$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem: Find the domain of the function $z=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}.$
question.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

- the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<1\}.
$$

last_observation.name: Question 10
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: The Domain of a Function Involving Reciprocals and Radicals
last_observation.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

- the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<1\}.
$$

question.html:
Question 10
?

Find the domain of the function z=11−x2−y2.

a
{(x,y)∈R2:x2+y2<0}
b
{(x,y)∈R2:x2+y2≤1}
c
{(x,y)∈R2:x2+y2>1}
d
The domain is the entire xy-plane
e
{(x,y)∈R2:x2+y2<1}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

  • the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

1−x2−y2>0⟹x2+y2<1

Therefore, the domain is {(x,y)∈R2:x2+y2<1}.
question.knowledge_point: The Domain of a Function Involving Reciprocals and Radicals

solution.reasoning: The square root is in the denominator, so its radicand must be strictly positive: 1−x²−y²>0. Equivalently, x²+y²<1, giving option e. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key; the worked example concerns a different function.

feedback.name: Question 10
feedback.problem: Find the domain of the function $z=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

- the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<1\}.
$$

a

c

The domain is the entire xy-plane
e

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

  • the expression under the square root is non-negative.

1−x2−y2>0⟹x2+y2<1

Therefore, the domain is {(x,y)∈R2:x2+y2<1}.

question.name: Question 11
question.problem: Find the domain of the function $z=\frac{{x}^{3}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})}.$
question.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities: 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\ne 0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0 \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0,\,{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 1\}.
$$

last_observation.name: Question 11
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: The Domain of a Function Containing Exponential, Logarithmic, and Trigonometric Functions
last_observation.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities: 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\ne 0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0 \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0,\,{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 1\}.
$$

question.html:
Question 11
?

Find the domain of the function z=x3ln⁡(x2−y2).

a
{(x,y)∈R2:x2−y2>0}
b
{(x,y)∈R2:x2−y2>0,x2−y2≠1}
c
{(x,y)∈R2:x2−y2≠0,1}
d
{(x,y)∈R2:x2−y2>1}
e
The domain is the entire xy-plane
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

  • the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

{x2−y2>0ln⁡(x2−y2)≠0⟹{x2−y2>0x2−y2≠1

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:x2−y2>0,x2−y2≠1}.
question.knowledge_point: The Domain of a Function Containing Exponential, Logarithmic, and Trigonometric Functions

solution.reasoning: The logarithm requires x²−y²>0. Since it is the denominator, ln(x²−y²) must also be nonzero, which excludes x²−y²=1. Thus option b is correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key; the worked example concerns a different function.

feedback.name: Question 11
feedback.problem: Find the domain of the function $z=\frac{{x}^{3}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities: 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\ne 0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0 \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0,\,{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 1\}.
$$

feedback.html:
Question 11
?

Find the domain of the function z=x3ln⁡(x2−y2).

a
{(x,y)∈R2:x2−y2>0}
b
{(x,y)∈R2:x2−y2>0,x2−y2≠1}
c
{(x,y)∈R2:x2−y2≠0,1}
d
{(x,y)∈R2:x2−y2>1}
e
The domain is the entire xy-plane
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

  • the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

{x2−y2>0ln⁡(x2−y2)≠0⟹{x2−y2>0x2−y2≠1

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:x2−y2>0,x2−y2≠1}.

question.name: Question 12
question.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-{x}^{2})}{y}.$
question.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities: 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}1-{x}^{2}>0 \\ y\ne 0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}-1<x<1 \\ y\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,-1<x<1,\,y\ne 0\}.
$$

b
{(x,y)∈R2:x>0,y≠0}

{(x,y)∈R2:x≠±1,y≠0}

The domain is the entire xy-plane
e
{(x,y)∈R2:−1<x<1,y>0}
Submit
Correct

{(x,y)∈R2:−1<x<1,y≠0}.

question.html:
Question 12
?

Find the domain of the function f(x,y)=ln⁡(1−x2)y.

a
{(x,y)∈R2:−1<x<1,y≠0}
b
{(x,y)∈R2:x>0,y≠0}
c
{(x,y)∈R2:x≠±1,y≠0}
d
The domain is the entire xy-plane
e
{(x,y)∈R2:−1<x<1,y>0}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

  • the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

{1−x2>0y≠0⟹{−1<x<1y≠0

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:−1<x<1,y≠0}.
question.knowledge_point: The Domain of a Function Containing Exponential, Logarithmic, and Trigonometric Functions

solution.reasoning: The logarithm requires 1−x²>0, equivalently −1<x<1. The denominator requires y≠0. Thus option a is correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key; the worked example concerns a different function.

feedback.name: Question 12
feedback.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-{x}^{2})}{y}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities: 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}1-{x}^{2}>0 \\ y\ne 0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}-1<x<1 \\ y\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,-1<x<1,\,y\ne 0\}.
$$

Find the domain of the function f(x,y)=ln⁡(1−x2)y.

a
{(x,y)∈R2:−1<x<1,y≠0}
b
{(x,y)∈R2:x>0,y≠0}
c
{(x,y)∈R2:x≠±1,y≠0}
d
The domain is the entire xy-plane
e
{(x,y)∈R2:−1<x<1,y>0}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

  • the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

{1−x2>0y≠0⟹{−1<x<1y≠0

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:−1<x<1,y≠0}.

question.name: Question 13
question.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡y}{{x}^{3}}.$
question.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities: 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y>0 \\ {x}^{3}\ne 0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}y>0 \\ x\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y>0,\,x\ne 0\}.
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

question.html:
Question 13
?

Find the domain of the function f(x,y)=ln2⁡yx3.

a
The domain is the entire xy-plane
b
{(x,y)∈R2:y>0}
c
{(x,y)∈R2:y≥0,x≠0}
d
{(x,y)∈R2:y≠0,x≠0}
e
{(x,y)∈R2:y>0,x≠0}
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

  • the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

{y>0x3≠0⟹{y>0x≠0

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:y>0,x≠0}.
question.knowledge_point: The Domain of a Function Containing Exponential, Logarithmic, and Trigonometric Functions

solution.reasoning: The expression (ln y)² requires y>0; squaring does not extend the logarithm's domain. The denominator x³ must be nonzero, so x≠0. Thus option e is correct. feedback.name: Question 13
feedback.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡y}{{x}^{3}}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities: 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y>0 \\ {x}^{3}\ne 0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}y>0 \\ x\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y>0,\,x\ne 0\}.
$$

question.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-y)}{{e}^{x}}.$
question.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

Notice that ${e}^{x}>0$ for all $x.$ Therefore, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y>0\,⟹\,x>y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,x>y\}.
$$

question.html:
Question 14
?

Find the domain of the function f(x,y)=ln⁡(x−y)ex.

a
{(x,y)∈R2:x≠y}
b
The domain is the entire xy-plane
c
{(x,y)∈R2:x>y}
d
{(x,y)∈R2:x≠y,x≠0}
e
{(x,y)∈R2:x>y,x≠0}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

  • the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

Notice that ex>0 for all x. Therefore, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

x−y>0⟹x>y Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:x>y}.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

question.html:
Question 14
?

Find the domain of the function f(x,y)=ln⁡(x−y)ex.

a
{(x,y)∈R2:x≠y}
b
The domain is the entire xy-plane
c
{(x,y)∈R2:x>y}
d
{(x,y)∈R2:x≠y,x≠0}
e
{(x,y)∈R2:x>y,x≠0}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

  • the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

Notice that ex>0 for all x. Therefore, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

x−y>0⟹x>y Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:x>y}.
question.knowledge_point: The Domain of a Function Containing Exponential, Logarithmic, and Trigonometric Functions

solution.reasoning: The logarithm requires x−y>0, equivalently x>y. Since e^x is positive for every real x, the denominator imposes no further restriction. Thus option c is correct. Question 14
?

Find the domain of the function f(x,y)=ln⁡(x−y)ex.

a
{(x,y)∈R2:x≠y}
b
The domain is the entire xy-plane
c
{(x,y)∈R2:x>y}
d
{(x,y)∈R2:x≠y,x≠0}
e
{(x,y)∈R2:x>y,x≠0}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

  • the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

Notice that ex>0 for all x. Therefore, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

x−y>0⟹x>y Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:x>y}.

question.name: Question 15
question.problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-y)}.$
question.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities: 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x-y>0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x-y)\ne 0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}x-y>0 \\ x-y\ne 1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,x-y>0,\,x-y\ne 1\}.
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

Find the domain of the function f(x,y)=1ln⁡(x−y).

a
{(x,y)∈R2:x−y≠0,1}
b
{(x,y)∈R2:x−y≥0}
c
The domain is the entire xy-plane
d
{(x,y)∈R2:x−y>0}
e
{(x,y)∈R2:x−y>0,x−y≠1}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

  • the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

{x−y>0ln⁡(x−y)≠0⟹{x−y>0x−y≠1

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:x−y>0,x−y≠1}.

question.html:
Question 15
?

Find the domain of the function f(x,y)=1ln⁡(x−y).

a
{(x,y)∈R2:x−y≠0,1}
b
{(x,y)∈R2:x−y≥0}
c
The domain is the entire xy-plane
d
{(x,y)∈R2:x−y>0}
e
{(x,y)∈R2:x−y>0,x−y≠1}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is well-defined at all points (x,y) for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

  • the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

{x−y>0ln⁡(x−y)≠0⟹{x−y>0x−y≠1

Therefore, the domain is

{(x,y)∈R2:x−y>0,x−y≠1}.
question.knowledge_point: The Domain of a Function Containing Exponential, Logarithmic, and Trigonometric Functions

solution.reasoning: The logarithm requires x−y>0. Its value must also be nonzero because it is the denominator; ln(x−y)=0 exactly when x−y=1. Thus option e is correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key; the worked example concerns a different function.

$$

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,x-y>0,\,x-y\ne 1\}.
$$

question.name: Question 16
question.problem: Which of the following shaded regions corresponds to the domain of the function $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2})?$
question.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
4-{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}>0\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}<4\,⟹\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}<1
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}<1\}.
$$

Since the expression involves the $<$ sign, the curve is *not* part of the domain. Therefore, we draw the dashed curve $\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}<1$ and shade the region *inside* the curve.

The resulting domain is as follows:

question.name: Question 17
question.problem: Which of the following shaded regions corresponds to the domain of the function $g(x,y)=\frac{1}{{x}^{3}+y}?$
question.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
{x}^{3}+y\ne 0\,⟹\,y\ne -{x}^{3}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y\ne -{x}^{3}\}.
$$

Since the expression involves the $\ne $ sign, the line is *not* part of the domain. Therefore, we draw the dashed curve $y=-{x}^{3}$ and shade *above* and *below* the curve.

The resulting domain is as follows:

questions.worked_solution:
The part is $32,$ the percentage is $40%,$ and we need to find the whole.

To do this, we can use the following formula:

$$
\text{whole}=\text{part}÷\text{percentage}
$$

Before we can substitute our numbers into the formula, we need to express $40%$ as a fraction:

$$
\frac{40}{100}=\frac{40÷20}{100÷20}=\frac{2}{5}
$$

We can now substitute our numbers into the formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{whole} & =32÷40% \\  & =32÷\frac{2}{5} \\  & =32\times \frac{5}{2} \\  & =\frac{32}{2}\times 5 \\  & =16\times 5 \\  & =80\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
By the segment addition postulate, we have

$$
AD=AB+BC+CD.
$$

To solve for $x,$ we can substitute the given information

$$
AD=17,\,AB=x-2,\,BC=9,\,CD=2x-5,
$$

 

and then solve the resulting equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}AD & =AB+BC+CD \\ 17 & =(x-2)+9+(2x-5) \\ 17 & =3x+2 \\ 3x & =15 \\ x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Speed is a special unit rate applied to moving objects. It is defined as *the distance traveled per unit of time*:

$$
\text{speed}=\frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}
$$

To find the speed in meters per minute, we divide the number of meters, $190,$ by the number of minutes, $2.$ This gives,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{190}{2} & =190÷2 \\  & =95.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the speed of the person is $95$ meters per minute. 

To find the distance covered in $5$ minutes, we multiply the speed by $5.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{distance} & =\text{speed}\times \text{time} \\  & =95\times 5 \\  & =475.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the person can cover $475$ meters in $5$ minutes.

questions.worked_solution:
First, note that $y=-\frac{7}{2}$ and $y=\frac{2}{5}$ cannot be solutions since division by $0$ is undefined.

To solve the equation, we move the negative sign onto the numerator of the fraction and then apply cross-multiplication:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2y+7} & =\frac{4}{5y-2} \\ \frac{-1}{2y+7} & =\frac{4}{5y-2} \\ (-1)\cdot (5y-2) & =(2y+7)\cdot 4 \\ -5y+2 & =8y+28\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the addition and multiplication principles, as usual:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5y+2 & =8y+28 \\ -5y+2+5y & =8y+28+5y \\ 2 & =13y+28 \\ 2-28 & =13y+28-28 \\ -26 & =13y \\ \frac{-26}{13} & =\frac{13y}{13} \\ -2 & =y\end{aligned}
$$

Since $y=-2$ is different from $y=-\frac{7}{2}$ and $y=\frac{2}{5},$ we can accept it as a solution. Thus, the solution is $y=-2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =129\,600 \\ 100\cdot {6}^{t} & =129\,600.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the lowest common denominator of two fractions, we first find the prime factorization of both denominators. 

Since the denominators $7$ and $2$ are prime numbers, they are already represented by their respective prime factorizations.

feedback.problem: If $\,\boxed{}\times 40%=32,$ then $\,\boxed{}=$
feedback.worked_solution:
The part is $32,$ the percentage is $40%,$ and we need to find the whole.

To do this, we can use the following formula:

$$
\text{whole}=\text{part}÷\text{percentage}
$$

Before we can substitute our numbers into the formula, we need to express $40%$ as a fraction:

$$
\frac{40}{100}=\frac{40÷20}{100÷20}=\frac{2}{5}
$$

We can now substitute our numbers into the formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{whole} & =32÷40% \\  & =32÷\frac{2}{5} \\  & =32\times \frac{5}{2} \\  & =\frac{32}{2}\times 5 \\  & =16\times 5 \\  & =80\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
By the segment addition postulate, we have

$$
AD=AB+BC+CD.
$$

To solve for $x,$ we can substitute the given information

$$
AD=17,\,AB=x-2,\,BC=9,\,CD=2x-5,
$$

 

and then solve the resulting equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}AD & =AB+BC+CD \\ 17 & =(x-2)+9+(2x-5) \\ 17 & =3x+2 \\ 3x & =15 \\ x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
The roots of the function are the values of $x$ such that $f(x)=0.$ In the given mapping diagram, we see that there is no value of $x$ that gives an output of zero. 

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ has no roots.

solution.reasoning: Inverse variation means xy=k. The given values give k=4·2=8. When x=4/5, y=8/(4/5)=10, current option a. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.problem: If $y$ varies inversely with $x$ and $y=2$ when $x=4,$ find the value of $y$ when $x=\frac{4}{5}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since $y$ varies inversely with $x,$ we use the equation

$$
y=\frac{k}{x}.
$$

We are told that $y=2$ when $x=4.$ We substitute this data into the equation to find $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =\frac{k}{4} \\ 2\cdot 4 & =k \\ 8 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the inverse variation is given by 

$$
y=\frac{8}{x}.
$$

Finally, substituting the value of $x=\frac{4}{5}$ into this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{8}{(\frac{4}{5})} \\  & =8÷\frac{4}{5} \\  & =8\cdot \frac{5}{4} \\  & =\frac{40}{4} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

solution.reasoning: Assuming a constant walking speed, the rate is 190/2=95 meters per minute. In 5 minutes, the distance is 95×5=475 meters, current option e. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.problem: It takes a particular person $2$ minutes to walk $190$ meters. Find the distance this person covers in $5$ minutes.
feedback.worked_solution:
Speed is a special unit rate applied to moving objects. It is defined as *the distance traveled per unit of time*:

$$
\text{speed}=\frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}
$$

To find the speed in meters per minute, we divide the number of meters, $190,$ by the number of minutes, $2.$ This gives,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{190}{2} & =190÷2 \\  & =95.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the speed of the person is $95$ meters per minute. 

To find the distance covered in $5$ minutes, we multiply the speed by $5.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{distance} & =\text{speed}\times \text{time} \\  & =95\times 5 \\  & =475.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the person can cover $475$ meters in $5$ minutes.

decision.exposure_note: KP association unavailable; use the base accuracy without pooling unknown skills

solution.reasoning: Cross-multiplying gives -(5y-2)=4(2y+7), so -5y+2=8y+28 and -13y=26. Thus y=-2. Both denominators are nonzero at this value, and both sides equal -1/3. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.worked_solution:
First, note that $y=-\frac{7}{2}$ and $y=\frac{2}{5}$ cannot be solutions since division by $0$ is undefined.

To solve the equation, we move the negative sign onto the numerator of the fraction and then apply cross-multiplication:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2y+7} & =\frac{4}{5y-2} \\ \frac{-1}{2y+7} & =\frac{4}{5y-2} \\ (-1)\cdot (5y-2) & =(2y+7)\cdot 4 \\ -5y+2 & =8y+28\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the addition and multiplication principles, as usual:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5y+2 & =8y+28 \\ -5y+2+5y & =8y+28+5y \\ 2 & =13y+28 \\ 2-28 & =13y+28-28 \\ -26 & =13y \\ \frac{-26}{13} & =\frac{13y}{13} \\ -2 & =y\end{aligned}
$$

Since $y=-2$ is different from $y=-\frac{7}{2}$ and $y=\frac{2}{5},$ we can accept it as a solution. Thus, the solution is $y=-2.$

solution.reasoning: Rearranging 4x-2y=15 gives y=2x-15/2. The coefficient of x is the slope, so the answer is 2, current option a. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.problem: What is the slope of the line $4x-2y=15?$
feedback.worked_solution:
We can find the slope of the line if we can express its equation in slope-intercept form. To do this, we solve for $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-2y & =15 \\ -2y & =-4x+15 \\ 2y & =4x-15 \\ \frac{2y}{2} & =\frac{4x-15}{2} \\ y & =\frac{4x}{2}-\frac{15}{2} \\ y & =2x-\frac{15}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

From the slope-intercept equation, we can tell that the slope of the line is $m=2.$

question.html:
Question 10

A particular nature reserve started with 100 rabbits. The number of rabbits is expected to increase sixfold each decade. What equation should we solve to determine the number of decades it will take for the rabbit population to increase to 129600?

a
 129600⋅6t=100
b
 100t=129600
c
 6t=129600
d
 100⋅6t=129600
e
 6⋅100t=129600

decision.exposure_note: KP association unavailable; use the base accuracy without pooling unknown skills

solution.reasoning: After t decades, the population is the initial 100 multiplied by 6^t. Setting this equal to the target gives 100·6^t=129600, current option d. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.problem: A particular nature reserve started with $100$ rabbits. The number of rabbits is expected to increase sixfold each decade. What equation should we solve to determine the number of decades it will take for the rabbit population to increase to $129\,600?$
feedback.worked_solution:
We know that the number of rabbits increases sixfold every decade. So the number of rabbits, which we'll call $y(t),$ grows exponentially with a growth factor of $6.$

The formula for exponential growth (in terms of a growth factor $b$) is

$$
y(t)=a{b}^{t}.
$$

From the given information, we have the following:

- $a=100$ is the initial number of rabbits.

- $b=6$ is the growth factor.

- $t$ is the time, in decades, since the opening of the nature reserve.

Therefore, the expression for $y(t)$ is

$$
y(t)=100\cdot {6}^{t}.
$$

So, to find the time it takes for the population to increase to $129\,600,$ we would need to solve the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =129\,600 \\ 100\cdot {6}^{t} & =129\,600.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11

Order the sides of △KLM above from the shortest to the longest.

a
 KM―,LM―,KL―
b
 LM―,KM―,KL―
c
 LM―,KL―,KM―
d
 KM―,KL―,LM―
e
 KL―,KM―,LM―

decision.exposure_note: KP association unavailable; use the base accuracy without pooling unknown skills

solution.reasoning: Sides opposite larger angles are longer. Since angle K=45° < angle L=48° < angle M=87°, the opposite sides satisfy LM < KM < KL, current option b. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14246462/assets/f2dc2ed0562e3d93888ab025195ada5da5ef9bf5312d6215dfb83253c81f9be7.png)

Order the sides of $△KLM$ above from the shortest to the longest.
feedback.worked_solution:
Since $∠K$ is the smallest angle, its opposite side $\overset{―}{LM}$ is the shortest side of the triangle.

Since $∠M$ is the largest angle, its opposite side $\overset{―}{KL}$ must be the longest side of the triangle. 

So, we have

$$
LM<KM<KL
$$

and therefore the required order is

$$
\overset{―}{LM},\,\overset{―}{KM},\,\overset{―}{KL}.
$$

feedback.problem: The lowest common denominator of $\frac{5}{7}$ and $\frac{1}{2}$ is{{field-1}}.
feedback.worked_solution:
To find the lowest common denominator of two fractions, we first find the prime factorization of both denominators. 

Since the denominators $7$ and $2$ are prime numbers, they are already represented by their respective prime factorizations. 

Now, we write down each prime factor, and we raise each factor to the highest power given in either factorization:

- the highest power of $7$ is $1$

- the highest power of $2$ is also $1$

Therefore, the lowest common denominator is ${7}^{1}\cdot {2}^{1}=14.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{5} & -\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{1}{5} & -\frac{7}{5}\end{aligned}]x(t)+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]
$$

A complementary solution to this system is given by

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}(t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]){e}^{-t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Then, the general solution of the system can be written as 
$x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t),$
where ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution. Determine the form of the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t).$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is constant. Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also constant, i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ are constants that are to be determined.

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations: $$ {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]x(t)+{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}-14 \\ -27\end{aligned}]. $$ The complementary solution to this system is given by $$ {x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R. $$ Then, the general solution of the system is
$x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+$ {{field-1}} $\cdot \,\,$ $2$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}-14 \\ -27\end{aligned}]
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is exponential. Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also exponential, i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}],
$$

where $a,b$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=-4{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]+{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}-14 \\ -27\end{aligned}] \\ -4[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-14 \\ -27\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-4a \\ -4b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3a \\ 5b\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-14 \\ -27\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-4a \\ -4b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3a-14 \\ 5b-27\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3a-14=-4a \\ 5b-27=-4b\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get

$$
3a-14=-4a\,⇒\,a=2.
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
5b-27=-4b\,⇒\,b=3.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations: $$ {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{3} & -\frac{8}{3} \\ -\frac{4}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]x(t)+[\begin{aligned}-6{t}^{2}+\frac{41}{3}t-8 \\ 3{t}^{2}-\frac{13}{3}t+5\end{aligned}] $$ The complementary solution to this system is given by $$ {x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R. $$ Then, the general solution of the system is
$x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+\,\,$ {{field-1}} $\,\,{t}^{2}+\,\,$ $-1$ $\,\,t+\,\,$ {{field-2}} .
$-1$ {{field-3}} $-2$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
[\begin{aligned}-6{t}^{2}+\frac{41}{3}t-8 \\ 3{t}^{2}-\frac{13}{3}t+5\end{aligned}]
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}]{t}^{2}+[\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{c}_{1},{c}_{2}$ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{3} & -\frac{8}{3} \\ -\frac{4}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-6{t}^{2}+\frac{41}{3}t-8 \\ 3{t}^{2}-\frac{13}{3}t+5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}(\frac{5{a}_{1}-8{a}_{2}}{3}){t}^{2}+(\frac{5{b}_{1}-8{b}_{2}}{3})t+(\frac{5{c}_{1}-8{c}_{2}}{3}) \\ (\frac{-4{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}}{3}){t}^{2}+(\frac{-4{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}}{3})t+(\frac{-4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}}{3})\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-6{t}^{2}+\frac{41}{3}t-8 \\ 3{t}^{2}-\frac{13}{3}t+5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0{t}^{2}+2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 0{t}^{2}+2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}(\frac{5{a}_{1}-8{a}_{2}-18}{3}){t}^{2}+(\frac{5{b}_{1}-8{b}_{2}+41}{3})t+(\frac{5{c}_{1}-8{c}_{2}-24}{3}) \\ (\frac{-4{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}+9}{3}){t}^{2}+(\frac{-4{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}-13}{3})t+(\frac{-4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+15}{3})\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding coefficients of like powers of $t,$ we get the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5{a}_{1}-8{a}_{2}-18}{3}=0 \\ \frac{-4{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}+9}{3}=0 \\ \frac{5{b}_{1}-8{b}_{2}+41}{3}=2{a}_{1} \\ \frac{-4{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}-13}{3}=2{a}_{2} \\ \frac{5{c}_{1}-8{c}_{2}-24}{3}={b}_{1} \\ \frac{-4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+15}{3}={b}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first and second equations, we get

$$
{a}_{1}=2,\,{a}_{2}=-1.
$$

Substituting these into the second and third equations, and solving for ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2},$ we get

$$
{b}_{1}=-1,\,{b}_{2}=3.
$$

Finally, substituting these last two values into the fourth and sixth equations, and solving for ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we have

$$
{c}_{1}=1,\,{c}_{2}=-2.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}-t+1 \\ -{t}^{2}+3t-2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{t}^{2}+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t)+{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the missing coefficients in the solution to the initial value problem, shown above.

$x(t)=$ 
{{field-1}} 
$\,\cdot \,[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,-$
{{field-2}}
$\,\cdot \,[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}]+{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
We are told that the general solution to the system is 

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}]+{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}$ are constants that are to be determined. 

Next, we find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(0)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0\cdot {e}^{2(0)} \\ {e}^{2(0)}\end{aligned}]+{e}^{-0}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}+1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}=3 \\ {c}_{2}+1=-2\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we have ${c}_{1}=3.$ From the second equation, we get ${c}_{2}=-3.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
x(t)=3\cdot [\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]-3\cdot [\begin{aligned}t{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}]+{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
