$$

Find the missing coefficients in the solution to the initial value problem, shown above.

$x(t)=$ 
{{field-1}} 
$\,\cdot \,[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,-$
{{field-2}}
$\,\cdot \,[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-t+1 \\ 2t-3\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
We are told that the general solution to the system is 

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-t+1 \\ 2t-3\end{aligned}]
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}$ are constants that are to be determined. 

Next, we find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{0} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{2(0)}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}-0+1 \\ 2(0)-3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+1 \\ {c}_{2}-3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+1=2 \\ {c}_{2}-3=-5\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get ${c}_{1}=1.$ From the second equation, we have ${c}_{2}=-2.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
x(t)=1\cdot [\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]-2\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-t+1 \\ 2t-3\end{aligned}].
$$

question.problem:
Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations:

$$

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}(t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]){e}^{-t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Then, the general solution of the system can be written as 
$x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t),$
where ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution. Determine the form of the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t).$

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}-14 \\ -27\end{aligned}]
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is exponential. Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also exponential, i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}],
$$

where $a,b$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=-4{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]+{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}-14 \\ -27\end{aligned}] \\ -4[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-14 \\ -27\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-4a \\ -4b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3a \\ 5b\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-14 \\ -27\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-4a \\ -4b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3a-14 \\ 5b-27\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3a-14=-4a \\ 5b-27=-4b\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get

$$
3a-14=-4a\,⇒\,a=2.
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
5b-27=-4b\,⇒\,b=3.
$$

question.problem:
Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{5} & -\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{1}{5} & -\frac{7}{5}\end{aligned}]x(t)+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]
$$

A complementary solution to this system is given by

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}(t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]){e}^{-t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Then, the general solution of the system can be written as 
$x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t),$
where ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution. Determine the form of the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t).$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is constant. Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also constant, i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ are constants that are to be determined.

x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)

$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{5} & -\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{1}{5} & -\frac{7}{5}\end{aligned}]x(t)+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]
$$

A complementary solution to this system is given by

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}(t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]){e}^{-t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Then, the general solution of the system can be written as 
$x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t),$
where ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution. Determine the form of the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t).$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations: $$ {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]x(t)+{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}-14 \\ -27\end{aligned}]. $$ The complementary solution to this system is given by $$ {x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R. $$ Then, the general solution of the system is
$x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+$ {{field-1}} $\cdot \,\,$ $2$
{{field-2}}
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}-14 \\ -27\end{aligned}]
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is exponential. Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also exponential, i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}],
$$

where $a,b$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=-4{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]+{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}-14 \\ -27\end{aligned}] \\ -4[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-14 \\ -27\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-4a \\ -4b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3a \\ 5b\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-14 \\ -27\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-4a \\ -4b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3a-14 \\ 5b-27\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3a-14=-4a \\ 5b-27=-4b\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get

$$
3a-14=-4a\,⇒\,a=2.
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
5b-27=-4b\,⇒\,b=3.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Given that $r$, $s$ and $t$ in the above diagram are parallel, find $m∠1.$
questions.worked_solution:
Consider $∠2$ in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14246974/assets/2bca55a68d4a0695c73f82ca82d5fae386d9b8d57b058bc1cf694bee902cff25.png)

Notice that $∠2$ and the angle whose measure is ${42}^{∘}$ are alternate exterior angles formed when the transversal $u$ cuts the parallel lines $r$ and $s.$ Hence, 

$$
m∠2={42}^{∘}.
$$

Also, notice that the angle determined by $∠1$ and $∠2$ and the angle whose measure is ${108}^{∘}$ are corresponding angles formed when the transversal $v$ cuts the parallel lines $s$ and $t.$ Hence, 

$$
m∠1+m∠2={108}^{∘}.
$$

Now, substituting $m∠2$ into the equation, we can find $m∠1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠1+m∠2 & ={108}^{∘} \\ m∠1+{42}^{∘} & ={108}^{∘} \\ m∠1 & ={66}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14246974/assets/5178d7f2910b4a28116022968e6a2d5580b9284d65bb7dc973e36f4c2a2f4ccd.png)

Given that $\overset{↔}{AB}∥\overset{↔}{CF},$ what is the measure of $∠AFB?$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that $∠BAF$  and $∠AFC$ are alternate interior angles formed when the transversal $\overset{↔}{AF}$ cuts the parallel lines $\overset{↔}{AB}$ and $\overset{↔}{CF}.$ Hence, 

$$
m∠AFC=m∠BAF={71}^{∘}.
$$

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14246974/assets/bfb1ce1e2aba3efe901251ad40f84fda062e8324c4dd7a1f2888081724679842.png)

Also, notice that $∠FBE$  and $∠BFC$ are alternate interior angles formed when the transversal $\overset{↔}{BF}$ cuts the parallel lines $\overset{↔}{AB}$ and $\overset{↔}{CF}.$ Hence, 

$$
m∠BFC=m∠FBE={139}^{∘}.
$$

Now, using the angle addition postulate, we can find $∠AFB:$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠AFB & =m∠BFC-m∠AFC \\  & ={139}^{∘}-{71}^{∘} \\  & ={68}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that r, s and t in the above diagram are parallel, find m∠1.

a
68∘
b
66∘
c
72∘
d
63∘
e
75∘
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Consider ∠2 in the diagram below.

Notice that ∠2 and the angle whose measure is 42∘ are alternate exterior angles formed when the transversal u cuts the parallel lines r and s. Hence, m∠2=42∘.

Also, notice that the angle determined by ∠1 and ∠2 and the angle whose measure is 108∘ are corresponding angles formed when the transversal v cuts the parallel lines s and t. Hence, m∠1+m∠2=108∘.

Now, substituting m∠2 into the equation, we can find m∠1: m∠1+m∠2=108∘m∠1+42∘=108∘m∠1=66∘

question.html:
Question 2
?

Given that r, s and t in the above diagram are parallel, find m∠1.

a
66∘
b
61∘
c
57∘
d
69∘
e
53∘
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Consider ∠2 in the diagram below.

Notice that ∠2 and the angle whose measure is 66∘ are alternate exterior angles formed when the transversal v cuts the parallel lines r and s. Hence, m∠2=66∘.

Also, notice that the angle determined by ∠1 and ∠2 and the angle whose measure is 127∘ are corresponding angles formed when the transversal u cuts the parallel lines s and t. Hence, m∠1+m∠2=127∘.

Now, substituting m∠2 into the equation, we can find m∠1: m∠1+m∠2=127∘m∠1+66∘=127∘m∠1=61∘

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14246974/assets/5178d7f2910b4a28116022968e6a2d5580b9284d65bb7dc973e36f4c2a2f4ccd.png)

Given that $\overset{↔}{AB}∥\overset{↔}{CF},$ what is the measure of $∠AFB?$
question.worked_solution:
Notice that $∠BAF$  and $∠AFC$ are alternate interior angles formed when the transversal $\overset{↔}{AF}$ cuts the parallel lines $\overset{↔}{AB}$ and $\overset{↔}{CF}.$ Hence, 

$$
m∠AFC=m∠BAF={71}^{∘}.
$$

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14246974/assets/bfb1ce1e2aba3efe901251ad40f84fda062e8324c4dd7a1f2888081724679842.png)

Also, notice that $∠FBE$  and $∠BFC$ are alternate interior angles formed when the transversal $\overset{↔}{BF}$ cuts the parallel lines $\overset{↔}{AB}$ and $\overset{↔}{CF}.$ Hence, 

$$
m∠BFC=m∠FBE={139}^{∘}.
$$

Now, using the angle addition postulate, we can find $∠AFB:$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠AFB & =m∠BFC-m∠AFC \\  & ={139}^{∘}-{71}^{∘} \\  & ={68}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Given that AB↔∥CF↔, what is the measure of ∠AFB?

a
65∘
b
75∘
c
66∘
d
68∘
e
71∘
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that ∠BAF and ∠AFC are alternate interior angles formed when the transversal AF↔ cuts the parallel lines AB↔ and CF↔. Hence, m∠AFC=m∠BAF=71∘.

Also, notice that ∠FBE and ∠BFC are alternate interior angles formed when the transversal BF↔ cuts the parallel lines AB↔ and CF↔. Hence, m∠BFC=m∠FBE=139∘.

Now, using the angle addition postulate, we can find ∠AFB: m∠AFB=m∠BFC−m∠AFC=139∘−71∘=68∘

$$

Equating the corresponding $x$- and $y$-coordinates in the equation above gives us

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}1=\frac{a-2}{2} \\ 1=\frac{b}{2}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}a=4 \\ b=2.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the midpoint of the line segment with endpoints (−w,7z) and (5w,−3z).

a
(−2w,−2z)
b
(−w,2z)
c
(−w,−z)
d
(2w,2z)
e
(2w,3z)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let (xm,ym) be the midpoint between (−w,7z)⏟(x1,y1) and (5w,−3z)⏟(x2,y2).

We use the midpoint formula as follows:

(xm,ym)=(x1+x22,y1+y22)=(−w+5w2,7z+(−3z)2)=(−w+5w2,7z−3z2)=(4w2,4z2)=(2w,2z).

Question 2
?

Find the midpoint of the line segment with endpoints (8p,−q) and (−2p,−9q).

a
(6p,−5q)
b
(4p,−2q)
c
(3p,−5q)
d
(2p,−5q)
e
(2p,−4q)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let (xm,ym) be the midpoint between (8p,−q)⏟(x1,y1) and (−2p,−9q)⏟(x2,y2).

We use the midpoint formula as follows:

(xm,ym)=(x1+x22,y1+y22)=(8p+(−2p)2,−q+(−9q)2)=(8p−2p2,−q−9q2)=(6p2,−10q2)=(3p,−5q).

Given that $(1,1)$ is the midpoint of the line segment $\overset{―}{PQ}$ above, find the values of $a$ and $b.$

$a=$
{{field-1}},
$\,b=$
{{field-2}}
question.worked_solution:
The given points are ${{(a,b)}_{⏟}}_{\text{(}{x}_{1},\,{y}_{1})}$, ${{(-2,0)}_{⏟}}_{\text{(}{x}_{2},\,{y}_{2})}$ and ${{(1,1)}_{⏟}}_{\text{(}{x}_{m},\,{y}_{m})}.$

We use the midpoint formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{m},{y}_{m}) & =(\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2},\frac{{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}}{2}) \\ (1,1) & =(\frac{a-2}{2},\frac{b+0}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding $x$- and $y$-coordinates in the equation above gives us

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}1=\frac{a-2}{2} \\ 1=\frac{b}{2}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}a=4 \\ b=2.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $a=4$ and $b=2.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y)=xy+{y}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =y\,\text{d}x+(x+2y)\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}y+{y}^{3}z-x{z}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =(2xy-{z}^{2})\,\text{d}x+({x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}z)\,\text{d}y+({y}^{3}-2xz)\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}).$
questions.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{2x\,\text{d}x}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}+\frac{\text{d}y}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}+\frac{3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz).$
questions.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{yz\,\text{d}x}{xyz}+\frac{xz\,\text{d}y}{xyz}+\frac{xy\,\text{d}z}{xyz} \\  & =\frac{\,\text{d}x}{x}+\frac{\,\text{d}y}{y}+\frac{\,\text{d}z}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2x\,\text{d}x+2y\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: Given a cylinder, find the differential $\text{d}V$ for the volume $V$ of the cylinder if the radius is $r=2$ and the height is $h=4.$
questions.worked_solution:
The volume of the cylinder is $V=\pi {r}^{2}h.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(r,h) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂r})\,\text{d}r+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =2\pi rh\,\text{d}r+\pi {r}^{2}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $r=2$ and $h=4,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(2,4) & =2\pi \cdot 2\cdot 4\,\text{d}r+\pi \cdot {2}^{2}\,\text{d}h \\  & =16\pi \,\text{d}r+4\pi \,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: Given a rectangular pyramid, find the differential $\text{d}V$ for the volume $V$ of the rectangular pyramid if the base is a square with the side of $a=6$ and the height is $h=5.$
questions.worked_solution:
The volume of the rectangular pyramid is $V=\frac{1}{3}{a}^{2}h.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,h) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{2ah}{3}\,\text{d}a+\frac{{a}^{2}}{3}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=6$ and $h=5,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(6,5) & =\frac{2\cdot 6\cdot 5}{3}\,\text{d}a+\frac{{6}^{2}}{3}\,\text{d}h \\  & =20\,\text{d}a+12\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem: Given a right triangular prism, find the differential $\text{d}V$ for the volume $V$ if the height is $h=1$ and the base is a right triangle with legs $a=2$ and $b=4.$
questions.worked_solution:
The volume of a given right triangular prism is $V=\frac{abh}{2}.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{bh}{2}\,\text{d}a+\frac{ah}{2}\,\text{d}b+\frac{ab}{2}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=2,$ $b=4,$ and $h=1,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(2,4,1) & =\frac{4\cdot 1}{2}\,\text{d}a+\frac{2\cdot 1}{2}\,\text{d}b+\frac{2\cdot 4}{2}\,\text{d}h \\  & =2\,\text{d}a+\text{d}b+4\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem: Given a rectangular solid, find the differential $\text{d}S$ for the surface area $S$ of the rectangular solid if the lengths of the sides are $a=4,$ $b=5,$ and $c=7.$
questions.worked_solution:
The  surface area of the rectangular solid is $S=2ab+2bc+2ac.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}S(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂S}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂S}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂S}{∂c})\,\text{d}c \\  & =2(b+c)\,\text{d}a+2(a+c)\,\text{d}b+2(a+b)\,\text{d}c\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=4,$ $b=5,$ and $c=7,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}S(4,5,7) & =2(5+7)\,\text{d}a+2(4+7)\,\text{d}b+2(4+5)\,\text{d}c \\  & =24\,\text{d}a+22\,\text{d}b+18\,\text{d}c.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem: Given a rectangular solid, find the differential $\text{d}V$ for the volume $V$ of the rectangular solid if the lengths of the sides are $a=2,$ $b=5,$ and $c=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The volume of the rectangular solid is $V=abc.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂V}{∂c})\,\text{d}c \\  & =bc\,\text{d}a+ac\,\text{d}b+ab\,\text{d}c\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=2,$ $b=5,$ and $c=1,$ the differential is

$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem: If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x+y,$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y)$ from $(4\pi ,8)$ to $(13,8.5).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x+1\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(4\pi ,8),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(4\pi ,8) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi \,\text{d}x+1\,\text{d}y \\  & =0\,\text{d}x+1\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(4\pi +Δx,8+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈0\,Δx+1\,Δy.
$$

Moving from $(4\pi ,8)$ to $(13,8.5),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =13-4\pi , \\ Δy & =8.5-8=0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈0\,Δx+1\,Δy \\  & ≈0\cdot (13-4\pi )+1\cdot (0.5) \\  & ≈0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y)$ increases by approximately $0.5.$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem: If $f(x,y,z)=y{e}^{x}+xz,$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y,z)$ from $(0,1,2)$ to $(-1,0,3).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}z \\  & =(y{e}^{x}+z)\,\text{d}x+{e}^{x}\,\text{d}y+x\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(0,1,2),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(0,1,2) & =(1\cdot {e}^{0}+2)\,\text{d}x+{e}^{0}\,\text{d}y+0\,\text{d}z \\  & =3\,\text{d}x+1\,\text{d}y+0\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(0+Δx,1+Δy,2+Δz),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈3\,Δx+1\,Δy+0\,Δz.
$$

Moving from $(0,1,2)$ to $(-1,0,3),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =-1-0=-1, \\ Δy & =0-1=-1 \\ Δz & =3-2=1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈3\,Δx+1\,Δy+0\,Δz \\  & ≈3\cdot (-1)+1\cdot (-1)+0\cdot (1) \\  & ≈-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y,z)$ decreases by approximately $-4.$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem: If $f(x,y,z)=x{e}^{2y-z},$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y,z)$ from $(-1,2,3)$ to $(1,0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}z \\  & ={e}^{2y-z}\,\text{d}x+2x{e}^{2y-z}\,\text{d}y-x{e}^{2y-z}\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(-1,2,3),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(-1,2,3) & ={e}^{2(2)-3}\,\text{d}x+2\cdot (-1)\cdot {e}^{2(2)-3}\,\text{d}y-(-1)\cdot {e}^{2(2)-3}\,\text{d}z \\  & =e\,\text{d}x-2e\,\text{d}y+e\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(-1+Δx,2+Δy,3+Δz),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈e\,Δx-2e\,Δy+e\,Δz.
$$

Moving from $(-1,2,3)$ to $(1,0,1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1-(-1)=2, \\ Δy & =0-2=-2 \\ Δz & =1-3=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈e\,Δx-2e\,Δy+e\,Δz \\  & ≈e\cdot (2)-2e\cdot (-2)+e\cdot (-2) \\  & ≈4e.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y,z)$ increases by approximately $4e.$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem: If $f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+y\operatorname{cos}⁡z,$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y,z)$ from $(1,0,\frac{\pi }{2})$ to $(0,1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}x+(x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{cos}⁡z)\,\text{d}y-y\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(1,0,\frac{\pi }{2}),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(1,0,\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)\,\text{d}x+(1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))\,\text{d}y-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}z \\  & =0\,\text{d}x+1\,\text{d}y+0\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(1+Δx,0+Δy,\frac{\pi }{2}+Δz),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈0\,Δx+1\,Δy+0\,Δz.
$$

Moving from $(1,0,\frac{\pi }{2})$ to $(0,1,1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =0-1=-1, \\ Δy & =1-0=1 \\ Δz & =1-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈0\,Δx+1\,Δy+0\,Δz \\  & ≈0\cdot (-1)+1\cdot (1)+0\cdot (1-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & ≈1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y,z)$ increases by approximately $1.$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem: If $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+4\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{3}-y),$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y,z)$ from $(2,-3,1)$ to $(1,-2,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =2x\,\text{d}x-(\frac{4}{{z}^{3}-y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{12{z}^{2}}{{z}^{3}-y})\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(2,-3,1),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(2,-3,1) & =(2\cdot 2)\,\text{d}x-(\frac{4}{{1}^{3}-(-3)})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{12\cdot {1}^{2}}{{1}^{3}-(-3)})\,\text{d}z \\  & =4\,\text{d}x-\,\text{d}y+3\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(2+Δx,-3+Δy,1+Δz),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈4\,Δx-\,Δy+3\,Δz.
$$

Moving from $(2,-3,1)$ to $(1,-2,2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1-2=-1, \\ Δy & =-2-(-3)=1 \\ Δz & =2-1=1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈4\,Δx-1\,Δy+3\,Δz \\  & ≈4\cdot (-1)-1\cdot 1+3\cdot 1 \\  & ≈-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y,z)$ decreases by approximately $-2.$

questions.name: Question 16
questions.problem: Estimate $\sqrt{{e}^{0.2}+0.1}$ using a differential $\text{d}f$ of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{e}^{x}+y}$ at the point $(0,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x}}{2\sqrt{{e}^{x}+y}}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{e}^{x}+y}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(0,0),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =\frac{{e}^{0}}{2\sqrt{{e}^{0}+0}}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{e}^{0}+0}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(0+Δx,0+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈\frac{1}{2}\,Δx+\frac{1}{2}\,Δy
$$

Note that 

$$
\sqrt{{e}^{0.2}+0.1}=f(0.2,0.1),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(0.2,0.1).$

Moving from $(0,0)$ to $(0.2,0.1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =0.2-0=0.2, \\ Δy & =0.1-0=0.1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈\frac{1}{2}(0.2)+\frac{1}{2}(0.1) \\  & =0.1+0.05 \\  & =0.15.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.15.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0.2,0.1) & ≈f(0,0)+0.15 \\ \sqrt{{e}^{0.2}+0.1} & ≈\sqrt{{e}^{0}+0}+0.15 \\  & =1+0.15 \\  & =1.15.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 17
questions.problem: Estimate $\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(0.12)$ using a differential $\text{d}f$ of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{3},0).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(\frac{\pi }{3},0),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,\text{d}x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{cos}⁡0\,\text{d}y \\  & =0\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(\frac{\pi }{3}+Δx,0+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈0\,Δx+\frac{1}{2}\,Δy
$$

Note that 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(0.12)=f(1,0.12),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(1,0.12).$

Moving from $(\frac{\pi }{3},0)$ to $(1,0.12),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1-\frac{\pi }{3}, \\ Δy & =0.12-0=0.12.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈0\cdot (1-\frac{\pi }{3})+\frac{1}{2}\cdot (0.12) \\  & ≈0+0.5\cdot 0.12 \\  & ≈0.06.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.06.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0.12) & ≈f(\frac{\pi }{3},0)+0.06 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(0.12) & ≈\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+0.06 \\  & ≈0+0.06 \\  & ≈0.06.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 18
questions.problem: Estimate $(1.81)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.91)$ using a differential $\text{d}f$ of the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ at the point $(2,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,\text{d}x+\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(2,1),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)\,\text{d}x+\frac{2}{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =0\,\text{d}x+2\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(2+Δx,1+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈0\,Δx+2\,Δy
$$

Note that 

$$
(1.81)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.91)=f(1.81,0.91),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(1.81,0.91).$

Moving from $(2,1)$ to $(1.81,0.91),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1.81-2=-0.19, \\ Δy & =0.91-1=-0.09.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈0\cdot (-0.19)+2\cdot (-0.09) \\  & ≈0-0.18 \\  & ≈-0.18.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ decreases by about $0.18.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.81,0.91) & ≈f(2,1)-0.18 \\ (1.81)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.91) & ≈2\operatorname{ln}⁡1-0.18 \\  & ≈0-0.18 \\  & ≈-0.18.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 19
questions.problem: Estimate the value of ${e}^{\sqrt{10}-3.2}$ using a differential $\text{d}f$ of the function $f(x,y)={e}^{\sqrt{x}-y}$ at the point $(9,3).$ Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{x}-y}}{2\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x-{e}^{\sqrt{x}-y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(9,3),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{9}-3}}{2\sqrt{9}}\,\text{d}x-{e}^{\sqrt{9}-3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{{e}^{0}}{6}\,\text{d}x-{e}^{0}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}x-1\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(9+Δx,3+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈\frac{1}{6}\,Δx-1\,Δy
$$

Note that 

$$
{e}^{\sqrt{10}-3.2}=f(10,3.2),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(10,3.2).$

Moving from $(9,3)$ to $(10,3.2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =10-9=1, \\ Δy & =3.2-3=0.2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈\frac{1}{6}\cdot 1-1\cdot 0.2 \\  & ≈0.167-0.2 \\  & ≈-0.033.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ decreases by about $0.033.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(10,3.2) & ≈f(9,3)-0.033 \\ {e}^{\sqrt{10}-3.2} & ≈{e}^{\sqrt{9}-3}-0.033 \\  & ≈1-0.033 \\  & ≈0.967.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Estimate $(1.06)^{4.1}$ using a differential $\text{d}f$ of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{y}$ at the point $(1,4).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =y{x}^{y-1}\,\text{d}x+{x}^{y}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(1,4),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =4\cdot {1}^{3}\,\text{d}x+{1}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =4\,\text{d}x+0\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(1+Δx,4+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈4\,Δx+0\,Δy.
$$

Note that 

$$
(1.06)^{4.1}=f(1.06,4.1),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(1.06,4.1).$

Moving from $(1,4)$ to $(1.06,4.1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1.06-1=0.06, \\ Δy & =4.1-4=0.1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈4\cdot (0.06)+0\cdot (0.1) \\  & ≈0.24+0 \\  & ≈0.24\,.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.24.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.06,4.1) & ≈f(1,4)+0.24 \\ (1.06)^{4.1} & ≈{1}^{4}+0.24 \\  & ≈1+0.24 \\  & ≈1.24\,.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function
canonical_examples.problem: Find the differential for $f(x,y) = x^2 \sin y.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =(2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}x+({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}x+{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Computing a Differential in a Geometrical Context
canonical_examples.problem: Given a cone, find the differential $\textrm d V$ for the volume $V$ of the cone if the radius is $r=6$ and the height is $h = 3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The volume of the cone is $V = \dfrac{1}{3} \pi r^2h.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(r,h) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂r})\,\text{d}r+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\pi rh\,\text{d}r+\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

For $r=6$ and $h=3,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(6,3) & =\frac{2}{3}\pi \cdot 6\cdot 3\,\text{d}r+\frac{1}{3}\pi \cdot {6}^{2}\,\text{d}h \\  & =12\pi \,\text{d}r+12\pi \,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Using Differentials to Approximate the Change in a Multivariable Function
canonical_examples.problem: If $f (x, y) = xe^y ,$ use the differential $\textrm d f$ to estimate the change $\Delta f$ in the value of $f(x, y)$ from $(5,0)$ to $(2,1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={e}^{y}\,\text{d}x+x{e}^{y}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(5,0),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(5,0) & ={e}^{0}\,\text{d}x+5{e}^{0}\,\text{d}y \\  & =1\,\text{d}x+5\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(5 + \Delta x, 0 + \Delta y),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
\Delta f \approx 1 \, \Delta x + 5 \, \Delta y.
$$

Moving from $(5,0)$ to $(2,1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =2-5=-3, \\ Δy & =1-0=1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈1\,Δx+5\,Δy \\  & ≈1\cdot (-3)+5\cdot (1) \\  & ≈2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y)$ increases by approximately $2.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Using Differentials to Approximate the Value of a Function
canonical_examples.problem: Estimate $\sin (3) + \cos (0.2)$ using a differential of the function $f(x,y) = \sin x + \cos y$ at the point $\left( \pi, 0 \right).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $\left( \pi, 0 \right),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \,\text{d}x-\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,\text{d}y \\  & =-1\,\text{d}x+0\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(\pi + \Delta x, 0 + \Delta y),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
\Delta f \approx  -1  \,  \Delta x + 0  \,  \Delta y
$$

Note that 

$$
\sin (3) + \cos (0.2)= f(3,0.2),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(3,0.2).$

Moving from $(\pi, 0)$ to $(3,0.2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =3-\pi ≈-0.141, \\ Δy & =0.2-0=0.2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈-1(-0.141)+0(0.2) \\  & ≈0.141.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.141.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3,0.2) & ≈f(\pi ,0)+0.141 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0.2) & ≈\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+0.141 \\  & ≈0+1+0.141 \\  & ≈1.141.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The **differential** of a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ is denoted $\textrm df(x,y)$ and represents the infinitesimal change in the function value that occurs when the inputs $x$ and $y$ are changed by infinitesimal amounts $\textrm dx$ and $\textrm dy.$

The formula for the differential comes from the multivariable chain rule, which can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the differential can be extended to any number of variables. For example, for a three-variable function $f(x,y,z),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Approximating Change Using Differentials
tutorials.problem:
Given a multivariable function $f(x,y),$ the differential

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

tells us how infinitesimal changes in $x$ and $y,$ denoted $\textrm dx$ and $\textrm dy,$ result in an infinitesimal change in $f,$ denoted $\textrm df.$

Consequently, we can use the differential to *approximate* the change in $f$ as we move from one point to another. If we move from a point $(x,y)$ to a point $(x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y),$ then the approximate change in $f$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf(x,y) & ≈(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,Δx+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,Δy.\end{aligned}
$$

The above formula is very similar to the differential formula, except the $\textrm d$'s are replaced with $\Delta$'s. The $\textrm d$'s refer to infinitesimal changes, while the $\Delta$'s refer to changes that can actually be measured.

question.html:
Question 1
?

Find the differential df for the function f(x,y)=xy+y2.

a
(y+y2)dx+(x+2y)dy
b
xydx+y2dy
c
ydx+2ydy
d
ydx+(x+2y)dy
e
 xydx+2ydy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We compute the differential using the formula:

df(x,y)=(∂f∂x)dx+(∂f∂y)dy=ydx+(x+2y)dy
question.knowledge_point: Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =(2xy-{z}^{2})\,\text{d}x+({x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}z)\,\text{d}y+({y}^{3}-2xz)\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}y+{y}^{3}z-x{z}^{2}.$
question.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =(2xy-{z}^{2})\,\text{d}x+({x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}z)\,\text{d}y+({y}^{3}-2xz)\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Find the differential df for the function f(x,y,z)=x2y+y3z−xz2.

a
(2xy−z2)dx+x2dy+y3dz
b
(2xy−z2)dx+(x2+3y2z)dy+(y3−2xz)dz
c
−z2dx+(y3−z2)dy+(y3−2xz)dz
d
z2dx+(x2+3y2z)dy−2xzdz
e
(2xy+x2)dx+(y3+3y2z)dy+(z2−2xz)dz
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We compute the differential using the formula:

df(x,y,z)=(∂f∂x)dx+(∂f∂y)dy+(∂f∂z)dz=(2xy−z2)dx+(x2+3y2z)dy+(y3−2xz)dz
question.knowledge_point: Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{2x\,\text{d}x}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}+\frac{\text{d}y}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}+\frac{3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}).$
question.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{2x\,\text{d}x}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}+\frac{\text{d}y}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}+\frac{3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Find the differential df for the function f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(x2+y+z3).

a
 dx2x+dy+3z2dz3z2
b
 2xdxx2+y+z3+dyx2+y+z3+3z2dzx2+y+z3
c
 dxx2+y+z3+dyx2+y+z3+dzx2+y+z3
d
 dx2x+dyy+3z2dz3z2
e
 2xdxx2+y+z3+2ydyx2+y+z3+2zdzx2+y+z3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We compute the differential using the formula:

df(x,y,z)=(∂f∂x)dx+(∂f∂y)dy+(∂f∂z)dz=2xdxx2+y+z3+dyx2+y+z3+3z2dzx2+y+z3
question.knowledge_point: Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{yz\,\text{d}x}{xyz}+\frac{xz\,\text{d}y}{xyz}+\frac{xy\,\text{d}z}{xyz} \\  & =\frac{\,\text{d}x}{x}+\frac{\,\text{d}y}{y}+\frac{\,\text{d}z}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz).$
question.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{yz\,\text{d}x}{xyz}+\frac{xz\,\text{d}y}{xyz}+\frac{xy\,\text{d}z}{xyz} \\  & =\frac{\,\text{d}x}{x}+\frac{\,\text{d}y}{y}+\frac{\,\text{d}z}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Find the differential df for the function f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(xyz).

a
 yzdx+xzdy+xydz
b
 dxx+dyy+dzz
c
 xdx+ydy+zdz
d
 dxxyz+dyxyz+dzxyz
e
 dxyz+dyxz+dzxy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We compute the differential using the formula:

df(x,y,z)=(∂f∂x)dx+(∂f∂y)dy+(∂f∂z)dz=yzdxxyz+xzdyxyz+xydzxyz=dxx+dyy+dzz
question.knowledge_point: Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2x\,\text{d}x+2y\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.$
question.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2x\,\text{d}x+2y\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The volume of the rectangular pyramid is $V=\frac{1}{3}{a}^{2}h.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,h) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{2ah}{3}\,\text{d}a+\frac{{a}^{2}}{3}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=6$ and $h=5,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(6,5) & =\frac{2\cdot 6\cdot 5}{3}\,\text{d}a+\frac{{6}^{2}}{3}\,\text{d}h \\  & =20\,\text{d}a+12\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Given a rectangular pyramid, find the differential $\text{d}V$ for the volume $V$ of the rectangular pyramid if the base is a square with the side of $a=6$ and the height is $h=5.$
question.worked_solution:
The volume of the rectangular pyramid is $V=\frac{1}{3}{a}^{2}h.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,h) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{2ah}{3}\,\text{d}a+\frac{{a}^{2}}{3}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=6$ and $h=5,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(6,5) & =\frac{2\cdot 6\cdot 5}{3}\,\text{d}a+\frac{{6}^{2}}{3}\,\text{d}h \\  & =20\,\text{d}a+12\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing a Differential in a Geometrical Context
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The volume of a given right triangular prism is $V=\frac{abh}{2}.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{bh}{2}\,\text{d}a+\frac{ah}{2}\,\text{d}b+\frac{ab}{2}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=2,$ $b=4,$ and $h=1,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(2,4,1) & =\frac{4\cdot 1}{2}\,\text{d}a+\frac{2\cdot 1}{2}\,\text{d}b+\frac{2\cdot 4}{2}\,\text{d}h \\  & =2\,\text{d}a+\text{d}b+4\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The  surface area of the rectangular solid is $S=2ab+2bc+2ac.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}S(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂S}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂S}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂S}{∂c})\,\text{d}c \\  & =2(b+c)\,\text{d}a+2(a+c)\,\text{d}b+2(a+b)\,\text{d}c\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=4,$ $b=5,$ and $c=7,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}S(4,5,7) & =2(5+7)\,\text{d}a+2(4+7)\,\text{d}b+2(4+5)\,\text{d}c \\  & =24\,\text{d}a+22\,\text{d}b+18\,\text{d}c.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 9

observed_steps.name: Question 10
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing a Differential in a Geometrical Context
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The volume of the rectangular solid is $V=abc.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂V}{∂c})\,\text{d}c \\  & =bc\,\text{d}a+ac\,\text{d}b+ab\,\text{d}c\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=2,$ $b=5,$ and $c=1,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(2,5,1) & =5\cdot 1\,\text{d}a+2\cdot 1\,\text{d}b+5\cdot 2\,\text{d}c \\  & =5\,\text{d}a+2\,\text{d}b+10\,\text{d}c.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 10
?

Given a rectangular solid, find the differential dV for the volume V of the rectangular solid if the lengths of the sides are a=2, b=5, and c=1.

a
4da+10db+2dc
b
4da+5db+10dc
c
5da+25db+4dc
d
5da+2db+10dc
e
2da+5db+4dc
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The volume of the rectangular solid is V=abc. Let's find the differential: dV(a,b,c)=(∂V∂a)da+(∂V∂b)db+(∂V∂c)dc=bcda+acdb+abdc

For a=2, b=5, and c=1, the differential is dV(2,5,1)=5⋅1da+2⋅1db+5⋅2dc=5da+2db+10dc.

tutorial.name: Approximating Change Using Differentials
tutorial.problem:
Given a multivariable function $f(x,y),$ the differential

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

tells us how infinitesimal changes in $x$ and $y,$ denoted $\textrm dx$ and $\textrm dy,$ result in an infinitesimal change in $f,$ denoted $\textrm df.$

Consequently, we can use the differential to *approximate* the change in $f$ as we move from one point to another. If we move from a point $(x,y)$ to a point $(x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y),$ then the approximate change in $f$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf(x,y) & ≈(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,Δx+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,Δy.\end{aligned}
$$

The above formula is very similar to the differential formula, except the $\textrm d$'s are replaced with $\Delta$'s. The $\textrm d$'s refer to infinitesimal changes, while the $\Delta$'s refer to changes that can actually be measured.

observed_steps.name: Example: Using Differentials to Approximate the Change in a Multivariable Function
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing a Differential in a Geometrical Context
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={e}^{y}\,\text{d}x+x{e}^{y}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(5,0),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(5,0) & ={e}^{0}\,\text{d}x+5{e}^{0}\,\text{d}y \\  & =1\,\text{d}x+5\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(5 + \Delta x, 0 + \Delta y),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
\Delta f \approx 1 \, \Delta x + 5 \, \Delta y.
$$

Moving from $(5,0)$ to $(2,1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =2-5=-3, \\ Δy & =1-0=1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈1\,Δx+5\,Δy \\  & ≈1\cdot (-3)+5\cdot (1) \\  & ≈2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y)$ increases by approximately $2.$

Question 11
?

If f(x,y)=cos⁡x+y, use the differential df to estimate the change Δf in the value of f(x,y) from (4π,8) to (13,8.5).

a
Δf≈0.5
b
Δf≈0.1
c
Δf≈0.3
d
Δf≈−0.3
e
Δf≈−0.5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's find the differential:

df(x,y)=(∂f∂x)dx+(∂f∂y)dy=−sin⁡xdx+1dy

At the point (4π,8), the differential is

df(4π,8)=−sin⁡4πdx+1dy=0dx+1dy

So, if we move to the point (4π+Δx,8+Δy), then we can approximate the change in f as

Δf≈0Δx+1Δy.

Moving from (4π,8) to (13,8.5), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $\left( \pi, 0 \right),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \,\text{d}x-\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,\text{d}y \\  & =-1\,\text{d}x+0\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}

$$
\Delta f \approx  -1  \,  \Delta x + 0  \,  \Delta y
$$

Note that 

$$
\sin (3) + \cos (0.2)= f(3,0.2),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(3,0.2).$

Moving from $(\pi, 0)$ to $(3,0.2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =3-\pi ≈-0.141, \\ Δy & =0.2-0=0.2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈-1(-0.141)+0(0.2) \\  & ≈0.141.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3,0.2) & ≈f(\pi ,0)+0.141 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0.2) & ≈\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+0.141 \\  & ≈0+1+0.141 \\  & ≈1.141.\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =4\cdot {1}^{3}\,\text{d}x+{1}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =4\,\text{d}x+0\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(1+Δx,4+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈4\,Δx+0\,Δy.
$$

Note that 

$$
(1.06)^{4.1}=f(1.06,4.1),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(1.06,4.1).$

Moving from $(1,4)$ to $(1.06,4.1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1.06-1=0.06, \\ Δy & =4.1-4=0.1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈4\cdot (0.06)+0\cdot (0.1) \\  & ≈0.24+0 \\  & ≈0.24\,.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.24.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.06,4.1) & ≈f(1,4)+0.24 \\ (1.06)^{4.1} & ≈{1}^{4}+0.24 \\  & ≈1+0.24 \\  & ≈1.24\,.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, let's find the differential:

df(x,y)=(∂f∂x)dx+(∂f∂y)dy=yxy−1dx+xyln⁡xdy.

At the point (1,4), the differential is

df(x,y)=4⋅13dx+14ln⁡(1)dy=4dx+0dy.

So, if we move to the point (1+Δx,4+Δy), then we can approximate the change in f as

Δf≈4Δx+0Δy.

Note that (1.06)4.1=f(1.06,4.1),

so we want to move to the point (1.06,4.1).

Moving from (1,4) to (1.06,4.1), we have

Δx=1.06−1=0.06,Δy=4.1−4=0.1.

So, we have

Δf≈4⋅(0.06)+0⋅(0.1)≈0.24+0≈0.24.

This means that the value of f increases by about 0.24. Consequently, we have

f(1.06,4.1)≈f(1,4)+0.24(1.06)4.1≈14+0.24≈1+0.24≈1.24.

question.html:
Question 1
?

Find the differential df for the function f(x,y)=xy+y2.

a
(y+y2)dx+(x+2y)dy
b
xydx+y2dy
c
ydx+2ydy
d
ydx+(x+2y)dy
e
 xydx+2ydy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We compute the differential using the formula:

df(x,y)=(∂f∂x)dx+(∂f∂y)dy=ydx+(x+2y)dy

last_observation.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =y\,\text{d}x+(x+2y)\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y)=xy+{y}^{2}.$
question.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =y\,\text{d}x+(x+2y)\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Find the differential df for the function f(x,y)=xy+y2.

a
(y+y2)dx+(x+2y)dy
b
xydx+y2dy
c
ydx+2ydy
d
ydx+(x+2y)dy
e
 xydx+2ydy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We compute the differential using the formula:

df(x,y)=(∂f∂x)dx+(∂f∂y)dy=ydx+(x+2y)dy
question.knowledge_point: Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function

solution.reasoning: The total differential is df=f_x dx+f_y dy. Here f_x=y and f_y=x+2y, so option d is mathematically correct. The supplied worked example concerns a different function and does not establish Math Academy's answer for this question.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y)=xy+{y}^{2}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =y\,\text{d}x+(x+2y)\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Question 2
?

Find the differential df for the function f(x,y,z)=x2y+y3z−xz2.

a
(2xy−z2)dx+x2dy+y3dz
b
(2xy−z2)dx+(x2+3y2z)dy+(y3−2xz)dz
c
−z2dx+(y3−z2)dy+(y3−2xz)dz
d
z2dx+(x2+3y2z)dy−2xzdz
e
(2xy+x2)dx+(y3+3y2z)dy+(z2−2xz)dz
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We compute the differential using the formula:

df(x,y,z)=(∂f∂x)dx+(∂f∂y)dy+(∂f∂z)dz=(2xy−z2)dx+(x2+3y2z)dy+(y3−2xz)dz

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function
last_observation.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =(2xy-{z}^{2})\,\text{d}x+({x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}z)\,\text{d}y+({y}^{3}-2xz)\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}y+{y}^{3}z-x{z}^{2}.$
question.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =(2xy-{z}^{2})\,\text{d}x+({x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}z)\,\text{d}y+({y}^{3}-2xz)\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Find the differential df for the function f(x,y,z)=x2y+y3z−xz2.

a
(2xy−z2)dx+x2dy+y3dz
b
(2xy−z2)dx+(x2+3y2z)dy+(y3−2xz)dz
c
−z2dx+(y3−z2)dy+(y3−2xz)dz
d
z2dx+(x2+3y2z)dy−2xzdz
e
(2xy+x2)dx+(y3+3y2z)dy+(z2−2xz)dz
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We compute the differential using the formula:

df(x,y,z)=(∂f∂x)dx+(∂f∂y)dy+(∂f∂z)dz=(2xy−z2)dx+(x2+3y2z)dy+(y3−2xz)dz
question.knowledge_point: Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function

solution.reasoning: Using df=f_x dx+f_y dy+f_z dz, the partial derivatives are f_x=2xy-z^2, f_y=x^2+3y^2z, and f_z=y^3-2xz. Thus option b is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key for this question.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}y+{y}^{3}z-x{z}^{2}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =(2xy-{z}^{2})\,\text{d}x+({x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}z)\,\text{d}y+({y}^{3}-2xz)\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Find the differential df for the function f(x,y,z)=x2y+y3z−xz2.

a
(2xy−z2)dx+x2dy+y3dz
b
(2xy−z2)dx+(x2+3y2z)dy+(y3−2xz)dz
c
−z2dx+(y3−z2)dy+(y3−2xz)dz
d
z2dx+(x2+3y2z)dy−2xzdz
e
(2xy+x2)dx+(y3+3y2z)dy+(z2−2xz)dz
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We compute the differential using the formula:

df(x,y,z)=(∂f∂x)dx+(∂f∂y)dy+(∂f∂z)dz=(2xy−z2)dx+(x2+3y2z)dy+(y3−2xz)dz
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}).$
question.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{2x\,\text{d}x}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}+\frac{\text{d}y}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}+\frac{3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Find the differential df for the function f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(x2+y+z3).

a
 dx2x+dy+3z2dz3z2
b
 2xdxx2+y+z3+dyx2+y+z3+3z2dzx2+y+z3
c
 dxx2+y+z3+dyx2+y+z3+dzx2+y+z3
d
 dx2x+dyy+3z2dz3z2
e
 2xdxx2+y+z3+2ydyx2+y+z3+2zdzx2+y+z3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We compute the differential using the formula:

df(x,y,z)=(∂f∂x)dx+(∂f∂y)dy+(∂f∂z)dz=2xdxx2+y+z3+dyx2+y+z3+3z2dzx2+y+z3

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function
last_observation.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{2x\,\text{d}x}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}+\frac{\text{d}y}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}+\frac{3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}).$
question.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{2x\,\text{d}x}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}+\frac{\text{d}y}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}+\frac{3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Find the differential df for the function f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(x2+y+z3).

a
 dx2x+dy+3z2dz3z2
b
 2xdxx2+y+z3+dyx2+y+z3+3z2dzx2+y+z3
c
 dxx2+y+z3+dyx2+y+z3+dzx2+y+z3
d
 dx2x+dyy+3z2dz3z2
e
 2xdxx2+y+z3+2ydyx2+y+z3+2zdzx2+y+z3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We compute the differential using the formula:

df(x,y,z)=(∂f∂x)dx+(∂f∂y)dy+(∂f∂z)dz=2xdxx2+y+z3+dyx2+y+z3+3z2dzx2+y+z3
question.knowledge_point: Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function

solution.reasoning: Let u=x^2+y+z^3. The chain rule gives df=du/u, where du=2x dx+dy+3z^2 dz. Thus option b is correct on the domain u>0. The supplied example addresses another function; no captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes the current key.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}).$
feedback.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{2x\,\text{d}x}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}+\frac{\text{d}y}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}+\frac{3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z}{{x}^{2}+y+{z}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Find the differential df for the function f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(x2+y+z3).

a
 dx2x+dy+3z2dz3z2
b
 2xdxx2+y+z3+dyx2+y+z3+3z2dzx2+y+z3
c
 dxx2+y+z3+dyx2+y+z3+dzx2+y+z3
d
 dx2x+dyy+3z2dz3z2
e
 2xdxx2+y+z3+2ydyx2+y+z3+2zdzx2+y+z3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We compute the differential using the formula:

df(x,y,z)=(∂f∂x)dx+(∂f∂y)dy+(∂f∂z)dz=2xdxx2+y+z3+dyx2+y+z3+3z2dzx2+y+z3
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz).$
question.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{yz\,\text{d}x}{xyz}+\frac{xz\,\text{d}y}{xyz}+\frac{xy\,\text{d}z}{xyz} \\  & =\frac{\,\text{d}x}{x}+\frac{\,\text{d}y}{y}+\frac{\,\text{d}z}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Find the differential df for the function f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(xyz).

a
 yzdx+xzdy+xydz
b
 dxx+dyy+dzz
c
 xdx+ydy+zdz
d
 dxxyz+dyxyz+dzxyz
e
 dxyz+dyxz+dzxy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We compute the differential using the formula:

df(x,y,z)=(∂f∂x)dx+(∂f∂y)dy+(∂f∂z)dz=yzdxxyz+xzdyxyz+xydzxyz=dxx+dyy+dzz
question.knowledge_point: Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function
last_observation.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{yz\,\text{d}x}{xyz}+\frac{xz\,\text{d}y}{xyz}+\frac{xy\,\text{d}z}{xyz} \\  & =\frac{\,\text{d}x}{x}+\frac{\,\text{d}y}{y}+\frac{\,\text{d}z}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz).$
question.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{yz\,\text{d}x}{xyz}+\frac{xz\,\text{d}y}{xyz}+\frac{xy\,\text{d}z}{xyz} \\  & =\frac{\,\text{d}x}{x}+\frac{\,\text{d}y}{y}+\frac{\,\text{d}z}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Find the differential df for the function f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(xyz).

a
 yzdx+xzdy+xydz
b
 dxx+dyy+dzz
c
 xdx+ydy+zdz
d
 dxxyz+dyxyz+dzxyz
e
 dxyz+dyxz+dzxy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We compute the differential using the formula:

df(x,y,z)=(∂f∂x)dx+(∂f∂y)dy+(∂f∂z)dz=yzdxxyz+xzdyxyz+xydzxyz=dxx+dyy+dzz
question.knowledge_point: Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function

solution.reasoning: By the chain rule, df=(yz dx+xz dy+xy dz)/(xyz)=dx/x+dy/y+dz/z on the domain xyz>0. Therefore option b is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key for this question.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz).$
feedback.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{yz\,\text{d}x}{xyz}+\frac{xz\,\text{d}y}{xyz}+\frac{xy\,\text{d}z}{xyz} \\  & =\frac{\,\text{d}x}{x}+\frac{\,\text{d}y}{y}+\frac{\,\text{d}z}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.$
question.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2x\,\text{d}x+2y\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Differential of a Multivariable Function
last_observation.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2x\,\text{d}x+2y\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.$
question.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2x\,\text{d}x+2y\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

 xdx+ydy

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem: Find the differential $\text{d}f$ for the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
We compute the differential using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2x\,\text{d}x+2y\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: Given a cylinder, find the differential $\text{d}V$ for the volume $V$ of the cylinder if the radius is $r=2$ and the height is $h=4.$
question.worked_solution:
The volume of the cylinder is $V=\pi {r}^{2}h.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(r,h) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂r})\,\text{d}r+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =2\pi rh\,\text{d}r+\pi {r}^{2}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $r=2$ and $h=4,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(2,4) & =2\pi \cdot 2\cdot 4\,\text{d}r+\pi \cdot {2}^{2}\,\text{d}h \\  & =16\pi \,\text{d}r+4\pi \,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 6
?

Given a cylinder, find the differential dV for the volume V of the cylinder if the radius is r=2 and the height is h=4.

a
8πdr+2πdh
b
16dr+4dh
c
4πdr+16πdh
d
16πdr+4πdh
e
4πdr+πdh
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The volume of the cylinder is V=πr2h. Let's find the differential: dV(r,h)=(∂V∂r)dr+(∂V∂h)dh=2πrhdr+πr2dh For r=2 and h=4, the differential is dV(2,4)=2π⋅2⋅4dr+π⋅22dh=16πdr+4πdh.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The volume of the cylinder is $V=\pi {r}^{2}h.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(r,h) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂r})\,\text{d}r+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =2\pi rh\,\text{d}r+\pi {r}^{2}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $r=2$ and $h=4,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(2,4) & =2\pi \cdot 2\cdot 4\,\text{d}r+\pi \cdot {2}^{2}\,\text{d}h \\  & =16\pi \,\text{d}r+4\pi \,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Given a cylinder, find the differential dV for the volume V of the cylinder if the radius is r=2 and the height is h=4.

a
8πdr+2πdh
b
16dr+4dh
c
4πdr+16πdh
d
16πdr+4πdh
e
4πdr+πdh
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The volume of the cylinder is V=πr2h. Let's find the differential: dV(r,h)=(∂V∂r)dr+(∂V∂h)dh=2πrhdr+πr2dh For r=2 and h=4, the differential is dV(2,4)=2π⋅2⋅4dr+π⋅22dh=16πdr+4πdh.
question.knowledge_point: Computing a Differential in a Geometrical Context

solution.reasoning: A cylinder has volume V=\pi r^2h, so dV=2\pi rh\,dr+\pi r^2\,dh. At r=2 and h=4 this becomes 16\pi\,dr+4\pi\,dh, matching option d. The supplied cone example does not establish Math Academy's answer for this question.

feedback.name: Question 6
feedback.problem: Given a cylinder, find the differential $\text{d}V$ for the volume $V$ of the cylinder if the radius is $r=2$ and the height is $h=4.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The volume of the cylinder is $V=\pi {r}^{2}h.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(r,h) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂r})\,\text{d}r+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =2\pi rh\,\text{d}r+\pi {r}^{2}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $r=2$ and $h=4,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(2,4) & =2\pi \cdot 2\cdot 4\,\text{d}r+\pi \cdot {2}^{2}\,\text{d}h \\  & =16\pi \,\text{d}r+4\pi \,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 7
question.problem: Given a rectangular pyramid, find the differential $\text{d}V$ for the volume $V$ of the rectangular pyramid if the base is a square with the side of $a=6$ and the height is $h=5.$
question.worked_solution:
The volume of the rectangular pyramid is $V=\frac{1}{3}{a}^{2}h.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,h) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{2ah}{3}\,\text{d}a+\frac{{a}^{2}}{3}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=6$ and $h=5,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(6,5) & =\frac{2\cdot 6\cdot 5}{3}\,\text{d}a+\frac{{6}^{2}}{3}\,\text{d}h \\  & =20\,\text{d}a+12\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 7
?

Given a rectangular pyramid, find the differential dV for the volume V of the rectangular pyramid if the base is a square with the side of a=6 and the height is h=5.

a
30da+15dh
b
20da+10dh
c
20da+12dh
d
10da+15dh
e
30da+12dh
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The volume of the rectangular pyramid is V=13a2h. Let's find the differential: dV(a,h)=(∂V∂a)da+(∂V∂h)dh=2ah3da+a23dh For a=6 and h=5, the differential is dV(6,5)=2⋅6⋅53da+623dh=20da+12dh.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The volume of the rectangular pyramid is $V=\frac{1}{3}{a}^{2}h.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,h) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{2ah}{3}\,\text{d}a+\frac{{a}^{2}}{3}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=6$ and $h=5,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(6,5) & =\frac{2\cdot 6\cdot 5}{3}\,\text{d}a+\frac{{6}^{2}}{3}\,\text{d}h \\  & =20\,\text{d}a+12\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(6,5) & =\frac{2\cdot 6\cdot 5}{3}\,\text{d}a+\frac{{6}^{2}}{3}\,\text{d}h \\  & =20\,\text{d}a+12\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 7
?

Given a rectangular pyramid, find the differential dV for the volume V of the rectangular pyramid if the base is a square with the side of a=6 and the height is h=5.

a
30da+15dh
b
20da+10dh
c
20da+12dh
d
10da+15dh
e
30da+12dh
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The volume of the rectangular pyramid is V=13a2h. Let's find the differential: dV(a,h)=(∂V∂a)da+(∂V∂h)dh=2ah3da+a23dh For a=6 and h=5, the differential is dV(6,5)=2⋅6⋅53da+623dh=20da+12dh.
question.knowledge_point: Computing a Differential in a Geometrical Context

solution.reasoning: The volume is V=a^2h/3, so dV=(2ah/3) da+(a^2/3) dh. Substituting a=6 and h=5 gives dV=20 da+12 dh, matching option c. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key for this question.

feedback.name: Question 7
feedback.problem: Given a rectangular pyramid, find the differential $\text{d}V$ for the volume $V$ of the rectangular pyramid if the base is a square with the side of $a=6$ and the height is $h=5.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The volume of the rectangular pyramid is $V=\frac{1}{3}{a}^{2}h.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,h) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{2ah}{3}\,\text{d}a+\frac{{a}^{2}}{3}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=6$ and $h=5,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(6,5) & =\frac{2\cdot 6\cdot 5}{3}\,\text{d}a+\frac{{6}^{2}}{3}\,\text{d}h \\  & =20\,\text{d}a+12\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem: Given a right triangular prism, find the differential $\text{d}V$ for the volume $V$ if the height is $h=1$ and the base is a right triangle with legs $a=2$ and $b=4.$
question.worked_solution:
The volume of a given right triangular prism is $V=\frac{abh}{2}.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{bh}{2}\,\text{d}a+\frac{ah}{2}\,\text{d}b+\frac{ab}{2}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=2,$ $b=4,$ and $h=1,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(2,4,1) & =\frac{4\cdot 1}{2}\,\text{d}a+\frac{2\cdot 1}{2}\,\text{d}b+\frac{2\cdot 4}{2}\,\text{d}h \\  & =2\,\text{d}a+\text{d}b+4\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 8
?

Given a right triangular prism, find the differential dV for the volume V if the height is h=1 and the base is a right triangle with legs a=2 and b=4.

a
4da+db+2dh
b
2da+4db+dh
c
da+2db+4dh
d
4da+2db+dh
e
2da+db+4dh
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The volume of a given right triangular prism is V=abh2. Let's find the differential: dV(a,b,c)=(∂V∂a)da+(∂V∂b)db+(∂V∂h)dh=bh2da+ah2db+ab2dh

For a=2, b=4, and h=1, the differential is dV(2,4,1)=4⋅12da+2⋅12db+2⋅42dh=2da+db+4dh.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The volume of a given right triangular prism is $V=\frac{abh}{2}.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{bh}{2}\,\text{d}a+\frac{ah}{2}\,\text{d}b+\frac{ab}{2}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=2,$ $b=4,$ and $h=1,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(2,4,1) & =\frac{4\cdot 1}{2}\,\text{d}a+\frac{2\cdot 1}{2}\,\text{d}b+\frac{2\cdot 4}{2}\,\text{d}h \\  & =2\,\text{d}a+\text{d}b+4\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem: Given a right triangular prism, find the differential $\text{d}V$ for the volume $V$ if the height is $h=1$ and the base is a right triangle with legs $a=2$ and $b=4.$
question.worked_solution:
The volume of a given right triangular prism is $V=\frac{abh}{2}.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{bh}{2}\,\text{d}a+\frac{ah}{2}\,\text{d}b+\frac{ab}{2}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=2,$ $b=4,$ and $h=1,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(2,4,1) & =\frac{4\cdot 1}{2}\,\text{d}a+\frac{2\cdot 1}{2}\,\text{d}b+\frac{2\cdot 4}{2}\,\text{d}h \\  & =2\,\text{d}a+\text{d}b+4\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

Given a right triangular prism, find the differential dV for the volume V if the height is h=1 and the base is a right triangle with legs a=2 and b=4.

a
4da+db+2dh
b
2da+4db+dh
c
da+2db+4dh
d
4da+2db+dh
e
2da+db+4dh
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The volume of a given right triangular prism is V=abh2. Let's find the differential: dV(a,b,c)=(∂V∂a)da+(∂V∂b)db+(∂V∂h)dh=bh2da+ah2db+ab2dh

For a=2, b=4, and h=1, the differential is dV(2,4,1)=4⋅12da+2⋅12db+2⋅42dh=2da+db+4dh.

feedback.name: Question 8
feedback.problem: Given a right triangular prism, find the differential $\text{d}V$ for the volume $V$ if the height is $h=1$ and the base is a right triangle with legs $a=2$ and $b=4.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The volume of a given right triangular prism is $V=\frac{abh}{2}.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{bh}{2}\,\text{d}a+\frac{ah}{2}\,\text{d}b+\frac{ab}{2}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=2,$ $b=4,$ and $h=1,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(2,4,1) & =\frac{4\cdot 1}{2}\,\text{d}a+\frac{2\cdot 1}{2}\,\text{d}b+\frac{2\cdot 4}{2}\,\text{d}h \\  & =2\,\text{d}a+\text{d}b+4\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 9
question.problem: Given a rectangular solid, find the differential $\text{d}S$ for the surface area $S$ of the rectangular solid if the lengths of the sides are $a=4,$ $b=5,$ and $c=7.$
question.worked_solution:
The  surface area of the rectangular solid is $S=2ab+2bc+2ac.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}S(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂S}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂S}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂S}{∂c})\,\text{d}c \\  & =2(b+c)\,\text{d}a+2(a+c)\,\text{d}b+2(a+b)\,\text{d}c\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=4,$ $b=5,$ and $c=7,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}S(4,5,7) & =2(5+7)\,\text{d}a+2(4+7)\,\text{d}b+2(4+5)\,\text{d}c \\  & =24\,\text{d}a+22\,\text{d}b+18\,\text{d}c.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 9
?

Given a rectangular solid, find the differential dS for the surface area S of the rectangular solid if the lengths of the sides are a=4, b=5, and c=7.

a
4da+5db+7dc
b
24da+22db+18dc
c
35da+28db+20dc
d
8da+10db+14dc
e
12da+11db+9dc
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The surface area of the rectangular solid is S=2ab+2bc+2ac. Let's find the differential: dS(a,b,c)=(∂S∂a)da+(∂S∂b)db+(∂S∂c)dc=2(b+c)da+2(a+c)db+2(a+b)dc

For a=4, b=5, and c=7, the differential is dS(4,5,7)=2(5+7)da+2(4+7)db+2(4+5)dc=24da+22db+18dc.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The  surface area of the rectangular solid is $S=2ab+2bc+2ac.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}S(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂S}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂S}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂S}{∂c})\,\text{d}c \\  & =2(b+c)\,\text{d}a+2(a+c)\,\text{d}b+2(a+b)\,\text{d}c\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=4,$ $b=5,$ and $c=7,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}S(4,5,7) & =2(5+7)\,\text{d}a+2(4+7)\,\text{d}b+2(4+5)\,\text{d}c \\  & =24\,\text{d}a+22\,\text{d}b+18\,\text{d}c.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 9
question.problem: Given a rectangular solid, find the differential $\text{d}S$ for the surface area $S$ of the rectangular solid if the lengths of the sides are $a=4,$ $b=5,$ and $c=7.$
question.worked_solution:
The  surface area of the rectangular solid is $S=2ab+2bc+2ac.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}S(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂S}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂S}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂S}{∂c})\,\text{d}c \\  & =2(b+c)\,\text{d}a+2(a+c)\,\text{d}b+2(a+b)\,\text{d}c\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=4,$ $b=5,$ and $c=7,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}S(4,5,7) & =2(5+7)\,\text{d}a+2(4+7)\,\text{d}b+2(4+5)\,\text{d}c \\  & =24\,\text{d}a+22\,\text{d}b+18\,\text{d}c.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The surface area of the rectangular solid is S=2ab+2bc+2ac. Let's find the differential: dS(a,b,c)=(∂S∂a)da+(∂S∂b)db+(∂S∂c)dc=2(b+c)da+2(a+c)db+2(a+b)dc

For a=4, b=5, and c=7, the differential is dS(4,5,7)=2(5+7)da+2(4+7)db+2(4+5)dc=24da+22db+18dc.

EXPLANATION

The surface area of the rectangular solid is S=2ab+2bc+2ac. Let's find the differential: dS(a,b,c)=(∂S∂a)da+(∂S∂b)db+(∂S∂c)dc=2(b+c)da+2(a+c)db+2(a+b)dc

question.name: Question 10
question.problem: Given a rectangular solid, find the differential $\text{d}V$ for the volume $V$ of the rectangular solid if the lengths of the sides are $a=2,$ $b=5,$ and $c=1.$
question.worked_solution:
The volume of the rectangular solid is $V=abc.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂V}{∂c})\,\text{d}c \\  & =bc\,\text{d}a+ac\,\text{d}b+ab\,\text{d}c\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=2,$ $b=5,$ and $c=1,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(2,5,1) & =5\cdot 1\,\text{d}a+2\cdot 1\,\text{d}b+5\cdot 2\,\text{d}c \\  & =5\,\text{d}a+2\,\text{d}b+10\,\text{d}c.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 10
?

Given a rectangular solid, find the differential dV for the volume V of the rectangular solid if the lengths of the sides are a=2, b=5, and c=1.

a
4da+10db+2dc
b
4da+5db+10dc
c
5da+25db+4dc
d
5da+2db+10dc
e
2da+5db+4dc
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The volume of the rectangular solid is V=abc. Let's find the differential: dV(a,b,c)=(∂V∂a)da+(∂V∂b)db+(∂V∂c)dc=bcda+acdb+abdc

For a=2, b=5, and c=1, the differential is dV(2,5,1)=5⋅1da+2⋅1db+5⋅2dc=5da+2db+10dc.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The volume of the rectangular solid is $V=abc.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂V}{∂c})\,\text{d}c \\  & =bc\,\text{d}a+ac\,\text{d}b+ab\,\text{d}c\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=2,$ $b=5,$ and $c=1,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(2,5,1) & =5\cdot 1\,\text{d}a+2\cdot 1\,\text{d}b+5\cdot 2\,\text{d}c \\  & =5\,\text{d}a+2\,\text{d}b+10\,\text{d}c.\end{aligned}
$$
