questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve. Given that the line integral

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$

 
represents the area of the region $D$ enclosed by any such curve in ${R}^{2},$ which of the following could be the vector field $F(x,y)?$

I. $F(x,y)=⟨y{e}^{x},\,x-{e}^{x}⟩$

II. $F(x,y)=⟨2y,\,x⟩$

III. $F(x,y)=⟨-\frac{y}{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡{x}^{2},\,\frac{2x}{3}+1⟩$
questions.worked_solution:
According to Green's theorem, if $F(x,y)=⟨P(x,y),\,Q(x,y)⟩,$ where

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,
$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y \\  & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Vector field I does *not* give the required area. In this case, 
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}={e}^{x}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1-{e}^{x},$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-2{e}^{x}\ne 1.
$$

- Vector field II does *not* give the required area. Notice that 
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1\ne 1.
$$

- Vector field III gives the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{3}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\frac{2}{3},$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.problem:

$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/ac9f6016ee4c93aec58f8fff0a8002057f89d7c1bae589e5357a25709ae5a76c.png)

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩$ for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{5\pi }{3}].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-y\,dx & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}-(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Area(D)=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∫π/35π/3AAAAAAAdt,

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/bfec7cbdb26a3db773ab1f6207de436ff0856b331cda183da530dbb6b91d91bd.png)

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨{cos}^{3}⁡t,\,{sin}^{3}⁡t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-y\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-{sin}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3{sin}^{4}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

7.?

Let D be the region enclosed by the curve C parametrized as r(t)=⟨cos3⁡t,sin3⁡t⟩ for t∈[0,2π]. The area of D can be written as

Area(D)=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∫02πAAAAAAAdt,

where P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0. Determine the missing part of the equation.

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/35b8ad6fd40daf95ba4f77288321d6a570e2df2944d056b9445e9ba4e36f97b7.png)

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/10f4094edb09afc7908bd0cd3df089387c8f5b762ea5ef86da152d1c9d08b5e4.png)

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨{sin}^{5}⁡t,\,{cos}^{5}⁡t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ 
The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.

*Hint: Note that $C$ is negatively oriented.*
questions.worked_solution:
Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since the path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨5{sin}^{4}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-5{cos}^{4}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-{sin}^{5}⁡t)\cdot (-5{cos}^{4}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }5{sin}^{6}⁡t{cos}^{4}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of $D$ can be written as

$$

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.

$$

$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/ef44f01fb462cdf608f66a60dd11b8df798603bd204dca9d579ed50b370a84e3.png)

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region enclosed by the curve 
$C$ parametrized as $r(t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\,j$ 
for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since our path is negatively oriented. 

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,i-4\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\text{d}u=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\cdot (-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡2t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =6{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}].$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}y\,dx & =-{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/52ec0dfc4590daf9306c2389bd321acbf80f263c799fa4ddd4e5b8f662e0a2b5.png)

Consider the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2},$ where 

- ${C}_{1}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{1}(t)={t}^{5}\,i+{t}^{4}\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1],$ and

- ${C}_{2}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{2}(t)=-t\,i+1\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1].$

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivatives of ${r}_{1}(t)$ and ${r}_{2}(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\, & {r}_{1}^{′}(t)=5{t}^{4}\,i+4{t}^{3}\,j \\ {C}_{2}:\, & {r}_{2}^{′}(t)=-i\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}}x\,dy \\  & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}}x\,dy+{∮}_{{C}_{2}}x\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{5}\cdot 4{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-t)\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{8}\,\text{d}t-0 \\  & =4[\frac{{t}^{9}}{9}]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{2}{9} \\  & =\frac{8}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/9ebabcf1e3c3c3d2f4850d425657e7314c0135c81a432bfbbc8ae31ee39cb85d.png)

Consider the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2},$ where 

- ${C}_{1}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{1}(t)={t}^{5}\,i-2{t}^{4}\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1],$ and

- ${C}_{2}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{2}(t)=-t\,i-2\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1].$

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ 

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and   

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since our path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-{∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivatives of ${r}_{1}(t)$ and ${r}_{2}(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\, & {r}_{1}^{′}(t)=5{t}^{4}\,i-8{t}^{3}\,j \\ {C}_{2}:\, & {r}_{2}^{′}(t)=-i\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}}x\,dy \\  & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}}x\,dy-{∮}_{{C}_{2}}x\,dy \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{5}\cdot (-8{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-t)\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{8}\,\text{d}t+0 \\  & =8[\frac{{t}^{9}}{9}]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =8\cdot \frac{2}{9} \\  & =\frac{16}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/41dc9af596ca43b1d0d61bb4273be46d3a3d1adc62f99a70fe53c72d69667093.png)

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region enclosed by the curve 
$C$ parametrized as $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j$ 
for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}].$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$

Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying Vector Fields That Satisfy the Unit Curl Property
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve. Given that the line integral

$$
\displaystyle \oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}
$$

 
represents the area of the region $D$ enclosed by any such curve in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ which of the following could be the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)?$

I. $\left\langle -y, \: y\right\rangle$

II. $\left\langle -2x, \: 2x\right\rangle$

III. $\left\langle 5y\sin x, \: x-5\cos x \right\rangle$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
According to Green's theorem, if $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \left\langle P(x,y), \: Q(x,y) \right\rangle,$ where

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 1,
$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y \\  & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Vector field I gives the required area. In this case, 
$\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = -1$
and
$\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = 0,$
which gives

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 1.
$$

- Vector field II does not give the required area. In this case, 
$\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 0$
and
$\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = 2,$
which gives

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 2.
$$

- Vector field III gives the required area. Notice that
$\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 5\sin x$
and
$\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = 1+5\sin x,$
which gives

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle 2\sin t, \: 2 \cos t \rangle$ for $t \in \left [0, 2\pi \right).$ 
The area of $D$ can be written as

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/45513e4aedd37b868d2020cbbb47f49938f6ca03487ded8b5e519a2ec8e4edf5.svg)

where $P(x,y) = -y$ and $Q(x,y) = 0.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.

*Hint: Note that $C$ is negatively oriented.*

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/a5eeb5db90f9ee0d86a49e5bbf02629c7886fa019db7cff3c4d0e1eb43e8fd75.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 0 - \left(-1\right) = 1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since the path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y) = -y$ and $Q(x,y) = 0,$ we get

$$
- \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y = \oint\limits_C y \: \text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is

$$
\mathbf{r}'(t) = \left\langle  2\cos t ,\:  -2 \sin t \right\rangle.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the missing expression is $4\cos^2 t.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating an Area Using Green's Theorem
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C=C_1 \cup C_2,$ where 

- $C_1$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}_1(t) =-2 t^4 \: \mathbf{i} + t^3 \: \mathbf{j}$ for $t \in \left[-1,1\right],$ and

- $C_2$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}_2(t) = -2\: \mathbf{i} -t \: \mathbf{j}$ for $t \in \left[-1,1\right].$

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/147e8fdd97fc938ae5482b70d7215483956a860ee3ce69ae5bbebd111dcc343b.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 0 - \left(-1\right) = 1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y) = -y$ and $Q(x,y) = 0,$ we get

$$
\oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y = -\oint\limits_C y \: \text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivatives of $\mathbf r_1(t)$ and $\mathbf r_2(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\, & {r}_{1}^{′}(t)=-8{t}^{3}\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j \\ {C}_{2}:\, & {r}_{2}^{′}(t)=-j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}}y\,dx \\  & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}}y\,dx-{∮}_{{C}_{2}}y\,dx \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{3}\cdot (-8{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-t)\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{6}\,\text{d}t+0 \\  & =8[\frac{{t}^{7}}{7}]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =8\cdot \frac{2}{7} \\  & =\frac{16}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that $\mathbf F =P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2,$ and a region $D$ is bounded by a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve $C,$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/fa3efbc9200a6acdda01e503999f7588cd44fd63af77fa0a6abf1b5303c9a889.png)

Green's theorem states that

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Let's now consider what happens when the scalar curl term on the left-hand side of the above equation equals unity everywhere on $D.$ In other words, let's consider what happens when

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}=1.
$$

In this case, the double integral gives the area of $D,$ because

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A={∬}_{D}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y=\text{Area}(D).\end{aligned}
$$

 

Thus, we've just discovered a new method of computing the area of $D.$ We simply choose a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ whose scalar curl equals unity everywhere on $D,$ and then compute its circulation over $C.$

There are infinitely many vector fields that we can use to compute the area of a region. Some of the most common for this purpose are as follows:

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y)= \left\langle -y, \: 0 \right\rangle, 
\qquad
\mathbf{G}(x,y)= \left\langle -\dfrac{y}{2}, \: \dfrac{x}{2} \right\rangle,
\qquad
\mathbf{H}(x,y)= \left\langle 0, \: x \right\rangle
$$

tutorials.name: A Concrete Example
tutorials.problem:
As a concrete example, let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C,$ parametrized as

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle 2\cos t, \: \sin t \rangle, \qquad t \in \left [0, 2\pi \right).
$$

The region $D$ and its positively oriented bounding curve $C$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/a6d9fe9cad4ccee56d5d61457c475b41371e0705f1aeccd3a18fb4a3fa8e127c.png)

To calculate the area of $D$ using Green's theorem, we need to find a vector field whose scalar curl equals unity everywhere on $D.$ So, let's choose

$$
P(x,y) = -y, \qquad Q(x,y) = 0.
$$

Indeed, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 0 - \left(-1\right) = 1. \qquad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}
$$

Therefore, since $C$ is a positively oriented path, the area of $D$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting our expressions for $P$ and $Q$ into the above, we get

$$
\oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y = -\oint\limits_C y \: \text{d}x.
$$

 

Let's now evaluate the integral using the usual methods. The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is

$$
\mathbf{r'}(t) = \langle -2\sin t, \: \cos t \rangle.
$$

So we can calculate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x & =-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2{sin}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2(\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt \\  & ={[t-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\textrm{Area}(D)  =2\pi.
$$

tutorials.name: Negatively Oriented Curves
tutorials.problem:
We've established that if a region $D$ is bounded by a positively oriented curve $C,$ and we select a vector field $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ such that

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} =  1,
$$

then the area of $D$ is given by

$$
\textrm{Area}(D) =  \oint\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y.
$$

Now, if $C$ is *negatively* oriented, then

$$
\textrm{Area}(D) =  -\oint\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = -\oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y.
$$

\mathbf{r'}(t) = \langle -2\sin t, \: \cos t \rangle.

$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\textrm{Area}(D)  =2\pi.
$$

tutorial.name: Negatively Oriented Curves
tutorial.problem:
We've established that if a region $D$ is bounded by a positively oriented curve $C,$ and we select a vector field $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ such that

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} =  1,
$$

then the area of $D$ is given by

$$
\textrm{Area}(D) =  \oint\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y.
$$

Now, if $C$ is *negatively* oriented, then

$$
\textrm{Area}(D) =  -\oint\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = -\oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y.
$$

According to Green's theorem, if $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \left\langle P(x,y), \: Q(x,y) \right\rangle,$ where

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 1,
$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y \\  & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Vector field I gives the required area. In this case, 
$\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = -1$
and
$\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = 0,$
which gives

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 1.
$$

$\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 0$
and
$\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = 2,$
which gives

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 2.
$$

$\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 5\sin x$
and
$\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = 1+5\sin x,$
which gives

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

observed_steps.name: Example: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying Vector Fields That Satisfy the Unit Curl Property
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 0 - \left(-1\right) = 1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since the path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y) = -y$ and $Q(x,y) = 0,$ we get

$$
- \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y = \oint\limits_C y \: \text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is

$$
\mathbf{r}'(t) = \left\langle  2\cos t ,\:  -2 \sin t \right\rangle.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the missing expression is $4\cos^2 t.$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Let D be the region enclosed by the curve C parametrized as r(t)=⟨cos⁡t−cos⁡2t,sin⁡t−sin⁡2t⟩ for t∈[π3,5π3]. The area of D can be written as

Area(D)=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∫π/35π/3AAAAAAAdt,

where P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0. Determine the missing part of the equation.

a
(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)(cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t)
b
(cos⁡t−cos⁡2t)(cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t)
c
(cos⁡2t−cos⁡t)(cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t)
d
(sin⁡2t−sin⁡t)(sin⁡t−2sin⁡2t)
e
(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)(sin⁡t−2sin⁡2t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Our simple, smooth, closed path C is positively oriented, and

∂Q∂x−∂P∂y=0−(−1)=1.

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region D enclosed by the curve C as follows:

Area(D)=∬DdA=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∮CPdx+Qdy

Substituting P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0, we get

∮CPdx+Qdy=∮C−ydx.

The derivative of r(t) is r′(t)=⟨−sin⁡t+2sin⁡2t,cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t⟩.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

∮C−ydx=∫π/35π/3−(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)⋅(−sin⁡t+2sin⁡2t)dt=∫π/35π/3(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)(sin⁡t−2sin⁡2t)dt.
question.knowledge_point: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem

observed_steps.name: Question 7
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-y\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-{sin}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3{sin}^{4}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Let D be the region enclosed by the curve C parametrized as r(t)=⟨cos3⁡t,sin3⁡t⟩ for t∈[0,2π]. The area of D can be written as

Area(D)=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∫02πAAAAAAAdt,

where P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0. Determine the missing part of the equation.

a
3sin3⁡tcos3⁡t
b
3sin3⁡tcos4⁡t
c
3sin2⁡tcos4⁡t
d
3sin3⁡tcos2⁡t
e
3sin4⁡tcos2⁡t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path C is positively oriented, and

∂Q∂x−∂P∂y=0−(−1)=1.

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region D enclosed by the curve C as follows:

Area(D)=∬DdA=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∮CPdx+Qdy

Substituting P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0, we get

∮CPdx+Qdy=∮C−ydx.

The derivative of r(t) is r′(t)=⟨−3cos2⁡tsin⁡t,3sin2⁡tcos⁡t⟩.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

∮C−ydx=∫02π(−sin3⁡t)⋅(−3cos2⁡tsin⁡t)dt=∫02π3sin4⁡tcos2⁡tdt.
question.knowledge_point: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem

observed_steps.name: Question 8
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 8
?

Let D be the region enclosed by the curve C parametrized as r(t)=⟨3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t,3sin⁡t−sin⁡3t⟩ for t∈[0,2π]. The area of D can be written as

Area(D)=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∫02πAAAAAAAdt,

where P(x,y)=0 and Q(x,y)=x. Determine the missing part of the equation.

a
3(3cos⁡t+cos⁡3t)(cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)
b
−3(sin⁡t+sin⁡3t)(3sin⁡t−3sin⁡3t)
c
3(3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)(cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)
d
−3(sin⁡t−sin⁡3t)(3sin⁡t−3sin⁡3t)
e
3(sin⁡t−sin⁡3t)(3sin⁡t−3sin⁡3t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path C is positively oriented, and

∂Q∂x−∂P∂y=1−0=1.

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region D enclosed by the curve C as follows:

Area(D)=∬DdA=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∮CPdx+Qdy

Substituting P(x,y)=0 and Q(x,y)=x, we get

∮CPdx+Qdy=∮Cxdy.

The derivative of r(t) is r′(t)=⟨−3sin⁡t+3sin⁡3t,3cos⁡t−3cos⁡3t⟩.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

∮Cxdy=∫02π(3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)⋅(3cos⁡t−3cos⁡3t)dt=∫02π3(3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)(cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)dt.
question.knowledge_point: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem

observed_steps.name: Question 9
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since the path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨5{sin}^{4}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-5{cos}^{4}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-{sin}^{5}⁡t)\cdot (-5{cos}^{4}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }5{sin}^{6}⁡t{cos}^{4}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of r(t) is r′(t)=⟨5sin4⁡tcos⁡t,−5cos4⁡tsin⁡t⟩.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 0 - \left(-1\right) = 1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y) = -y$ and $Q(x,y) = 0,$ we get

$$
\oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y = -\oint\limits_C y \: \text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivatives of $\mathbf r_1(t)$ and $\mathbf r_2(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\, & {r}_{1}^{′}(t)=-8{t}^{3}\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j \\ {C}_{2}:\, & {r}_{2}^{′}(t)=-j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}}y\,dx \\  & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}}y\,dx-{∮}_{{C}_{2}}y\,dx \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{3}\cdot (-8{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-t)\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{6}\,\text{d}t+0 \\  & =8[\frac{{t}^{7}}{7}]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =8\cdot \frac{2}{7} \\  & =\frac{16}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}y\,dx & =-{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve. Given that the line integral

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$

 
represents the area of the region $D$ enclosed by any such curve in ${R}^{2},$ which of the following could be the vector field $F(x,y)?$

I. $F(x,y)=⟨y{e}^{x},\,x-{e}^{x}⟩$

II. $F(x,y)=⟨2y,\,x⟩$

III. $F(x,y)=⟨-\frac{y}{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡{x}^{2},\,\frac{2x}{3}+1⟩$
question.worked_solution:
According to Green's theorem, if $F(x,y)=⟨P(x,y),\,Q(x,y)⟩,$ where

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,
$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y \\  & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Vector field I does *not* give the required area. In this case, 
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}={e}^{x}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1-{e}^{x},$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-2{e}^{x}\ne 1.
$$

- Vector field II does *not* give the required area. Notice that 
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1\ne 1.
$$

- Vector field III gives the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{3}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\frac{2}{3},$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve. Given that the line integral

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$

 
represents the area of the region $D$ enclosed by any such curve in ${R}^{2},$ which of the following could be the vector field $F(x,y)?$

I. $F(x,y)=⟨y,\,y⟩$

II. $F(x,y)=⟨\frac{y}{7},\,\frac{6x}{7}⟩$

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y \\  & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Vector field I does *not* give the required area. In this case, 
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=0,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1\ne 1.
$$

- Vector field II does *not* give the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{1}{7}$

and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={e}^{-y}+1,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/ac9f6016ee4c93aec58f8fff0a8002057f89d7c1bae589e5357a25709ae5a76c.png)

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩$ for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{5\pi }{3}].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.
question.worked_solution:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-y\,dx & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}-(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Let D be the region enclosed by the curve C parametrized as r(t)=⟨cos⁡t−cos⁡2t,sin⁡t−sin⁡2t⟩ for t∈[π3,5π3]. The area of D can be written as

Area(D)=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∫π/35π/3AAAAAAAdt,

where P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0. Determine the missing part of the equation.

a
(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)(cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t)
b
(cos⁡t−cos⁡2t)(cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t)
c
(cos⁡2t−cos⁡t)(cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t)
d
(sin⁡2t−sin⁡t)(sin⁡t−2sin⁡2t)
e
(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)(sin⁡t−2sin⁡2t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Our simple, smooth, closed path C is positively oriented, and

∂Q∂x−∂P∂y=0−(−1)=1.

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region D enclosed by the curve C as follows:

Area(D)=∬DdA=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∮CPdx+Qdy

Substituting P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0, we get

∮CPdx+Qdy=∮C−ydx.

The derivative of r(t) is r′(t)=⟨−sin⁡t+2sin⁡2t,cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t⟩.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

∮C−ydx=∫π/35π/3−(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)⋅(−sin⁡t+2sin⁡2t)dt=∫π/35π/3(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)(sin⁡t−2sin⁡2t)dt.

last_observation.name: Question 6
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem
last_observation.worked_solution:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-y\,dx & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}-(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩$ for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{5\pi }{3}].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$

where $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.

question.html:
Question 6
?

Let D be the region enclosed by the curve C parametrized as r(t)=⟨cos⁡t−cos⁡2t,sin⁡t−sin⁡2t⟩ for t∈[π3,5π3]. The area of D can be written as

Area(D)=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∫π/35π/3AAAAAAAdt,

where P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0. Determine the missing part of the equation.

a
(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)(cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t)
b
(cos⁡t−cos⁡2t)(cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t)
c
(cos⁡2t−cos⁡t)(cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t)
d
(sin⁡2t−sin⁡t)(sin⁡t−2sin⁡2t)
e
(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)(sin⁡t−2sin⁡2t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Our simple, smooth, closed path C is positively oriented, and

∂Q∂x−∂P∂y=0−(−1)=1.

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region D enclosed by the curve C as follows:

Area(D)=∬DdA=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∮CPdx+Qdy

Substituting P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0, we get

∮CPdx+Qdy=∮C−ydx.

The derivative of r(t) is r′(t)=⟨−sin⁡t+2sin⁡2t,cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t⟩.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

∮C−ydx=∫π/35π/3−(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)⋅(−sin⁡t+2sin⁡2t)dt=∫π/35π/3(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)(sin⁡t−2sin⁡2t)dt.
question.knowledge_point: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem

solution.reasoning: The parametrization traverses C counterclockwise: at t=π, it passes through (−2,0) moving downward. Green's theorem therefore gives area = ∮C −y dx. Since y(t)=sin t−sin 2t and x′(t)=−sin t+2sin 2t, the integrand is −y(t)x′(t)=(sin t−sin 2t)(sin t−2sin 2t), option e. feedback.name: Question 6
feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/ac9f6016ee4c93aec58f8fff0a8002057f89d7c1bae589e5357a25709ae5a76c.png)

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩$ for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{5\pi }{3}].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.
feedback.worked_solution:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-y\,dx & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}-(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Let D be the region enclosed by the curve C parametrized as r(t)=⟨cos⁡t−cos⁡2t,sin⁡t−sin⁡2t⟩ for t∈[π3,5π3]. The area of D can be written as

Area(D)=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∫π/35π/3AAAAAAAdt,

where P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0. Determine the missing part of the equation.

a
(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)(cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t)
b
(cos⁡t−cos⁡2t)(cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t)
c
(cos⁡2t−cos⁡t)(cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t)
d
(sin⁡2t−sin⁡t)(sin⁡t−2sin⁡2t)
e
(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)(sin⁡t−2sin⁡2t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Our simple, smooth, closed path C is positively oriented, and

∂Q∂x−∂P∂y=0−(−1)=1.

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region D enclosed by the curve C as follows:

Area(D)=∬DdA=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∮CPdx+Qdy

Substituting P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0, we get

∮CPdx+Qdy=∮C−ydx.

The derivative of r(t) is r′(t)=⟨−sin⁡t+2sin⁡2t,cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t⟩.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

∮C−ydx=∫π/35π/3−(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)⋅(−sin⁡t+2sin⁡2t)dt=∫π/35π/3(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)(sin⁡t−2sin⁡2t)dt.

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/bfec7cbdb26a3db773ab1f6207de436ff0856b331cda183da530dbb6b91d91bd.png)

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨{cos}^{3}⁡t,\,{sin}^{3}⁡t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.
question.worked_solution:
Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-y\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-{sin}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3{sin}^{4}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Let D be the region enclosed by the curve C parametrized as r(t)=⟨cos3⁡t,sin3⁡t⟩ for t∈[0,2π]. The area of D can be written as

Area(D)=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∫02πAAAAAAAdt,

where P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0. Determine the missing part of the equation.

a
3sin3⁡tcos3⁡t
b
3sin3⁡tcos4⁡t
c
3sin2⁡tcos4⁡t
d
3sin3⁡tcos2⁡t
e
3sin4⁡tcos2⁡t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path C is positively oriented, and

∂Q∂x−∂P∂y=0−(−1)=1.

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region D enclosed by the curve C as follows:

Area(D)=∬DdA=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∮CPdx+Qdy

Substituting P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0, we get

∮CPdx+Qdy=∮C−ydx.

The derivative of r(t) is r′(t)=⟨−3cos2⁡tsin⁡t,3sin2⁡tcos⁡t⟩.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

∮C−ydx=∫02π(−sin3⁡t)⋅(−3cos2⁡tsin⁡t)dt=∫02π3sin4⁡tcos2⁡tdt.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-y\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-{sin}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3{sin}^{4}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 7
?

Let D be the region enclosed by the curve C parametrized as r(t)=⟨cos3⁡t,sin3⁡t⟩ for t∈[0,2π]. The area of D can be written as

Area(D)=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∫02πAAAAAAAdt,

where P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0. Determine the missing part of the equation.

a
3sin3⁡tcos3⁡t
b
3sin3⁡tcos4⁡t
c
3sin2⁡tcos4⁡t
d
3sin3⁡tcos2⁡t
e
3sin4⁡tcos2⁡t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path C is positively oriented, and

∂Q∂x−∂P∂y=0−(−1)=1.

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region D enclosed by the curve C as follows:

Area(D)=∬DdA=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∮CPdx+Qdy

Substituting P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0, we get

∮CPdx+Qdy=∮C−ydx.

The derivative of r(t) is r′(t)=⟨−3cos2⁡tsin⁡t,3sin2⁡tcos⁡t⟩.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

∮C−ydx=∫02π(−sin3⁡t)⋅(−3cos2⁡tsin⁡t)dt=∫02π3sin4⁡tcos2⁡tdt.
question.knowledge_point: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem

solution.reasoning: The curve is traversed counterclockwise, so Green's theorem gives area = ∮C −y dx. Here x′(t)=−3cos²t sin t and y(t)=sin³t, hence −y(t)x′(t)=3sin⁴t cos²t, option e. feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/bfec7cbdb26a3db773ab1f6207de436ff0856b331cda183da530dbb6b91d91bd.png)

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨{cos}^{3}⁡t,\,{sin}^{3}⁡t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.
feedback.worked_solution:
Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-y\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-{sin}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3{sin}^{4}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Let D be the region enclosed by the curve C parametrized as r(t)=⟨cos3⁡t,sin3⁡t⟩ for t∈[0,2π]. The area of D can be written as

Area(D)=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∫02πAAAAAAAdt,

where P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0. Determine the missing part of the equation.

a
3sin3⁡tcos3⁡t
b
3sin3⁡tcos4⁡t
c
3sin2⁡tcos4⁡t
d
3sin3⁡tcos2⁡t
e
3sin4⁡tcos2⁡t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path C is positively oriented, and

∂Q∂x−∂P∂y=0−(−1)=1.

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region D enclosed by the curve C as follows:

Area(D)=∬DdA=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∮CPdx+Qdy

Substituting P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0, we get

∮CPdx+Qdy=∮C−ydx.

The derivative of r(t) is r′(t)=⟨−3cos2⁡tsin⁡t,3sin2⁡tcos⁡t⟩.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

∮C−ydx=∫02π(−sin3⁡t)⋅(−3cos2⁡tsin⁡t)dt=∫02π3sin4⁡tcos2⁡tdt.

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/35b8ad6fd40daf95ba4f77288321d6a570e2df2944d056b9445e9ba4e36f97b7.png)

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.
question.worked_solution:
Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Let D be the region enclosed by the curve C parametrized as r(t)=⟨3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t,3sin⁡t−sin⁡3t⟩ for t∈[0,2π]. The area of D can be written as

Area(D)=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∫02πAAAAAAAdt,

where P(x,y)=0 and Q(x,y)=x. Determine the missing part of the equation.

a
3(3cos⁡t+cos⁡3t)(cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)
b
−3(sin⁡t+sin⁡3t)(3sin⁡t−3sin⁡3t)
c
3(3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)(cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)
d
−3(sin⁡t−sin⁡3t)(3sin⁡t−3sin⁡3t)
e
3(sin⁡t−sin⁡3t)(3sin⁡t−3sin⁡3t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path C is positively oriented, and

∂Q∂x−∂P∂y=1−0=1.

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region D enclosed by the curve C as follows:

Area(D)=∬DdA=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∮CPdx+Qdy

Substituting P(x,y)=0 and Q(x,y)=x, we get

∮CPdx+Qdy=∮Cxdy.

The derivative of r(t) is r′(t)=⟨−3sin⁡t+3sin⁡3t,3cos⁡t−3cos⁡3t⟩.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

∮Cxdy=∫02π(3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)⋅(3cos⁡t−3cos⁡3t)dt=∫02π3(3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)(cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)dt.
question.knowledge_point: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem
last_observation.worked_solution:
Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 8
?

Let D be the region enclosed by the curve C parametrized as r(t)=⟨3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t,3sin⁡t−sin⁡3t⟩ for t∈[0,2π]. The area of D can be written as

Area(D)=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∫02πAAAAAAAdt,

where P(x,y)=0 and Q(x,y)=x. Determine the missing part of the equation.

a
3(3cos⁡t+cos⁡3t)(cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)
b
−3(sin⁡t+sin⁡3t)(3sin⁡t−3sin⁡3t)
c
3(3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)(cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)
d
−3(sin⁡t−sin⁡3t)(3sin⁡t−3sin⁡3t)
e
3(sin⁡t−sin⁡3t)(3sin⁡t−3sin⁡3t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path C is positively oriented, and

∂Q∂x−∂P∂y=1−0=1.

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region D enclosed by the curve C as follows:

Area(D)=∬DdA=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∮CPdx+Qdy

Substituting P(x,y)=0 and Q(x,y)=x, we get

∮CPdx+Qdy=∮Cxdy.

The derivative of r(t) is r′(t)=⟨−3sin⁡t+3sin⁡3t,3cos⁡t−3cos⁡3t⟩.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

∮Cxdy=∫02π(3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)⋅(3cos⁡t−3cos⁡3t)dt=∫02π3(3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)(cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)dt.
question.knowledge_point: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem

solution.reasoning: The curve is traversed counterclockwise. With P=0 and Q=x, Green's theorem gives area = ∮C x dy. Since y′(t)=3cos t−3cos 3t, the integrand is x(t)y′(t)=3(3cos t−cos 3t)(cos t−cos 3t), option c. feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/35b8ad6fd40daf95ba4f77288321d6a570e2df2944d056b9445e9ba4e36f97b7.png)

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.
feedback.worked_solution:
Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8

Let D be the region enclosed by the curve C parametrized as r(t)=⟨3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t,3sin⁡t−sin⁡3t⟩ for t∈[0,2π]. The area of D can be written as

Area(D)=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∫02πAAAAAAAdt,

where P(x,y)=0 and Q(x,y)=x. Determine the missing part of the equation.

a
3(3cos⁡t+cos⁡3t)(cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)
b
−3(sin⁡t+sin⁡3t)(3sin⁡t−3sin⁡3t)
c
3(3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)(cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)
d
−3(sin⁡t−sin⁡3t)(3sin⁡t−3sin⁡3t)
e
3(sin⁡t−sin⁡3t)(3sin⁡t−3sin⁡3t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path C is positively oriented, and

∂Q∂x−∂P∂y=1−0=1.

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region D enclosed by the curve C as follows:

Area(D)=∬DdA=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∮CPdx+Qdy

Substituting P(x,y)=0 and Q(x,y)=x, we get

∮CPdx+Qdy=∮Cxdy.

The derivative of r(t) is r′(t)=⟨−3sin⁡t+3sin⁡3t,3cos⁡t−3cos⁡3t⟩.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

∮Cxdy=∫02π(3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)⋅(3cos⁡t−3cos⁡3t)dt=∫02π3(3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)(cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)dt.

question.name: Question 9
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/10f4094edb09afc7908bd0cd3df089387c8f5b762ea5ef86da152d1c9d08b5e4.png)

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨{sin}^{5}⁡t,\,{cos}^{5}⁡t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ 
The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.

*Hint: Note that $C$ is negatively oriented.*
question.worked_solution:
Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since the path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨5{sin}^{4}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-5{cos}^{4}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-{sin}^{5}⁡t)\cdot (-5{cos}^{4}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }5{sin}^{6}⁡t{cos}^{4}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 9
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem
last_observation.worked_solution:
Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since the path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨5{sin}^{4}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-5{cos}^{4}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-{sin}^{5}⁡t)\cdot (-5{cos}^{4}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }5{sin}^{6}⁡t{cos}^{4}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/10f4094edb09afc7908bd0cd3df089387c8f5b762ea5ef86da152d1c9d08b5e4.png)

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨{sin}^{5}⁡t,\,{cos}^{5}⁡t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ 
The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.

*Hint: Note that $C$ is negatively oriented.*

$$

$$

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ 
The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.

*Hint: Note that $C$ is negatively oriented.*
question.worked_solution:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since the path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }6{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 10
?

Let D be the region enclosed by the curve C parametrized as r(t)=⟨2sin⁡t,3cos⁡t⟩ for t∈[0,2π]. The area of D can be written as

Area(D)=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∫02πAAAAAAAdt,

where P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0. Determine the missing part of the equation.

Hint: Note that C is negatively oriented.

a
−6cos2⁡t
b
6sin⁡tcos⁡t
c
−6sin⁡tcos⁡t
d
6cos2⁡t
e
−6sin2⁡t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Our simple, smooth, closed path C is negatively oriented, and

∂Q∂x−∂P∂y=0−(−1)=1.

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region D enclosed by the curve C as follows:

Area(D)=∬DdA=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=−∮CPdx+Qdy

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since the path is negatively oriented.

Substituting P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0, we get

−∮CPdx+Qdy=∮Cydx.

The derivative of r(t) is r′(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,−3sin⁡t⟩.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

∮Cydx=∫02π3cos⁡t⋅2cos⁡tdt=∫02π6cos2⁡tdt.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since the path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }6{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since our path is negatively oriented. 

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,i-4\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\text{d}u=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\cdot (-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡2t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =6{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region enclosed by the curve 
$C$ parametrized as $r(t)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,j$ 
for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}].$
question.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}y\,dx & =-{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, let P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0.

Our simple, smooth, closed path C is positively oriented, and

∂Q∂x−∂P∂y=0−(−1)=1.

question.name: Question 13
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/52ec0dfc4590daf9306c2389bd321acbf80f263c799fa4ddd4e5b8f662e0a2b5.png)

Consider the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2},$ where 

- ${C}_{1}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{1}(t)={t}^{5}\,i+{t}^{4}\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1],$ and

- ${C}_{2}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{2}(t)=-t\,i+1\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1].$

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region.
question.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivatives of ${r}_{1}(t)$ and ${r}_{2}(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\, & {r}_{1}^{′}(t)=5{t}^{4}\,i+4{t}^{3}\,j \\ {C}_{2}:\, & {r}_{2}^{′}(t)=-i\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}}x\,dy \\  & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}}x\,dy+{∮}_{{C}_{2}}x\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{5}\cdot 4{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-t)\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{8}\,\text{d}t-0 \\  & =4[\frac{{t}^{9}}{9}]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{2}{9} \\  & =\frac{8}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

Consider the region D enclosed by the curve C=C1∪C2, where

  • C1 is parametrized by r1(t)=t5i+t4j for t∈[−1,1], and

  • C2 is parametrized by r2(t)=−ti+1j for t∈[−1,1].

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region.

a
54
b
5
c
23
d
4
e
89
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, let P(x,y)=0 and Q(x,y)=x.

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path C is positively oriented and

∂Q∂x−∂P∂y=1−0=1.

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region D enclosed by the curve C as follows:

Area(D)=∬DdA=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∮CPdx+Qdy

Substituting P(x,y)=0 and Q(x,y)=x, we get

∮CPdx+Qdy=∮Cxdy.

The derivatives of r1(t) and r2(t) are as follows:

C1:r1′(t)=5t4i+4t3jC2:r2′(t)=−i

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

∮Cxdy=∮C1∪C2xdy=∮C1xdy+∮C2xdy=∫−11t5⋅4t3dt+∫−11(−t)⋅0dt=4∫−11t8dt−0=4[t99]−11=4⋅29=89.

solution.reasoning: The boundary is counterclockwise. Choosing P=−y and Q=0, Green's theorem gives area = −∮C y dx. On C₁ the contribution is −∫₋₁¹ t⁴(5t⁴) dt = −10/9. On C₂ it is −∫₋₁¹ 1(−1) dt = 2. Thus the area is 2−10/9=8/9, option e. No current-question Math Academy answer or grade is captured; the worked example concerns a different region.

feedback.name: Question 13
feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/52ec0dfc4590daf9306c2389bd321acbf80f263c799fa4ddd4e5b8f662e0a2b5.png)

Consider the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2},$ where 

- ${C}_{1}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{1}(t)={t}^{5}\,i+{t}^{4}\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1],$ and

- ${C}_{2}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{2}(t)=-t\,i+1\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1].$

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region.
feedback.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivatives of ${r}_{1}(t)$ and ${r}_{2}(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\, & {r}_{1}^{′}(t)=5{t}^{4}\,i+4{t}^{3}\,j \\ {C}_{2}:\, & {r}_{2}^{′}(t)=-i\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}}x\,dy \\  & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}}x\,dy+{∮}_{{C}_{2}}x\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{5}\cdot 4{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-t)\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{8}\,\text{d}t-0 \\  & =4[\frac{{t}^{9}}{9}]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{2}{9} \\  & =\frac{8}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$
